translation: But what am I?  Everyone does this; they brag about their illnesses. And perhaps I do it more than anyone else. Let's not argue; my objection is foolish. But still, I am firmly convinced that not only is a great deal of consciousness an illness, but even all consciousness is an illness. I stand by that. Let us leave that for a moment. Tell me this: why was it that, as if on purpose, in precisely those minutes, yes, in precisely those same minutes, when I was most capable of perceiving all the nuances of “all that is beautiful and lofty,”{2} as we used to say, I would find myself not only aware of, but also doing such unsightly deeds, such deeds that… well, in a word, which, though everyone perhaps does, came about in me precisely when I was most aware that I should not do them at all? The more I became aware of good and of all this “beautiful and lofty,” the deeper I sank into my mire and the more capable I became of becoming completely entangled in it. But the main thing was that all of this seemed not to be accidental in me, but as if it were meant to be so. As if this were my normal state, and not an illness or a corruption, so that, in the end, I even lost the desire to struggle with this corruption. It ended with my almost believing (and perhaps I did believe), that this, perhaps, was indeed my normal state. And at first, in the beginning, how much suffering I endured in this struggle! I didn’t believe that this could happen to others, and therefore all my life I kept this secret to myself. I was ashamed (and perhaps even now I am ashamed); I even reached the point of feeling a certain secret, abnormal, mean pleasure in returning, say, to another foul St. Petersburg night and my own corner, and to feel intensely that I had again done something bad, that what was done could never be undone, and to gnaw, to gnaw at myself inwardly, secretly, with my teeth, to the point where the bitterness finally turned into some sort of shameful, accursed sweetness and finally into a decisive, serious pleasure! Yes, into pleasure, into pleasure! I stand by that. That is why I began to speak, because I want to know, perhaps, if others experience such pleasures? I will explain: the pleasure came from the excessively sharp awareness of my humiliation; from the fact that you yourself feel that you have reached the last wall; that this is bad, but that it cannot be otherwise; that there is no escape for you, that you will never become a different person; that even if there were still time and faith to change into something else, you probably wouldn’t want to change; and that if you did want to, you wouldn’t do anything anyway, because in reality there is probably nothing to change into. And the main thing, the end result, is that all this happens according to the normal and fundamental laws of heightened consciousness and the inertia that directly follows from these laws, and consequently, not only can you not change, you can’t even do anything. For example, as a result of heightened consciousness, you become aware that you are a scoundrel, as if this were a consolation for the scoundrel, since he himself feels that he is indeed a scoundrel. But enough… Ah, I have said so much, but what have I explained? What explains this pleasure? But I will explain myself! I will bring it to an end! I took up the pen for this very reason…

K. waited from day to day throughout the next week for a new communication, he couldn't believe that his renunciation of interrogations had been taken literally. And as the expected communication did not arrive by Saturday evening, he assumed that he had been tacitly summoned back to the same house for the same length of time.  Therefore, he went there again on Sunday, this time going straight up the stairs and down the corridors; some people who remembered him greeted him at their doors, but he no longer had to ask anyone and soon came to the right door.  At his knock, it was immediately opened, and without looking further at the familiar woman who remained by the door, he was about to step into the next room. "There's no session today," said the woman. "Why shouldn't there be a session?" he asked, not wanting to believe it. But the woman convinced him by opening the door to the next room. It was really empty and looked even more pathetic in its emptiness than last Sunday. On the table, which stood unchanged on the platform, lay some books. "Can I look at the books?" asked K., not out of particular curiosity, but simply so as not to have been completely useless here. "No," said the woman and closed the door again, "that's not allowed. The books belong to the investigating judge."

Ether from a crack in the door. I started pacing back and forth. It occurred to me that I'd been sent here, to these people, to this overcrowded, general consultation. It was as if it were the first public confirmation that I belonged among the castoffs; had the doctor seen it in me? But I had made my visit in a decent suit, I had sent in my card. Nonetheless, he must have found out somehow, perhaps I had betrayed myself. Now that it was a fact, I didn't find it so bad; the people sat still and paid no attention to me. Some had pain and swung a leg slightly to make it more bearable. Various men had their heads in their flat hands, others slept deeply with heavy, blotched faces. A stout man with a red, swollen neck sat slumped over, stared at the floor and from time to time spat with a clap onto a spot that seemed fitting. A child was sobbing in a corner; it had pulled its long, thin legs up onto the bench and now held them close and pressed against itself, as if taking leave of them.

"Keep it brief, please. The gentlemen are pressed for time. It felt strange, unbearable, really. The young people sat and looked at me with that superior, professional curiosity they'd learned. The doctor I knew stroked his black pointed beard and smiled absentmindedly. I thought I was about to burst into tears, but I found myself saying in French, 'I have already had the honor of giving you, sir, all the information I can. If you deem it necessary for these gentlemen to be informed, then, after our conversation, you are certainly capable of doing so in a few words, whereas it is very difficult for me.' The doctor rose with a polite smile, approached the window with his assistants, and said a few words, accompanying them with a horizontal, swaying hand gesture. After three minutes, one of the young men, short-sighted and fidgety, returned to the table and said, trying to look stern, 'You are sleeping well, sir?' 'No, poorly.' Upon which he sprang back to the group. They discussed amongst themselves for a while longer, then the doctor turned to me and informed me that they would call for me. I reminded him that I had an appointment for a specific time. He smiled and made a few quick, jerky movements with his small white hands, signifying that he was extremely busy. I returned to my corridor, where the air had become much heavier, and began to pace again, even though I was exhausted. Finally, the damp, oppressive smell made me dizzy; I stopped at the entrance door and opened it a little. I saw that it was still afternoon outside and there was a bit of sunshine, and that did me an immense amount of good."

Keep it brief, please. They didn't have much time. I found it strange. The young men sat there and looked at me with that superior, professional curiosity they had learned. The doctor I knew stroked his black, pointed beard and smiled faintly. I thought I would burst into tears, but I heard myself say in French: "I have already had the honor of giving you, sir, all the information I can. If you deem it necessary for these gentlemen to be informed, you are certainly capable of doing so with a few words, whereas it is very difficult for me." The doctor rose with a polite smile, went to the window with his assistants and said a few words, accompanying them with a horizontal, swaying hand gesture. After three minutes, one of the young men, shortsighted and flustered, returned to the table and said, trying to look stern at me: "Are you sleeping well, sir?" "No, poorly." Whereupon he sprang back to the group. They talked amongst themselves for a while longer, then the doctor turned to me and informed me that they would call me. I reminded him that I had been summoned at a specific time. He smiled and made a few quick, jerky movements with his small white hands, which meant he was incredibly busy. So I returned to my corridor, where the air had become much heavier, and started pacing again, although I was utterly exhausted. Finally, the damp, oppressive smell made me feel dizzy; I stopped at the entrance door and opened it a little. I saw that it was still afternoon and there was a little sunshine outside, and that did me an immense amount of good.

The newcomer seemed to avoid speaking much about himself; if he did speak, it was with commonplaces, with noticeable modesty, and his conversation took on a somewhat bookish tone: that he was an insignificant worm in this world and unworthy of much attention, that he had experienced much in his lifetime, endured much in service for the truth, had many enemies who had even tried to take his life, and that now, desiring peace, he was looking to finally choose a place to live, and that, arriving in this city, he considered it his duty to pay his respects to its first officials. This was all that was known about this new arrival, who very soon made an appearance at the governor’s party.

Preparation for the party took over two hours, and the newcomer displayed such attention to his toilette as was rarely seen. After a short afternoon nap, he ordered himself to be washed and scrubbed his cheeks with soap for an unusually long time, pressing his tongue against them from the inside. Then, taking a towel from the innkeeper's shoulder, he wiped his entire face with it, starting behind his ears and snorting twice into the innkeeper's face. He then put on a waistcoat in front of the mirror, plucked out two hairs that had stuck out of his nose, and immediately found himself in a cranberry-colored frock coat with a sparkle. Thus dressed, he rode in his own carriage along the infinitely wide streets, illuminated by meager lighting from the occasional flickering lanterns. However, the governor’s house was brightly lit, even for a ball; the carriage with its lanterns, two gendarmes at the entrance, the cries of footmen in the distance - in a word, everything was in order. Entering the hall, Chikchov had to close his eyes for a moment, because the brilliance from the candles, lamps, and ladies’ dresses was overwhelming. Everything was bathed in light. Black frock coats flickered and darted around, here and there, like flies buzzing around a brilliant, white lump of sugar on a hot July day when an old maid breaks it into sparkling fragments in front of an open window; children all gathered around, watching with curious eyes the movements of her stiff hands as she lifted the hammer, and the aerial squadrons of flies, lifted by a gentle breeze, boldly entered, behaving as though they were the owners, and, taking advantage of the old woman’s poor eyesight and the sun, which dazzled her eyes, showered down morsels of the sweet treat, breaking it here in fragments, there in clumps. Full of the richness of summer, and spreading delectable dishes at every step, they flew in not at all to eat, but simply to show themselves, to walk back and forth over the sugar mound, rub their hind or front legs against each other, or scratch themselves under their wings, or, stretching out both front legs, rub them above their heads, turn around, and fly away again, only to return with new, annoying squadrons. Before Chikchov could take in the scene, he was already seized by the hand by the governor, who immediately introduced him to the governor’s wife. The newcomer did not disappoint himself: he said some compliment, quite appropriate for a man of middle age with a middling rank. When the established dancing couples pressed everyone against the wall, he, folding his arms behind his back, observed them for two minutes with great attention. Many ladies were well dressed and fashionable; others were dressed as God had sent them in this provincial town. The men were, as everywhere, of two kinds: some were slender, who all revolved around the ladies; some were such that it was hard to distinguish them from the St. Petersburg men, they had the same thoughtfully and tastefully trimmed whiskers or simply handsome, very smoothly shaved oval faces, they would settle next to the ladies just as nonchalantly, talk in French just as easily, and make them laugh just as easily as in Petersburg. The other kind of men were stout or, like Chikchov, that is, not so much stout as not slender. These, on the contrary, looked sideways at the ladies and only looked around, wondering if the governor's steward was setting up a green table for whist. Their faces were full and round, some even had warts, some were red-haired, their hair on their heads was either in shaven tufts or slicked back, not like the French say, “damn me,” - their hair was either closely cropped or combed back, and their facial features were more rounded and strong. These were the respected officials in the town. Alas! the stout ones are better at managing their affairs in this world than the slender ones. The slender ones serve more for special errands or simply exist and flit about; their existence is somehow too light, airy, and unreliable. But the stout ones never occupy indirect positions, they always hold the direct ones, and if they do sit down somewhere, they sit securely and firmly, so that the place is more likely to crack and bend under them than they will move. They do not like outward brilliance; their frock coats are not as well-tailored as those of the slender ones, but in their jewel boxes there is divine grace. A slender man doesn't have a single soul left in three years that isn’t pawned; a stout man has a calm life, look - there is a house in the end of the town, bought in his wife's name, then in another part of town another house, then a village near the town, then a village with all the lands. Finally, the stout man, having served God and the state, having earned universal respect, leaves service, moves to the countryside, and becomes a glorious Russian landowner, a hospitable host, and lives well. And after him, his slender heirs, according to Russian custom, send out on courier service the entire paternal property. It is impossible to deny that these kinds of thoughts occupied Chikchov as he observed the company, and as a result, he finally joined the stout ones, where he met almost all the familiar faces: the prosecutor with very dark, thick eyebrows and blinking his left eye somewhat, as if saying: “Come, brother, into another room, I’ll tell you something,” - a man, however, serious and silent; the postmaster, a short man, but witty and philosophical; the chairman of the board, a very thoughtful and pleasant man, - who all greeted him as an old acquaintance, to which Chikchov bowed slightly, although not without pleasure. There he also met a very polite and courteous landowner, Manilov, and the somewhat clumsy Sobakevich, who stepped on his foot right away, saying, “Excuse me.” He was immediately handed a whist card, which he accepted with the same polite bow. They sat down at the green table and did not get up until dinner. All conversation ceased, as always happens when people finally devote themselves to the game. Although the postmaster was very talkative, he too, taking the cards in his hands, immediately expressed a thoughtful expression on his face, covered his lower lip with the upper one, and kept that position throughout the game. When exiting, he struck the table firmly with his hand, saying, “Go away, old woman!” if it was a lady, and “Go away, Tambov peasant!” if it was a king. The chairman would say, “I’ll get you by the whiskers! The thin serve more often on special assignments or just exist and flit about; their existence is too easy, airy, and unreliable. The stout, however, never take indirect positions; if they sit down, they sit down firmly and securely, so that the place is more likely to crack and bend under them, rather than they will move. They don't like outward show; their frock coats don't fit as neatly as those of the thin men, but they have treasures in their coffers. A thin man doesn't have a single soul not pawned in three years; a stout man has a calm life—you look around and there is a house bought in the name of his wife at one end of the city, then another house at the other end, then a village near the city, then a village with all its lands. Finally, the stout man, after serving God and the state, having earned universal respect, leaves service, moves to the countryside, and becomes a glorious Russian master, a generous host, and lives well. And after him, the thin heirs, according to Russian custom, receive all his paternal property on courier. One cannot deny that Chikchov was considering these kinds of thoughts as he observed the company, and as a result, he joined the stout men, where he met almost all familiar faces: the prosecutor with very black, thick eyebrows and who winked his left eye slightly as if to say, "Come, let's go to another room, I'll tell you something there,"— a man, however, serious and taciturn; the postmaster, a short man, but witty and a philosopher; the chairman of the chamber, a very reasonable and pleasant man—all of whom greeted him as an old friend, to which Chikchov bowed slightly, though not without pleasure. There he also met the very courteous and polite landowner Manilov and the somewhat clumsy Sobakevich, who, at the first attempt, stepped on his foot, saying, "Excuse me." Then he was handed a card for whist, which he accepted with a courteous bow. They sat down at the green table and did not get up until dinner.

All conversation ceased entirely, as always happens when people finally turn to a serious occupation. Even the postmaster, though very talkative, when he took the cards in his hands, immediately assumed a thoughtful expression, covered his lower lip with his upper one, and maintained that position throughout the game. When he discarded a card, he struck the table sharply with his hand, saying, "Go away, old hag!" if it was a queen, "Go away, Tambov peasant!" if it was a king. And the chairman would say, "I'll catch you by the whiskers! I'll catch you by the whiskers!" Sometimes, when cards were laid on the table, exclamations like, "Oh, it was or it wasn't, no reason to, so with a tambourine!" or simply, "Worms! Wormholes! Pik!" or, "Pikendra! Pichurushuh! Pichura!" and even just, "Pichuk!"—these were the names they gave the suits in their society. After the game, they argued, as is customary, quite loudly. Our guest also argued, but so skillfully that everyone saw he was arguing, but in a pleasant way. He never said, "You're going," but rather, "You were pleased to go," "I had the honor of covering your pair," and so on. To further agree with his opponents on something, he would always offer them his silver snuffbox with lilies of the valley at the bottom. The newcomer was particularly interested in the landowners Manilov and Sobakevich, mentioned above. He immediately inquired about them, addressing the chairman and the postmaster aside. A few questions, asked of them, showed in the guest not only curiosity, but also diligence; first of all, he asked how many peasant souls each of them owned and what the condition of their estates was, and then he inquired about their names and patronymics. In a short time, he had completely managed to enchant them.

 landowner Manilov, still a young man, with eyes as sweet as sugar, and who squinted every time he smiled, was completely captivated by him. He shook his hand for a very long time and earnestly requested that he would do him the honor of visiting his estate, which, according to him, was only fifteen miles from the city tollgate. To which Chikchov, with a very courteous inclination of his head and a sincere handshake, replied that he was not only happy to do so, but would even consider it his sacred duty. Sobakevich also said rather laconically, "Come to me too,"—stamping his foot, which was shod in a boot of such a gigantic size, that it would be difficult to find a foot to fit it, especially in these times, when heroes are beginning to appear even in Russia.

— Actually, we don’t know exactly what proposals he was writing with, but he wrote every day, every hour, and letter after letter! He was terribly worried. That is, I should have said “Make peace with Emperor Alexander,” but like a child, I naively expressed my whole thought. “Oh, my child!” he answered, pacing back and forth in the room, “Oh, my child!” He seemed not to notice then that I was ten years old, and even loved to talk to me, “Oh, my child, I’m ready to kiss the feet of Emperor Alexander, but not the Prussian king, but the Austrian emperor, oh, eternal hatred for them, and… finally… you understand nothing of politics!”  As if suddenly remembering who he was speaking to, he fell silent, but his eyes still darted sparks. Well, if I were to describe all these facts, — and I was a witness to the greatest of them, — if I were to publish them now, and all these critics, all these literary vanity, all these jealousies, factions, and… no, your obedient servant!

“You murderer!” the old man shouted, but only managed to get that out; he suddenly collapsed as if struck by lightning. Mitka jumped back into the garden and bent over the fallen man. He had a copper pestle in his hand, and he mechanically threw it onto the grass. The pestle landed not in the grass, but on the path, in the most conspicuous place, two paces from Grigory. For several seconds, he stared at the man lying before him. The old man’s head was covered in blood; Mitka reached out and began to touch it. He remembered afterwards with perfect clarity that he desperately wanted at that moment “to be completely sure,” had he cracked the old man’s skull or had he merely “stunned” him with the pestle to the back of the head? But the blood was flowing, flowing terribly, and in an instant it soaked the trembling fingers of Mitka with its hot stream. He recalled pulling out his white new handkerchief, which he had taken with him when going to see Kholkhlakova, and pressing it against the old man’s head, trying senselessly to wipe the blood from his forehead and face. But the handkerchief was soaked in blood in an instant. “Lord, why did I do this?” Mitka suddenly came to his senses, “If I did crack his skull, then how can I now know… And what does it all matter now!” he suddenly added despairingly, “I’ve killed, I’ve killed… The old man fell and now I’m caught!” he said aloud and suddenly darted towards the fence, leaped into the alley, and ran. The handkerchief, soaked in blood, was crumpled in his right fist, and he shoved it into the back pocket of his coat as he ran. He ran headlong, and several rare passersby he encountered in the darkness of the city streets later remembered how they had met a man running wildly in that night.  He ran again towards Morozova’s house. Earlier that evening, Fenechka, the moment he left, had rushed to the senior janitor, Nazar Ivanovich, and begged him, “By Christ, please don’t let the captain in anymore, not today, not tomorrow.” Nazar Ivanovich, having listened, agreed, but on a whim went upstairs to the mistress, where he was suddenly called, and on the way, meeting his nephew, a young man of about twenty, who had just arrived from the village, ordered him to stay in the courtyard, but forgot to tell him about the captain. Reaching the gates, Mitka knocked. The young man immediately recognized him: Mitka had given him tea many times before. He immediately opened the gate, let him in, and, smiling cheerfully, hastened to warn him, that “Agfena Alexandrovna isn’t even at home now.”

But Grigory Vasilyevich doesn’t come, so now I am alone in the rooms – that’s how they decided the moment they began this scheme with Aglaya Alexandrovna, and at night, by their orders, I too retire to the dacha and remain awake until midnight, patrolling the grounds, waiting for Aglaya Alexandrovna to arrive, since they’ve been waiting for her for days now, as if possessed. Wukong bowed again and said, "Reporting to the master, I have been away from home for twenty years. Although I yearn to look back at my old friends and family, I am mindful of the master's great kindness and haven't been able to repay it, so I dare not leave."

The master said, "What kindness and righteousness are there? You just need to not cause trouble and not involve me."

K. was interrupted from the end of the hall by a scream. He shielded his eyes to see, for the dim daylight made the haze appear white and blinding. It was the laundress, whom K. had recognized immediately upon her entry as a significant disturbance. Whether she was guilty or not was unclear. K. only saw that a man had pulled her into a corner by the door and was pressing against her. But it wasn't her who was screaming, but the man. He had his mouth wide open and was looking at the ceiling. A small circle had formed around the two of them, the gallery attendees near seemed delighted that the seriousness with which K. had introduced himself to the assembly was interrupted in this way. K. wanted to run towards them immediately, and he thought everyone would be concerned about establishing order and at least ushering the couple out of the hall, but the first rows in front of him remained completely still, no one moved, and no one let K. through. On the contrary, they hindered him, old men held out their arms, and some hand – he didn't have time to turn around – grasped him by the collar. K. no longer really thought about the couple; it felt as though his freedom was being restricted, as if he were being arrested, and he jumped recklessly from the podium. Now he stood face to face with the crowd. Had he misjudged the people? Had he given his speech too much impact? Had they been pretending while he spoke, and were they now, as he came to his conclusions, satisfied with the pretense? What faces surrounded him! Small, black eyes darted around, cheeks hung down, as if with those who had drunk too much, the long beards were stiff and sparse, and if you reached into them, it was as if you were touching claws, not beards. But under the beards – and that was the actual discovery K. made – insignia of various sizes and colors shimmered on the collar. Everyone had these insignia, as far as one could see. They all belonged together, the apparent parties on the right and left, and as he suddenly turned around, he saw the same insignia on the collar of the examining magistrate, who, with his hands in his pockets, looked down calmly. "So," K. exclaimed, throwing his arms into the air, the sudden realization needed space, "you are all officials, as I see it, you are the corrupt band I spoke against, you have gathered here as listeners and spies, you have formed apparent parties, and one has applauded to test me, you wanted to learn how to seduce the innocent! Well, you haven't been useless here, I hope, either you have discussed among yourselves that someone expected the defense of innocence from you, or – let me go, or I'll hit," K. shouted to a trembling old man who had pushed himself particularly close to him – "or you have really learned something. And with that, I wish you luck in your profession." He quickly grabbed his hat, which lay on the edge of the table, and, under a complete and absolute silence, forced his way to the exit. "I just wanted to point out to you," said the examining magistrate, "that you have deprived yourself today – it may not have occurred to you yet – of the advantage that an interrogation for the arrested always entails." K. laughed at the door. "You scoundrels," he cried, "I give you all the interrogations," opened the door, and hurried down the stairs. Behind him, the noise of the revived assembly rose, which probably began to discuss the events in the manner of students.

He shouted, "Master, don't be so pathetic! Sit down! Sit down! I'll go find that creature and get our horse back."  The Tripitaka grabbed him and said, "Disciple, where are you going to find him?"

He whistled, leapt into the air, with hawk eyes, shielding his face from the sun, scanning the surroundings, yet he saw no trace of the horse. Falling Cloud reported, "Master, our horse must have been eaten by that dragon. We can't find it anywhere else." The Tripitaka said, "Disciple, how could that creature's mouth be so large as to have swallowed the horse whole, saddle and reins included? It must have bolted in fear, escaped its reins, and wandered into a mountain hollow. Look again carefully." The行者 said, "You don't know my abilities. These eyes of mine can see good fortune and misfortune a thousand li away in daylight. If a dragonfly flaps its wings within a thousand li, I can see it. How could I not see that horse?" The Tripitaka said, "If it was eaten by that beast, how can I continue? It's so pitiful! How can we possibly travel through these ten thousand mountains and rivers?" Saying this, tears streamed down his face like rain. The行者 saw him weeping, and he couldn't bear it. He shouted, "Master, don't act so helpless! Sit down! Sit down! Just wait here while I go find that beast and get my horse back." The Tripitaka pulled him back and said, "Disciple, where would you go to find him?"

And when the painter did not answer, she said, "Please, don't paint him, such an ugly man." A flurry of unintelligible, agreeing noises followed. The staff clashed with the spear, the sound ringing out loudly, the spear reflecting the light of the iron staff.  Sun Wukong transformed into many forms, a rarity amongst the worldly monsters. One wanted the Buddhist robes for a birthday celebration, the other refused to return the cassock willingly. This arduous battle couldn't be resolved, even if a living Buddha descended to earth. The two of them fought from the mouth of the cave to the mountain peak, then from the mountain peak to beyond the clouds, spitting mist, wind, and sand, rocks flying everywhere. They battled until the red sun sank in the west, neither gaining an advantage. The monster said, "You, Sun, stop your attacks! The day is late, it's not suitable for a prolonged standoff. You go, go! I'll meet you tomorrow morning, and we'll settle this for good." Sun Wukong said, "Wait, monster! If you want to fight, fight like a proper fight, don't use the evening as an excuse to back down." Seeing the monster's cowardly retreat, Sun Wukong could only swing his staff.  The black-faced demon then turned into a clear breeze and returned to the cave, quickly closing the stone door from the inside.

Seeing his shameless demeanor, the Monkey King simply raised his staff and struck, the black-faced man then vanished, transforming into a gust of wind, retreating back into the cave and firmly shutting the stone door.

Thousand officials with jeweled ornaments surround the throne, the five guards' banners stand guard on both sides. Holding gold gourds and axes, they stand in pairs; red silk candles and incense from ceremonial censors fill the hall with a magnificent aroma. Dragons soar and phoenixes dance, falcons and eagles ascend; the holy emperor's presence shines, surrounded by loyal and righteous ministers. 

They outshine the virtues of Emperor Shun and Yu, reigning for a thousand years; they surpass the achievements of Emperors Yao and Tang, bringing peace for ten thousand generations. 

Observe, the ivory-handled umbrella, the dragon-embroidered robe, radiant and intermingled; jade bracelets and phoenix fans, auspicious fumes drifting everywhere. 

A crown of jewels, a jade sash, purple bands with gold insignia adorn him. Thousands of guards flanking the emperor, two lines of bearers carrying him.

The emperor bathes, with devout respect, offering incense to Buddha, embracing the good fruits. 

King Tang arrived early, before the temple, ordered the musical instruments silenced, stepped out of his carriage, leading a multitude of officials. He bowed to Buddha and offered incense.

After three circumambulations, he looked up, truly a magnificent hall. The banners fluttered and danced, the jeweled canopy soared. Banners fluttered and danced, revealing streaks of colorful clouds; the jeweled canopy soared, reflecting the sunlight, with crimson flashes. 

Shakyamuni, the golden elephant form majestic, Arhats with jade faces, fiercely dignified.  Flower vases filled with immortal blooms, sandalwood incense burning. Flower vases filled with immortal blooms, the jeweled trees shimmered, illuminating the entire temple.  Sandalwood incense burned, the fragrance rose, piercing the clear sky. 

Fresh fruits arranged on a vermilion platter,  unusual candy and sesame pastries piled high on colorful tables. High monks lined up, chanting the true scriptures, wishing to liberate souls from suffering.

Emperor Taizong, both civil and military, offered incense, bowed to the golden Buddha statue, and paid homage to the Arhats.

Then, the great master Xuanzang, head of the Eastern Capital, led the monks to bow to King Tang. 

After the ceremony, they each took their meditation positions, and the master presented the "Pledge for the Liberation of Souls" scroll to Emperor Taizong.

It read: "Transcendent virtue boundless, Zen is extinguished. 

Pure and lucid, permeating the Three Realms.

Ever-changing, embracing Yin and Yang.

Embodiment of truth, boundless and endless.

Observing those lonely souls, compassion is urged.

By the Mandate of Emperor Taizong, monks are selected to practice Zen and preach the Dharma.  The gate of convenient access is opened wide, the boat of compassion is launched, relieving all beings in the sea of suffering, freeing them from the six realms of misery.

Returning to the true path, playing freely in the primordial chaos; stillness and movement, non-action, merging into purity.  

Relying on this good opportunity, we invite them to appreciate the clear and bright Jade Palace;

Taking advantage of this great gathering, they will escape the hellish prison of the world.

Soar to Ultimate Bliss, with freedom and ease,

Traveling West whenever they please.

A few scrolls, the manuals for rebirth. 
Endless wondrous Dharma, boundless Heavenly Grace.
All grievances cease, all souls are freed from prison.

May you bless my nation, for ten thousand years of peace and prosperity."

Emperor Taizong read it with delight and said to the monks, "You all hold sincerity in your hearts, and must not neglect the affairs of the Buddha. When your deeds are completed, and each of you has achieved your full merit, I will surely reward you, and never leave you in vain." 

The one thousand and two hundred monks, all bowed their heads together, expressing their gratitude.

Thousand officials surrounded the Emperor, their emblems fanning out before and behind. The guards stood in rows on either side, swords and axes gleaming, in pairs facing each other.  Red silk candles flickered, while incense burned in ornate censers, filling the hall with a rich, palpable fragrance. Dragons soared and phoenixes took flight, as eagles and falcons spread their wings. The divinely appointed Son of Heaven, the Emperor, sat upright, surrounded by loyal and righteous ministers. His virtues have surpassed those of Shun and Yu from a thousand years past, his rule will rival that of Yao and Tang, bringing prosperity for ten thousand generations.

A sight to behold! The Emperor's scepter and throne are covered in brocade, their brilliance intermingling. Jade bracelets and intricately painted fans adorned with phoenixes cast down a scattering of auspicious light.  He wears a crown of jewels and a sash of purple, adorned with golden emblems. Thousands of soldiers stand guard, escorting the Emperor in two long lines. This Emperor, in utmost sincerity and reverence, bathes in the presence of the Buddha, taking refuge in the teachings and offering fragrant incense. 

Before the temple, the Tang King arrived early, silencing the music and instruments. He stepped out of his carriage, accompanied by many officials, prostrated himself before the Buddha, and offered incense. After three circuits, he looked up and saw indeed a magnificent assembly hall. Flags and banners fluttered, their colors brilliant.  The banners danced in the air, the swirling rainbow clouds seemed to shimmer. The jeweled canopy shone, its reflections illuminating the vibrant, crimson streaks of sunlight.

The Buddha, with his golden elephant-like form, emanates an aura of serenity. The Bodhisattvas, adorned with jade, radiate an aura of unwavering strength.  The incense burner offered an array of beautiful flowers, while sandalwood burned, releasing its sweet fragrance.  The fragrant sandalwood rose high, filling the air with a gentle mist. On a red lacquer tray were arranged exquisite fruits, and on a colorful altar, unique candies and pastries were stacked high. High priests and monks chanted the sacred sutras, praying to liberate lost souls from their suffering.

Emperor Taizong, both civil and military officials, offered incense, bowed before the golden Buddha, and respectfully paid homage to the Bodhisattvas. He saw Master Xuanzang, the renowned Buddhist master, leading the assembled monks in a respectful bow towards the Tang King. The ceremony completed, the monks took their designated meditation spots, and the Master presented the Emperor with a scroll titled, "A Charter for Liberating Souls," which read:

"Great virtue transcends understanding, Zen embodies emptiness. Pure and insightful, it flows through the three realms. Its forms are ever-changing, encompassing both yin and yang. Its essence is true and eternal, boundless and limitless. Observing those lost souls, one should feel deep compassion. Following the Emperor's holy command, we have gathered these monks to practice Zen and preach the Dharma. We open the door to convenience, spreading our compassionate vessel,  to ferry all living beings across the ocean of suffering, freeing them from the ailments of the six realms. Guide them to the true path, immerse them in the primordial chaos; let stillness and action be without striving, blending into pure simplicity. Relying on this auspicious occasion, we invite blessings upon the peaceful capital; utilize this fortunate gathering, free yourselves from the confines of hell and the mortal world.  Ascend to the Pure Land, enjoy boundless freedom, and come and go freely to the West.

"So let her be your beloved then," said Leni, "You wouldn't miss her very much if you lost her, or exchanged her for someone else, say, for me."

"Certainly," said K. smiling, "that's conceivable, but she has one great advantage over you, she knows nothing of my trial, and even if she did, she wouldn't think about it. She wouldn't try to persuade me to be more accommodating."

"That's no advantage," said Leni. "If she has no other advantages, I won't lose heart. Does she have any physical flaw?"

"A physical flaw?" asked K.

"Yes," said Leni, "I have a small one, see." She spread her middle and ring finger of her right hand apart, between which the webbing stretched almost to the top joint of the short finger. K. couldn't make out in the dark what she wanted to show him, so she guided his hand towards it.

"What a curious quirk of nature," said K., and adding, as he took in the whole hand, "What a pretty claw!"

With a certain pride, Leni watched as K., full of wonder, repeatedly spread and closed her two fingers, until he finally kissed them fleetingly and let go.

"Oh!" she exclaimed, "You kissed me!" Eagerly, with her mouth open, she climbed onto his lap with her knees. K. looked at her almost in alarm, now that she was so close, a bitter, pungent smell like pepper emanated from her, she took his head, leaned over him, and bit and kissed his neck, even biting into his hair.

"You've exchanged me!" she cried from time to time, "See, now you've exchanged me!"

Suddenly her knee slipped, and with a little cry she almost fell onto the rug. K. grasped her to keep her from falling and was pulled down towards her.

"Now you belong to me," she said.

On the very first day, the father went through the entire financial situation and prospects, both of the mother and the sister. Every now and then he would rise from the table and, from his small Wertheim safe, which he had salvaged from the collapse of his business five years prior, pull out some document or memorandum book. One could hear the intricate lock clicking open, and then click shut again as he retrieved and returned the desired item. These explanations from the father were, for the most part, the first agreeable thing Gregor had heard since his confinement. He had believed that the father had nothing left from that business, at least he had not been told otherwise, and Gregor, in fact, hadn't asked him. Gregor's worry back then had only been to help the family forget the business misfortune as quickly as possible, which had thrown them into complete despair. And so he had begun to work with unprecedented fervor, transforming practically overnight from a lowly clerk into a traveling salesman, which naturally offered him far greater earning possibilities, and whose work successes immediately materialized in the form of commission payments, in cash, which could be placed on the astonished and delighted family's table at home. Those were beautiful times, and they never reappeared, at least not with that same brilliance. Though Gregor later earned so much money that he could and did support the entire family. They had simply become accustomed to both the family and Gregor, accepting the money gratefully. He was happy to provide it, but a special warmth no longer arose. Only his sister remained close to Gregor, and it was his secret plan, without considering the considerable costs that would be incurred, costs they would already have to find elsewhere, to send her, the one who, unlike Gregor, loved music deeply and played the violin touchingly, to the conservatory the following year. During Gregor's short stays in the city, the conservatory was often mentioned in conversations with his sister, but always only as a beautiful dream, the realization of which was unthinkable. The parents didn't even like to hear these innocent mentions. But Gregor thought about it with great determination and intended to announce it ceremoniously on Christmas Eve.

One could hear the complicated lock being opened and then closed again as he retrieved what he needed. These explanations from the father were, in part, the first pleasant thing Gregor had heard since his imprisonment. He had thought that his father had lost everything from that business, at least his father had not said anything to the contrary, and Gregor hadn’t asked him about it. Gregor’s worry at the time had only been to get the family to forget about the business misfortune as quickly as possible, which had plunged them all into utter hopelessness. And so he had started working with renewed fervor, becoming almost overnight from a small clerk a traveling salesman who, of course, had far greater opportunities to earn money, and whose work successes immediately materialized in the form of commissions, which were brought home as cash to the astonished and overjoyed family. Those had been wonderful times, and they never repeated themselves, not even in that splendor, even though Gregor later earned so much money that he was able to, and did, support the entire family’s expenses.  They had simply gotten used to it, both the family and Gregor; they gratefully accepted the money, he gladly provided it, but no special warmth arose. Only his sister remained close to Gregor, and it was his secret plan to send her, who, unlike Gregor, loved music dearly and played the violin movingly, to the conservatory the following year, regardless of the great expense that would be incurred, which they would find a way to manage. During Gregor’s short stays in the city, the conservatory was mentioned in conversations with his sister, but always only as a beautiful dream, the realization of which was unthinkable, and the parents did not even like to hear these innocent mentions; but Gregor thought about it very determinedly and intended to announce it ceremoniously on Christmas Eve.

It took unbelievable caution to live with this blood. The duke was enclosed within himself, and at times he feared it, crouching and lurking around him. It could feel strangely foreign to him, this quick, half-Portuguese blood, which he scarcely knew. Often it frightened him that it might attack him in his sleep and tear him apart. He pretended to have it under control, but he was always consumed by his fear. He never dared to love a woman, for fear it would become jealous, and so consuming was it that wine never passed his lips; instead of drinking, he soothed himself with rosewater. But once, he drank, in his camp before Lausanne, when Granson was lost; he was ill and isolated then and drank much pure wine. But then his blood was asleep. In his senseless final years, it sometimes fell into this heavy, animal sleep. Then it showed how much he was at its mercy; for when it slept, he was nothing. Then no one from his surroundings could approach him; he did not understand what they said. He could not show himself to the foreign ambassadors, as barren as he was. Then he sat and waited for it to wake.

It's not so hard that the hero will displease the reader, but it's hard that in his soul lives the irrefutable conviction that the same hero, the same Chikchov, would have pleased the reader. If the author didn't delve deeper into his soul, didn't stir up what slips away and hides from the light at its bottom, didn't reveal the innermost thoughts that a person doesn't confide in anyone else, and simply showed him as he appeared to the whole town, to Manilov and other people, then everyone would have been delighted and taken him for an interesting person. There is no need for his face or his whole image to come alive before our eyes; instead, upon finishing the reading, the soul would remain undisturbed, and one could return to the card table, which delights all of Russia. Yes, my dear readers, wouldn't you prefer not to see the exposed human poverty? Why, you might say, what is the point of this? Don't we already know that there is much contemptible and foolish in life? And so we often see things that are not at all comforting. It's better to present us with the beautiful and captivating. Let us forget about it all! "Why, brother," says the landowner to the clerk, "are you telling me that things are going badly on the estate? - I, brother, know that without you, and don't you have other things to say? Dunia and her husband could take little comfort from these news, especially at first. Sonya reported incessantly that he was constantly gloomy, taciturn, and barely interested in the news she relayed from the letters she received; that he sometimes inquired about his mother; and when she, sensing he was already anticipating the truth, finally told him about her death, to her surprise, even the news of his mother's demise did not seem to affect him greatly, at least not outwardly. 

She reported, among other things, that despite the fact that he seemed so absorbed in himself and shut off from everyone, he had taken to his new life very straightforwardly and simply; that he clearly understood his situation, did not expect anything better in the near future, harbored no frivolous hopes (which were so typical in his position), and was hardly surprised by anything in his new surroundings, so unlike anything he had known before. She said that his health was satisfactory. He went to work, from which he did not shirk and to which he did not volunteer; he was almost indifferent to food, but since, except for Sundays and holidays, it was so wretched, he finally accepted some money from her to have tea every day.  About everything else, he asked her not to worry, assuring her that all these concerns about him only annoyed him. 

Further, Sonya reported that his lodging in the prison was shared with everyone; she hadn't seen the interior of the barracks, but concluded that it was cramped, unsightly, and unhealthy; that he slept on bunks, laying a piece of felt under him, and didn't want to arrange anything else for himself. But that he lived so crudely and poorly was not at all due to some preconceived plan or intention, but simply out of inattention and outward indifference to his fate. Sonya wrote directly that he, especially at first, not only showed no interest in her visits, but even seemed annoyed by them, was taciturn, and even rude to her; but that towards the end these meetings had become a habit for him, and almost a necessity, so that he was very sad when she was ill for several days and couldn't visit him.  They met on holidays at the prison gates or in the guardhouse, where they were allowed to see each other for a few minutes; on weekdays, she would visit him at work, in the workshops, on the brickworks, or in the sheds on the banks of the Irtysh. For herself, Sonya informed him that she had managed to acquire some acquaintances and patronage in the city; that she was doing sewing, and since there were hardly any dressmakers in the city, she had become almost indispensable in many homes; she didn't mention, however, that through her, Raskolnikov had also received patronage from the authorities, which had made his work easier. Finally, news arrived (Dunia even noticed a certain special excitement and anxiety in her last letters) that he was shunning everyone, that the convicts in the prison hadn't taken to him; that he was silent for whole days and was becoming very pale. Suddenly, in her last letter, Sonya wrote that he had become seriously ill and was lying in the hospital, in the convict ward...

Finally, news arrived (Dunya even noticed some unusual excitement and anxiety in her recent letters) that he shunned everyone, that the convicts in the prison had not taken to him; that he remained silent for entire days and was growing pale. Suddenly, in her last letter, Sonya wrote that he had become seriously ill and was lying in the hospital ward.

This was the third time Ivan Fedorovich went to see Smerdyakov upon his return from Moscow. The first time he had seen him and spoken with him was on the very first day of his arrival; then he visited him again two weeks later. But after that second meeting, he ceased visiting Smerdyakov, so that now it was over a month since he had seen him and he had heard almost nothing about him. Ivan Fedorovich had returned from Moscow only on the fifth day after his father’s death, so he had not even seen the coffin: the burial had taken place the very day before his arrival. The reason for Ivan Fedorovich's delay was that Alyosha, not knowing his exact Moscow address, had resorted to sending a telegram to Katerina Ivanovna, and she, also unaware of his current address, had telegraphed to her sister and aunt, hoping that Ivan Fedorovich would visit them immediately upon his arrival in Moscow. But he only visited them on the fourth day after arriving and, upon reading the telegram, immediately, of course, set off at top speed to see us. Here, he first encountered Alyosha, but after speaking with him, was very surprised that the latter did not even suspect Mitka, but directly pointed to Smerdyakov as the murderer, which contradicted all other opinions in our town. After seeing the police inspector and the prosecutor, learning the details of the accusation and the arrest, he was even more surprised by Alyosha and attributed his opinion to the brotherly feelings, excited to the highest degree, and compassion for Mitka, whom Alyosha, as Ivan knew, had loved very much. Incidentally, let us just say two words once and for all about Ivan’s feelings towards his brother, Dmitry Fyodorovich: he decidedly did not love him and often felt a mixture of pity and great contempt for him, bordering on disgust. Mitka, with his entire being, even with his entire figure, was extremely unsympathetic to him. He viewed Katya Ivanovna's love for him with indignation. However, he did meet with the accused Mitka on his first day in town, and this meeting did not weaken his conviction of his guilt but rather strengthened it. He found his brother to be in a state of anxiety and painful agitation. Mitka was talkative, but scattered and incoherent, spoke very sharply, accused Smerdyakov and became confused. He spoke most of all about the three thousand rubles which, he claimed, the deceased had "stolen" from him. "My money, they were mine," Mitka kept repeating, "even if I had stolen them, I would have been right." He barely contested most of the evidence against him, and if he tried to interpret the facts in his favor, it was again very disjointed and illogical – generally as if he did not even want to defend himself before Ivan or anyone else, but rather became angry, proudly disregarded the accusations, swore, and grew heated. He even sneered at Grigory’s testimony about the open door, claiming that “the devil had opened it.” But he could not offer any coherent explanation for this fact. He even managed to insult Ivan Fedorovich during this first meeting, sharply saying to him that he shouldn’t be questioned or interrogated by those who themselves claim that "everything is allowed."  In general, he was very unfriendly towards Ivan Fedorovich this time.  After this meeting with Mitka, Ivan Fedorovich then went to see Smerdyakov.

He sat there for a long time, uncertain of what was truly troubling him, only occasionally glancing back over his shoulder with a touch of fear towards the door to the anteroom, where he had mistakenly thought he heard a noise. Since no one came, however, he grew calmer, went to the washbasin, washed his face with cold water, and returned to his window seat with a lighter heart. 

The decision to take his own defense into his hands presented itself as more daunting than he had initially imagined. As long as he had left the defense to the lawyer, he had still been largely unaffected by the trial; he had observed it from a distance and had barely been touched by it directly. He had been able to check on the progress of his case whenever he wanted, and had also been able to withdraw his head when he wanted. Now, however, if he were to conduct his own defense, he would have to expose himself completely to the court – at least for the moment. The success of this was supposed to be his complete and final liberation in the future, but to achieve that, he would have to put himself in far greater danger than before. Had he still doubted this, today’s meeting with the deputy director and the factory owner would have convinced him otherwise. How he had sat there, already completely disoriented by the mere decision to defend himself! How would it be later? What days lay ahead of him? Would he find the path that led through it all to a good end? Did a careful defense – and everything else was pointless – not simultaneously mean the necessity of tying himself as closely as possible to everything else? Would he manage to get through that? And how was he supposed to carry this out at the bank? It wasn’t just about the submission, for which a vacation might have sufficed, although asking for one right now would have been a great risk; it was about a whole trial, the duration of which was unpredictable. What a sudden obstacle had been thrown in K.’s path!

There was so little to do. I wandered through the city and found that it had changed. It was pleasant to step out of the hotel where I had stayed and see that it was now a city for adults, one that held itself together, almost like a stranger. Everything had become a little smaller, and I strolled along the Langelinie out to the lighthouse and back again. When I came to the area of Amaliengade, it was certainly possible that something would emerge from somewhere that had been accepted for years and that was trying its power again. There were certain corner windows or archways or lampposts that knew a lot about me and threatened me with it. I looked them in the face and let them feel that I lived in the 'Phönix' Hotel and could travel again at any moment. But my conscience was not at ease with this. The suspicion arose in me that none of these influences and connections had really been mastered. They had been secretly abandoned one day, unfinished as they were. Childhood, too, would thus have to be fulfilled, if one didn't want to lose it forever. And as I realized how I was losing it, I simultaneously felt that I would never have anything else to fall back on.

Everything had become a bit smaller, and I strolled along the Langelinie out to the lighthouse and back again. When I came to the area around Amaliengade, it could happen, of course, that something would emerge from somewhere that had been acknowledged for years and that was trying its power once again. There were certain corner windows or archways or lampposts that knew a great deal about me and threatened me with it. I looked them in the face and let them feel that I was staying at the 'Phönix' Hotel and could travel again at any moment. But my conscience wasn't at peace with it. The suspicion rose in me that none of these influences and connections had really been mastered. They had been secretly abandoned one day, unfinished as they were. Even childhood, then, would have to be accomplished in a way, if one didn't want to lose it forever. And as I realized how I was losing it, I simultaneously felt that I would never have anything else to call upon.

Just as they were shouting, the True Monarch arrived and asked, "Brothers, did you not see him over there?" The gods replied, "We were just surrounding him here, and he vanished." Erlang opened his phoenix eyes wide and saw that the Great Sage had transformed into a sparrow, nailed to a tree. He then retracted his magical form, sheathed his divine blade, removed his slingshot, and in a flash, transformed into a hawk, spreading his wings and flying to attack. 

The Great Sage, seeing this, with a flutter of his wings, took flight, transforming into a large cormorant and soaring into the sky. Erlang, upon seeing this, shook his feathers, transformed into a giant crane, and ascended into the clouds to pursue. The Great Sage then lowered himself, diving into the stream, and transformed into a fish, disappearing into the water. Erlang arrived at the stream’s edge but saw no trace of him.  He thought to himself, “This monkey must have gone into the water. He must have transformed into some sort of fish or shrimp. I’ll just transform and catch him.” He immediately transformed into a fish eagle, gliding across the surface of the water. 

After a while, the Great Sage, as a fish, swam along, when suddenly he saw a flying creature, resembling a kite, yet not entirely blue; like a heron, but without a plume on its head; like a stork, but with legs that weren't red. "Must be Erlang, transformed to wait for me!" ... He quickly turned his head and darted away. 

Erlang saw, "The fish, it swishes its tail, but it's not red like a carp; it has scales, but not the patterns of a Mandarin fish; it's black, but lacks the stars on its head; it has gills, but no prickles. Why did he flee upon seeing me? It must be that monkey!" He swooped down, snapping his beak. 

The Great Sage shot out of the water and, in a flash, transformed into a water snake, swimming near the shore and disappearing into the grass. Erlang, unable to catch him, heard a splash in the water and saw a snake slither out. He recognized it as the Great Sage. He quickly turned around and transformed into a gray crane with a crimson crest, stretching out a long beak resembling a sharp, iron pincers, and headed to devour the water snake. 

The water snake leaped and transformed into a common peafowl, standing stiffly on the bank. Erlang, seeing that he had become such a lowly creature – a common peafowl, the most despicable and promiscuous bird, mingling with peacocks, phoenixes, hawks, and crows – decided not to approach, and instead returned to his original form and walked away. He picked up his slingshot, loaded it, and fired a stone, striking the Great Sage's [foot dragon] heel.

The Great Sage, seeing this, flapped his wings and soared into the sky, transforming into a large old cormorant and ascending into the heavens. The Second Brother, seeing this, shook his feathers, transformed into a great white crane, and soared into the clouds to pursue him.

Recognizing it as the Great Sage, he turned around and transformed into a gray crane with a crimson crest, stretching out a long beak that resembled a sharp iron claw, and flew towards the water snake. The water snake jumped and transformed into a common pheasant, standing stiffly on a reed mat. 

Seeing that he had transformed into something lowly - the pheasant being the most humble and licentious bird, mingling with peacocks, phoenixes, hawks, and crows - the Second Brother did not approach. Instead, he returned to his original form and strode away.  He picked up his crossbow, filled it, and shot a bolt that struck the pheasant's [ankle-like] tendon.

Despite how unlikely it was, I had somehow managed to slip out of the house alone in the evening. I ran, turned a corner, and in that very moment, I bumped into him. I can’t fathom how what happened next could have unfolded in roughly five seconds. Even if one tells it, it takes much longer. I had hurt myself stumbling into him; I was small, it already seemed like a lot that I didn’t cry, and I also involuntarily expected to be comforted. Since he didn’t, I took him for embarrassed; it didn’t occur to him, I suspected, what the right joke would be in which to resolve this. I was already happy enough to help him with that, but for that, it was necessary to look him in the face. I had said that he was big. Now, he hadn’t bent down over me, as would have been natural, so that he was at a height I wasn’t prepared for. Still, there was nothing in front of me but the smell and the peculiar stiffness of his suit that I had felt. Suddenly, his face appeared. How it was? I don’t know, I don’t want to know. It was the face of an enemy. And next to that face, close by, at the height of those terrifying eyes, stood, like a second head, his fist. Before I even had time to duck my face, I was already running; I dodged past him to the left and ran straight down an empty, terrifying alleyway, the alleyway of a foreign city, a city where nothing is forgiven.

Many busy people do the same thing, and yet no one thinks to call them the Outcastes. Because it’s clear to me that the Outcastes are not just beggars; no, they’re not really beggars, we have to make distinctions. They are the waste, the shells of people that fate has spit out. Wet with the saliva of fate, they cling to a wall, a lamppost, a billboard, or they slowly trickle down the alleyway, leaving a dark, dirty trail behind them. What in the world did that old woman want from me, who, with a nightstand drawer containing a few buttons and needles rolling around, crawled out of some hole? Why did she always walk beside me and watch me? As if she was trying to recognize me with her leaky eyes, which looked as if a sick person had spat green slime into her bloody eyelids. And how did that gray, little woman come to stand for a quarter of an hour in front of a shop window beside me, while she showed me an old, long pencil that infinitely slowly extended from her bad, closed hands. I acted as if I was looking at the displayed items and noticed nothing. But she knew that I had seen her, she knew that I stood there thinking about what she was actually doing. Because

“I don’t want oratorical success,” said K., reasoning thus, “that probably wouldn’t be within my grasp anyway. The Examining Magistrate probably speaks much better; it’s part of his profession, after all. What I want is simply a public discussion of a public wrong. Listen: I was arrested about ten days ago, and I laugh at the fact of the arrest itself, but that doesn’t belong here now. I was seized in bed early in the morning; perhaps they – it’s not excluded, as the Examining Magistrate said – had the order to arrest some equally innocent house painter, but they chose me. The adjacent room was occupied by two rough guards. If I were a dangerous robber, they couldn’t have taken less precaution. Besides, these guards were demoralized riff-raff, they talked my ear off, they wanted to bribe me, they wanted to get me to hand over my clothes and laundry under false pretenses, they wanted money, allegedly to bring me breakfast after they shamelessly devoured my own breakfast in front of me. And that wasn’t all. I was taken to a third room in front of the jailer. It was the room of a lady whom I greatly esteem, and I had to watch, for my sake, but without any fault of mine, how this room was more or less defiled by the presence of the guards and the jailer. It wasn’t easy to remain calm, but I managed it, and I asked the jailer, completely calmly – if he were here, he would confirm it – why I had been arrested. What answer did this jailer, whom I still see before me, sitting on the chair of the aforementioned lady as a manifestation of the most obtuse arrogance, give me? Gentlemen, he basically said nothing, perhaps he really knew nothing; he had arrested me and was satisfied with that. He even went so far as to bring three low employees of my bank into the room of that lady, who then busied themselves with groping and disarranging photographs, the property of the lady. The presence of these employees naturally had another purpose; they, just like my landlady and her maid, were meant to spread the news of my arrest, damage my public image, and especially to shake my position at the bank. Now, none of this, not even in the slightest, has succeeded. Even my landlady, a very simple person – I want to mention her name here in a respectful way, she is called Frau Grubach – even Frau Grubach was intelligent enough to see that such an arrest meant no more than an attack carried out by unsupervised boys in the street. I repeat, it has only caused me inconvenience and temporary annoyance, but it could have had worse consequences.”

Only because the Queen Mother was holding a peach feast, opening the Yaochi Palace to invite many guests. At that time, intoxicated and dizzy, he stumbled about, east and west, and wreaked havoc. He showed no deference, grabbing Chang’e, wanting her to rest with him. When she refused again and again, he became impatient, hiding east and west, but his heart was displeased.  His lust and courage were like thunder, nearly shaking the heavens' gate. The Inspecting Spirit Officials reported to the Jade Emperor, that day my destiny was clumsy. The Guanghan Palace was besieged, with no way in or out, making it difficult to escape. But I was caught by the gods, and the wine in my heart did not make me cowardly. Led to Lingxiao to see the Jade Emperor, according to the law, I was to be sentenced. Fortunately, the White Emperor, Li Jinxing, stepped down from the heavens to plead on my behalf. The sentence was changed to two thousand hammerings, breaking skin, flesh, and about to break bones. After being released, I was demoted outside the heavenly gate and fell to Fuling Mountain to make a living. I was born into the mortal realm due to my crime, my common name is Pigsy.  The traveler heard this and said, “You, you turned out to be the Tianpeng Water God, no wonder you know my name, Lao Sun.” The monster roared, "You, you lying flatterer, back then when you caused that havoc, you didn't know how many of us you implicated. Today, you come here to deceive people! Don't be disrespectful, take this!" The traveler wouldn't tolerate it, lifting his staff and striking him down. The two of them fought in the middle of the mountain under the darkness. 
 
The traveler’s golden eyes shone like lightning, the demons around him glistened like silver flowers. The monster spat colorful mist, the traveler exhaled red clouds. The red clouds filled the dusk, the colorful mist illuminated the night. The golden-hooded staff, the nine-toothed trident, the two heroes are truly worthy of praise: one is the Great Sage traveling in the mortal world, and the other is the Marshal descending to earth. The trident went forth like a dragon's claws, the staff met the air like a phoenix piercing a flower.

From the second watch, they battled until the east turned white. Unable to resist, the monster retreated, again transforming into a gust of wind and returning to his cave, tightly closing the door, no longer emerging.

If he had wanted to think about it a little, he would have been astonished at how he could have spoken to them like that just a minute ago, even trying to impose his feelings on them. Something completely unfamiliar, new, sudden, and unprecedented was happening to him. One day, the four valiant generals hosted a feast in their cave, inviting the six kings to drink. They slaughtered oxen and horses, sacrificed to heaven and earth, and had strange creatures dance and sing. Everyone ate until they were completely drunk.  As they sent the six kings away, the generals rewarded the chieftains and, leaning under the shade of the iron-plated bridge, fell asleep in an instant. The four valiant generals and their troops surrounded them, daring not to speak loudly. Suddenly, two men appeared in the Monkey King's sleep, carrying a decree bearing the words "Sun Wukong" written upon it. They approached without hesitation, bound him with rope, and snatched away his soul. They staggered along, dragging him toward a city. 

The Monkey King gradually sobered up and, looking up, saw a plaque on the city gate with three large characters: "Realm of the Underworld." The Monkey King suddenly understood, "The Realm of the Underworld is where the King of Hell resides. What brings me here?" The two men said, "Your earthly lifespan is coming to an end. We have a decree to lead you here."  

The Monkey King retorted, "Old Sun transcends the three realms and is not within the five elements. He is no longer under his jurisdiction. How dare you come for me?" The two grim reapers tugged and pulled, determined to drag him inside. The Monkey King, enraged, pulled out a precious object from his ear, flicking it, it grew thick and long. With a slight raise of his hand, he smashed the two grim reapers into a bloody paste. He broke free from his bonds, tossed the rope aside, and, wielding his staff, charged into the city.

This frightened the bull-headed ghost to hide and the horse-faced ghost to run in all directions. The ghost soldiers fled to the Hall of Ten Kings and shouted, "Your Majesty! Disaster! Disaster! A hairy-faced thunder god is attacking!"

I'm informing you, my dear, that a truly pitiful incident has occurred in our apartment, something truly worthy of pity! Today, at five in the morning, little Goroshkov died. I don't know exactly what from, perhaps scarlet fever, who knows! I went to visit the Goroshkovs. Well, mother, oh how wretched they are! And what a mess! And no wonder: the whole family lives in one room, only partitioned off with screens for decency's sake. They already have a coffin – simple, but quite pretty; they bought it ready-made, the boy was nine years old; he was said to have shown promise. And it's just heartbreaking to look at them, Varvara! The mother isn't crying, but so gloomy, poor thing. Perhaps it's even easier for them that one is gone; they still have two others left, a babe and a little girl, about six years old. What a pleasure, indeed, to see a child suffering, especially one's own child, and not even to be able to help! The father is sitting in his old, greasy frock, on a broken-down chair. Tears are streaming down his face, though, perhaps, not from grief, but out of habit, his eyes are weeping. Such a peculiar fellow! He blushes all red when you speak to him, stammers and doesn't know what to say. The little girl, his daughter, stands by the coffin, so sad, pensive, poor thing! And I don't like it, Varvara, when a child is pensive; it's unpleasant to look at! Some rag doll lies on the floor by her, – she's not playing; she holds her finger on her lips; she stands there – won't move. The mistress gave her a candy; she took it, but didn't eat it. It's sad, Varvara – isn't it?

And he glanced at the clock on the cabinet, which ticked away. "Heavenly Father!" he thought, it was half past six, and the hands were moving calmly forward, it was even half past, it was approaching three-quarters. Shouldn't the alarm have rung? From the bed one could see that it was set for four o'clock correctly; certainly it had rung. Yes, but was it possible to sleep through this furniture-shaking ringing? Well, he hadn't slept calmly, but probably all the more soundly. But what should he do now? The next train was at seven o'clock; to catch it, he would have had to rush senselessly, and the collection was still not packed, and he himself did not feel particularly fresh and agile. And even if he caught the train, a thunderbolt from the boss was unavoidable, because the business assistant had waited at the five o'clock train and had long since reported his absence. It was a creature of the boss, without backbone and intelligence. Now, what if he called in sick? But that would be extremely embarrassing and suspicious, for Gregor had not even been ill during his five years of service. Certainly the boss would come with the insurance doctor, would make accusations to his parents about the lazy son and cut off all objections with the reference to the insurance doctor, for whom there were only perfectly healthy, but work-shy people anyway. And would he, by the way, be entirely wrong in this case? Gregor actually felt, apart from a sleepiness that was really superfluous after the long sleep, quite well and even had a particularly strong appetite.

Anxiety was the beginning, anxiety and lust, and a horrified curiosity for what was to come. Night reigned, and his senses listened; for from afar approached a tumult, a din, a mixture of noise: rattling, crashing and a dull booming, shrill cries added to it, and a specific howling in a drawn-out u-sound, all pervaded and grotesquely sweet overlain by deep, whirring, relentlessly persistent flute playing, which shamelessly intrusive enchanted the bowels. But he knew a word, dark, yet naming what was coming: "The foreign God!" A nauseating glow kindled: there he recognized the highlands, similar to those around his summer house. And in fragmented light, from a wooded height, between trunks and moss-covered rock fragments it writhed and tumbled down in a whirl: people, animals, a swarm, a raging pack, and flooded the plateau with bodies, flames, turmoil and a reeling, whirling dance. Women, stumbling over their long fur garments hanging from their belts, shook rattles over their groaningly thrown-back heads, swung blazing torches and bare daggers, held flickering snakes in the middle of their bodies, or carried their screaming breasts in both hands. Men, with horns over their foreheads, clad in furs and bristly with skin, bent their necks and raised their arms and thighs, let iron kettledrums resonate, and struck furiously on drums, while smooth boys with smeared staffs prodded goats, to whose horns they clung and from whose leaps they let themselves be dragged joyfully. And the devotees cried out the call in soft harmonies and drawn-out u-sounds at the end, sweet and wild at once, like nothing ever heard: here it rang out, into the air lifted, as if from deer, and there it was given back, multi-voiced, in a wild triumph, they spurred each other on to dance and flinging their limbs and never let it fall silent. – It’s a long story, Avdotya Romanovna. It’s, how shall I put it, a sort of theory, the same sort of thing that makes me think, for instance, that a single act of villainy is permissible if the ultimate goal is good. One evil and a hundred good deeds! It’s also, of course, offensive to a young man with dignity and excessive pride to know that if there had only been three thousand, his whole career, his whole future, the formation of his life’s purpose, would have been different, and yet those three thousand are missing. Add to that the irritation from hunger, from the cramped apartment, from the construction site, from the sharp awareness of the beauty of his social standing, but also from the status of his sister and mother. Above all, however, it’s vanity, pride and vanity, and yet, who knows, maybe with good inclinations… I don’t blame him, you understand, please don’t think that; it’s not my business either. There was also his own little theory – a theory, you see – according to which people are divided, as it were, into material and exceptional people, that is, people for whom, due to their high position, the law is not written, but who, on the contrary, create laws for the rest of the people, the material, the common folk. Nothing, a rather trivial theory; une théorie, c'est une autre. [88] Napoleon captivated him terribly, that is, what really captivated him was that many brilliant people did not pay attention to single acts of evil and walked over them without thinking. He, it seems, imagined himself to be a brilliant man – he was, in fact, quite convinced of this for a while. He suffered a lot and still suffers from the thought that he was able to come up with the theory, but he couldn’t simply step over it without thinking, and therefore he wasn’t a genius. Well, and that, for a young man with pride, is humiliating, especially in our age…

Mother never came at night—or did she? Once, she did. I had screamed and screamed, and Mademoiselle and Sieversen, the housekeeper, and Georg, the coachman, had come, but it hadn’t helped. Finally, they had sent the carriage to my parents, who were at a grand ball, I think for the Crown Prince. Suddenly, I heard it pulling into the courtyard, and I went still, sitting and staring at the door. Then there was a rustling in the other rooms, and Mother came in wearing her grand ball gown, not even noticing it, and nearly ran in, dropping her white fur behind her. She scooped me up in her bare arms, and I felt, astonished and enchanted like never before, her hair and her small, well-tended face and the cold stones in her ears and the silk at the edge of her shoulders, which smelled of flowers. And we stayed there, weeping tenderly and kissing each other, until we felt that Father was there and that we had to separate. “He has a high fever,” I heard Mother say softly, and Father took my hand and felt my pulse. He was in his Huntsman’s uniform with the beautiful, wide, watered blue band of the Elephant. “What nonsense to call us,” he said into the room, without looking at me.
