Evening came on. The wind began to rustle more strongly in the old firs, a powerful wind rushed through and roared through the thick boughs. It sounded so beautiful to Heidi's ears and heart that she became quite joyful and hopped and skipped around the firs as if she had experienced unheard-of happiness. Grandfather stood in the doorway and watched the child. Now a sharp bleating sound rang out. Heidi stopped her jumps, and Grandfather stepped out. From above they came leaping down, goats one after another, like a hunt, and in the middle of it Peter. With a cry of joy Heidi dashed into the midst of the flock and greeted her old friends from this morning, one by one. When they reached the hut, everything fell still, and from the herd two beautiful, slender goats, one white and one brown, came to Grandfather and licked his hands, for he always held a little salt in them, as he did every evening to welcome his two little animals. Peter disappeared with his flock. Heidi stroked one goat gently and then the other, jumping around them to stroke them on the other side, and was completely happy and joyful about the animals. "Are they ours, Grandfather? Are they both ours? Do they come into the stable? Will they always stay with us?" Heidi asked, one question after the other, in her delight, and Grandfather could barely squeeze his constant "Yes, yes!" between one question and the next. When the goats had licked their salt, the old man said, "Go and fetch your little bowl and the bread."

Perhaps some readers will think that my young man was a sickly, ecstatic, underdeveloped soul, a pale dreamer, a frail, emaciated creature. On the contrary, Alyosha was at that time a stately, rosy-cheeked young man with a bright gaze, radiating health at nineteen. He was even very handsome, well-built, of medium height, dark-haired, with a regular, though slightly elongated oval face, with shining dark-gray widely spaced eyes, very pensive and seemingly very calm. They might say that red cheeks don't prevent fanaticism or mysticism; but it seems to me that Alyosha was even more of a realist than anyone. Oh, of course, in the monastery he completely believed in miracles, but, it seems to me, miracles never truly disconcert a realist. It is not miracles that incline a realist to faith. A true realist, if he is not a believer, will always find in himself the strength and ability not to believe even in a miracle, and if a miracle becomes an undeniable fact before him, he will rather not believe his senses than admit the fact. If he does admit it, he will admit it as a natural fact, but one that was previously unknown to him. In a realist, faith is not born of a miracle, but a miracle is born of faith. If a realist once believes, then, by the very nature of his realism, he must necessarily admit a miracle. Apostle Thomas declared that he would not believe until he saw, and when he saw, he said: “My Lord and my God!” Did the miracle make him believe? It is most likely that no, but he believed only because he desired to believe, and perhaps already believed completely, in the secret recesses of his being, even when he said: “I will not believe until I see.”

Once, when it was almost dark over this story, I was close to telling Maman about the ‘Hand’: in that moment I could have done it. I was already drawing breath to begin, but then I remembered how well I had understood the servant, that he hadn’t been able to look at their faces. And I was afraid, despite the darkness, of Maman’s face, should it see what I had seen. I took a quick breath again, so it would appear as though I had wanted nothing else. A few years later, after that strange night in the gallery at Urnekloster, I went around for days trying to confide in young Erik. But he had withdrawn completely from me after our nocturnal conversation, he avoided me; I believe he despised me. And precisely for that reason I wanted to tell him about the ‘Hand’. I imagined that I would gain his opinion (and that I desperately wished for, for some reason), if I could make it comprehensible to him that I had really experienced it. But Erik was so skilled at dodging the subject that it never came to pass. And then we traveled, and so, strangely enough, it is the first time that I (and finally, only to myself) tell an event that now lies far back in my childhood.

One day, the Master was playing with his disciples at the front of the Sanxing Cave as the evening light faded. The Master said, "Sun Wukong, is it done?" Sun Wukong said, "Many thanks to Master for your kindness, disciple has fulfilled his task and is ready to ascend to heaven." The Master said, "Show me your flying skills." Sun Wukong used his magic and with a heave, did a somersault, jumping several feet off the ground. He stepped onto the clouds and headed off, it took a moment's time, then he returned, no more than three miles away, landing in front of them and clasped his hands together saying, "Master, this is what it means to fly and ride the clouds." The Master laughed and said, "This is not yet considered riding the clouds, only climbing them. As the old saying goes, 'Immortals stroll the North Sea in the morning and Mount Cangwu in the evening.' To be like you, only going a half day's journey and not reaching three miles, it's not even considered climbing the clouds!" Sun Wukong said, "How is it 'strolling the North Sea in the morning and Mount Cangwu in the evening'?" The Master said, "Those who can truly ride the clouds, start their journey in the early morning from the North Sea, travel over the East Sea, the West Sea, the South Sea, and return to Mount Cangwu. Mount Cangwu is just another name for the North Sea." To have traveled beyond the four seas and covered them all in a single day, that's when one can truly be said to ride the clouds." Sun Wukong said, "That's difficult! Extremely difficult!" The Master said, "There's nothing difficult in the world, only those who lack the will." Upon hearing this, Sun Wukong bowed his head and said, "Master, 'one must be thorough in one's pursuits.' In that case, I would like to ask for your great compassion. Teach me this technique of riding the clouds, I promise not to forget your kindness." The Master said, "All immortals who ride the clouds start with a stomping motion, but you haven't done so. You simply jumped up after doing a somersault. I'll teach you my 'cloud-hopping' technique, based on that move." Sun Wukong bowed again, begging further, and the Master gave him a spell, saying, "This cloud, focus your mind, recite the mantra, clench your fist, shake your body, and jump. With a single somersault, you'll cover 100,000 or 80,000 miles!" The disciples heard this and burst into laughter, saying, "Sun Wukong is lucky! If you master this, you can work as a delivery man, carry messages, even become a messenger, and have endless opportunities for making a living!" As night fell, the Master and his disciples returned to their respective caves. That very night, Sun Wukong focused his mind and practiced, mastering the cloud-hopping technique. From then on, he could travel freely, boundless and carefree, enjoying the eternal bliss of immortality.

“Mother, Mother,” Gregor said softly and looked up at her. For a moment the traveling salesman had entirely disappeared from his mind; however, he couldn’t help but snap his jaws several times at the empty air when he saw the flowing coffee. At that, his mother would scream anew, flee the table, and throw herself into her husband’s arms as he came running. But Gregor had no time for his parents now; the traveling salesman was already on the stairs; his chin on the railing, he looked back one last time. Gregor took a run at him, hoping to catch him as quickly as possible; the traveling salesman must have sensed something, for he leaped over several steps and disappeared; “Hmph!” he cried out, the sound echoing through the whole stairwell. Unfortunately, this flight of the traveling salesman seemed to completely confuse his father, who had been relatively composed until now, for instead of chasing after the traveling salesman himself or at least not hindering Gregor in his pursuit, he grabbed the traveling salesman’s cane, which he had left on a chair with his hat and overcoat, snatched a large newspaper from the table with his left hand, and, with stamping feet, began to drive Gregor back into his room by swinging the cane and newspaper. No pleading from Gregor helped, no pleading was even understood; even when he bowed his head as humbly as possible, his father only stamped his feet harder.  Across the room, the mother, despite the cold weather, had opened a window, and leaning out, she pressed her face far beyond the windowpane into her hands. A strong draft blew in between the alley and the stairwell, the window curtains flew open, the newspapers on the table rustled, and individual sheets danced across the floor. Unrelenting, the father pressed on, letting out hissing sounds like a wild animal. Now Gregor hadn’t had any practice in backing up; it was really very slow. If only he could have turned around, he would have been in his room at once, but he feared that the father’s patience might be exhausted by this time-consuming maneuver, and yet every moment threatened a deadly blow from the cane in his father’s hand to his back or his head. Finally, however, Gregor had no choice but to turn, for he realized with horror that he didn’t even understand how to keep his direction while backing up. And so he began, under constant anxious glances at his father, to turn as quickly as possible, in reality, however, only very slowly.  Perhaps the father sensed his good intentions, for he did not hinder him, but even directed the turning movement from a distance with the tip of his cane. If only it hadn’t been for this unbearable hissing of the father! Gregor completely lost his composure. He was almost completely turned around when, always listening for that hissing, he even got lost and turned back a little. But when he finally managed to get his head in front of the doorway, it turned out that his body was too wide to pass through without difficulty. It naturally wouldn’t have occurred to his father, in his present state, to open the other door leaf to create a passage for Gregor. His fixed idea was simply that Gregor had to get back into his room as quickly as possible. He would never have allowed the cumbersome preparations that Gregor needed to straighten himself up and perhaps get through the door in that way. Perhaps, as if there were no obstacle, he now drove Gregor forward with particular noise; it no longer sounded like the voice of just one father behind Gregor; now there was truly no more fun, and Gregor pushed himself – whatever happened – into the door. One side of his body lifted, he was wedged in the doorway, his side was completely rubbed raw, ugly stains remained on the white door, he was stuck and couldn’t move on his own; his legs on one side hung trembling in the air, while the ones on the other were painfully pressed to the ground – then his father gave him a truly welcome, strong push from behind, and he flew, bleeding profusely, far into his room. The door was slammed shut with the cane, and finally, there was silence.

I am going because of passion, because of a calling, because I have a grand goal. You think I’ll get seventy-five thousand and immediately buy a carriage? No, sir! I would have to wear a third-year-old frock coat and abandon all my club acquaintances. We have few who can stand the test, even though they are all usurers. And I want to withstand it. The main thing here is to see it through to the end — that’s the whole point! Ptitsyn slept on the street at seventeen, sold pen knives, and started from a penny; now he has sixty thousand, but only after what a workout! I’ll jump over that whole workout and start straight from capital; in fifteen years they’ll say, “Here’s Ivlogin, the king of the Jews!” You tell me that I am not an original person. Notice, dear prince, that there’s nothing more offensive to a person of our time and breed than to tell him that he is not original, weak-willed, without special talents, and an ordinary person. You didn’t even deem me a good scoundrel, and, you know, I wanted to eat you for that the other day! You offended me more than Epantchin, who considers me (and without conversation, without temptation, in the simplicity of his soul, notice that!) capable of selling him his wife! This, father, has been bothering me for a long time, and I want money. When I have money, you know, I will be an utterly original person. Money is the most insidious and hateful thing, because it even gives talent. And it will continue to give it until the end of the world. You might say that this is all childish or, perhaps, poetry, — well, the more fun it will be for me, but the deed will still be done. I will see it through and endure. Rira bien qui rira le dernier! 1 Why does Epantchin offend me so much? Out of spite, do you think? Never. Simply because I am too insignificant. Well then… But enough, it’s time. Kolya has already stuck his nose out twice: he’s inviting you to dinner. And I’m going to the yard. I’ll sometimes drop by to see you. You’ll have it good with us; now you’ll be accepted into the family. Just be careful not to let it slip. It seems to me that we will either be friends or enemies. And what do you think, prince, if I had kissed your hand the other day (as sincerely as I offered), would I have become your enemy afterwards?

After this manner, he had removed the woman's objections, the quiet conversation at the window became too long for him; he tapped with his knuckles on the podium and then with his fist. The student glanced briefly over the woman's shoulder at K., but he let himself not be disturbed, indeed he even pressed closer to the woman and embraced her. She lowered her head deeply, as if listening to him attentively, he kissed her, as she bent down, loudly on the neck, without interrupting his speech much. K. saw in this the tyranny that the student exercised over him, as the woman had complained, stood up, and paced the room. He considered, with sidelong glances at the student, how he could get him out of there as quickly as possible, and it was not unwelcome to him when the student, apparently disturbed by K.'s pacing, which had by now become a trampling, remarked: "If you are impatient, you can leave. You could have left earlier, no one would have missed you. Yes, you should even have left, and that right from my entrance, and quickly." This remark may have expressed all possible anger, but it also contained the arrogance of the future magistrate speaking to a disliked defendant. K. stood very close to him and said with a smile: "I am impatient, that's true, but this impatience will be most easily eliminated by your leaving us. But if you have perhaps come to study – I heard that you are a student – then I will gladly make room for you and leave with the woman. You will have to study a lot more, however, before you become a judge. I don't know your legal system very well yet, but I assume that it's not enough to simply deliver those coarse speeches, which you already know how to do quite shamelessly." "One shouldn't have let him run around so freely," said the student, as if to give the woman an explanation for K.'s insulting speech, "it was a mistake. I told the examining magistrate. One should have kept him in his room at least between the interrogations. The examining magistrate is sometimes incomprehensible." "Useless talk," said K. and reached for the woman, "come." "Oh no," said the student, "no, no, you won't get her," and with a strength one wouldn't have attributed to him, he lifted her onto one arm and ran towards the door, bending his back and gazing at her tenderly. There was a certain fear of K. in this, nonetheless, he dared to provoke him further by stroking and pressing the woman's arm with his free hand. K. ran a few steps alongside him, ready to grab him and, if necessary, strangle him, when the woman said: "It's no use, the examining magistrate is going to fetch me, I'm not allowed to go with you, this little monster," she slapped the student's face, "this little monster won't let me go." "And you don't want to be freed!" K. cried and placed his hand on the student's shoulder, who snapped his teeth at her. "No!" cried the woman and pushed K. away with both hands, "no, no, not that, what are you thinking about! That would be my ruin. Let him be, oh please, let him be. He is only carrying out the examining magistrate's orders and bringing me to him." "Then let him run and I will never want to see you again," said K. angrily, overwhelmed with disappointment, and gave the student a shove in the back, so that he stumbled for a moment, only to then jump even higher with his burden, pleased that he hadn't been knocked down. K. walked slowly after them, he realized that this was the first undeniable defeat he had suffered from these people. It was naturally no reason to worry, he only suffered this defeat because he had sought out the fight. If he stayed at home and led his usual life, he was a thousand times superior to any of these people and could sweep any of them off his path with a single kick. And he pictured the most ridiculous scene imaginable, which would happen for example, if this pathetic student, this puffed-up child, this crooked beard wearer would kneel before Elsa's bed and beg for mercy with folded hands. K. liked this idea so much that he decided, if only the opportunity arose, to take the student to Elsa sometime.

His sleep was fleeting; the deliciously monotonous days were separated by short nights full of happy unrest. Although he would retire early, for when Tadzio had disappeared from the scene at nine o’clock, the day seemed finished to him, yet at the first glimmer of dawn, a delicate, penetrating alarm would awaken him; his heart remembered its adventure, it no longer allowed him to lie in the pillows, he would rise, and lightly wrapped against the chill of the early morning, he would sit by the open window, awaiting the sunrise. The wonderful event filled his soul, consecrated by sleep, with devotion. The sky, the earth, and the sea were still shrouded in a ghostly, glassy twilight; still, a fading star swam in the emptiness. But a breeze arrived, a buoyant message from unattainable dwelling places, that Eos was rising from the side of her husband, and that first, sweet blush of the most distant celestial and marine strokes occurred, through which the becoming sensuality of creation manifested. The goddess approached, the nymph-thief who had snatched away Kleitos, Kephalos, and despite the envy of all the Olympians, enjoyed the love of the beautiful Orion. A rose-shower began at the edge of the world, an unimaginably lovely radiance and blooming, childish clouds, clarified, illuminated, floated like serving Cupids in the rosy, bluish fragrance. Purple fell upon the sea, which seemed to swell and push it forward, golden spears shot up from below to the height of the heavens, the radiance became fire, silently, with divine might, surges of flame and molten heat welled up, and with thundering hooves, the sacred steeds of the brother climbed the circle of the earth. Bathed in the splendor of the god, the Lonely Watcher sat, he closed his eyes and let the glory kiss his eyelids. Former feelings, early, delicious yearnings of the heart, which had died in the strict service of his life and now so strangely returned—he recognized them with a bewildered, astonished smile. He mused, he dreamed, slowly his lips formed a name, and still smiling, with his face turned upward, his hands folded in his lap, he fell asleep in his chair once more.

K. stood stock-still and looked down at the floor. For the moment he was still free, he could still go on and through one of the three small, dark wooden doors, not far in front of him, escape. It would just mean that he hadn't understood, or that he had understood but didn't want to care. If he turned around, however, he would be trapped, for then he would have admitted that he understood well, that he was indeed the one called, and that he wanted to follow. Had the priest called out again, K. would certainly have left, but as everything remained silent as long as K. waited, he turned his head slightly, because he wanted to see what the priest was doing now. He stood calmly on the pulpit as before, but it was clearly visible that he had noticed K.'s head movement. It would have been a childish game of hide-and-seek if K. hadn't now turned completely around. He did so and was beckoned closer by the priest with a flick of his finger. Now that everything could happen openly, he ran - he did it also out of curiosity and to shorten the affair - with long, sweeping strides towards the pulpit. At the first pews he stopped, but the distance seemed too great for the priest; he stretched out his hand and pointed with his sharply lowered index finger to a spot just in front of the pulpit. K. followed suit; he had to bend his head back far to still see the priest. "You are Josef K.," said the priest and raised a hand on the railing in an indefinite movement. "Yes," said K., he thought of how openly he had always pronounced his name, it had been a burden to him for some time now, and even now people he met for the first time knew his name, how nice it was to be introduced first and then to be recognized. "You are accused," said the priest, especially softly. "Yes," said K., "I have been informed of that." "Then you are the one I'm looking for," said the priest. "I am the prison chaplain." "Oh, so," said K. "I called you here," said the priest, "to speak with you." "I didn't know that," said K. "I came here to show a visitor from Italy the cathedral." "Leave the unimportant matters aside," said the priest. "What do you have in your hand? Is it a prayer book?" "No," replied K., "it's an album of the city's sights." "Lay it down," said the priest. K. threw it away so violently that it opened and slid across the floor with crushed pages. "Do you know that your trial is going badly?" asked the priest. "It seems so to me too," said K. "I've tried my best, but so far without success. However, I haven't finished the appeal yet." "How do you imagine the end?" asked the priest. "Before, I thought it had to end well," said K., "now I sometimes doubt it myself. I don't know how it will end. Do you know?" "No," said the priest, "but I fear it will end badly. They hold you guilty. Your trial may not even get past a lower court. They at least provisionally consider you guilty." "But I'm not guilty," said K., "it's a mistake. How can a human being be guilty at all? We're all human beings here, one like the other." "That's true," said the priest, "but that's what the guilty always say." "Do you also have a prejudice against me?" asked K. "I have no prejudice against you," said the priest. "Thank you," said K., "but all the others involved in the proceedings have a prejudice against me. They even instill it in those who are uninvolved. My position is becoming increasingly difficult." "You misunderstand the facts," said the priest, "the verdict doesn't come all at once, the process gradually leads to the verdict." "So it is," said K. and lowered his head. "What do you intend to do next in your case?" asked the priest. "I want to seek help," said K. and raised his head to see how the priest assessed it. "There are still some possibilities I haven't used." "You are seeking too much outside help," said the priest disapprovingly, "and especially from women. Don't you see that it is not the true help?" "Sometimes and even often I could agree with you," said K., "but not always. Women have great power. If I could persuade some of the women I know to work together for me, I would break through. Especially with this court, which consists almost entirely of womanizers. Show the investigating judge a woman from afar, and he will rush, in order to arrive on time, over the judge's table and the accused." The priest leaned his head against the railing, now the canopy of the pulpit seemed to press down on him. What kind of storm must it be outside? It was no longer a gloomy day, it was deep night. Not a single stained-glass window was able to break the dark wall with even a glimmer. And just now the church warden began to extinguish the candles on the main altar, one by one. It was shouted in anger, but at the same time like someone who sees someone falling and, because he himself is startled, shouts out inadvertently, without will.

Mrs. Margarete Brigge had always, as far as I can remember, been a tall, inaccessible old woman. I can't imagine she was any younger than the chamberlain. She lived her life right amongst us, without considering anyone else. She was dependent on none of us and always had a companion of sorts, an aging Countess Oxe, whom she had obligated indefinitely through some unspecified kindness. This must have been a singular exception, because doing good was not her way. She disliked children and animals were not allowed near her. I don't know if she loved anything else. It was said that she had been betrothed to the handsome Felix Lichnowski when she was very young, who then met such a cruel end in Frankfurt. And indeed, after her death, there was a portrait of the prince, which, if I'm not mistaken, was returned to the family. Perhaps, I think now, she yearned for a different, more brilliant life, her natural one, amidst this increasingly rural existence that life on Ulsgaard had become year after year. It's hard to say if she mourned it. Perhaps she scorned it for not having come to pass, for having missed the opportunity to live it with skill and talent. She had absorbed all this within herself and had placed over it bowls, many, brittle, slightly metallic-looking bowls, each new and cool to the touch. Occasionally, though, she would betray herself with a naive impatience, not being sufficiently noticed; at my time, she would suddenly choke at the table in some conspicuous and intricate way, which ensured the attention of all and made her appear, if only for a moment, as sensational and captivating as she might have been in the grand scheme of things. However, I suspect that my father was the only one who took these all too frequent occurrences seriously. He would look at her, politely leaning forward, one could see how he offered her his own, proper windpipe in thought, and put it completely at her disposal. The chamberlain, of course, had naturally stopped eating; he took a small sip of wine and abstained from any opinion.

Mrs. Margarete Brigge had always been, as far as I can remember, a tall, inaccessible old woman. I can't imagine her being any younger than the chamberlain. She lived her life right among us, taking no notice of anyone. She was dependent on none of us and always had some kind of companion, an aging Countess Oxe, whom she had obligated herself to indefinitely through some unspecified act of kindness. This must have been a singular exception, because doing good was not otherwise her way. She disliked children, and animals were not allowed near her. I don't know if she loved anything else. It was said that she had been engaged to the handsome Felix Lichnowski when she was very young, who then met a cruel death in Frankfurt. And indeed, after her death, there was a portrait of the Prince, which, if I'm not mistaken, was returned to the family. Perhaps, I think now, she regretted this withdrawn rural life, which Ulsgaard's life had become more and more each year, a different, brilliant one: her natural one. It's hard to say if she mourned it. Perhaps she scorned it for not having come to pass, for having missed the opportunity to be lived with skill and talent. She had absorbed all this so deeply within herself and had placed upon it shells, many, brittle, slightly metallic-looking shells, each of which presented a new and cool outer layer. Sometimes, however, she betrayed herself with a naive impatience at not being sufficiently noticed; in my time she could suddenly choke at the table in some clear and complicated way, which ensured the attention of all and made her, for a moment at least, appear as sensational and exciting as she might have been on a grander scale.  However, I suspect that my father was the only one who took these all too frequent occurrences seriously. He looked at her, politely leaning forward, one could tell how he offered her his own, orderly windpipe in thought, placing it entirely at her disposal. The chamberlain, of course, had also stopped eating; he took a small sip of wine and abstained from any opinion.

Seeing that the street sweepers weren't going to budge from my words, because, they said, it was already late, and perhaps they'd even be angry that they hadn't come sooner, I felt offended, and I made up my mind, and started to inquire. Having found out yesterday, I went today. I came the first time – he wasn't there. After a while I came again – they wouldn't let me in. The third time I came – they let me in. I began to tell him everything as it happened, and he started pacing the room and beating himself in the chest: “What are you doing to me, you robbers!” he said. “If I had known about this, I would have demanded a guard!” Then he rushed out, called someone, and began talking to them in the corner, and then he came back to me and started questioning and scolding me. And he scolded me a lot. But I told him everything and said that from my words yesterday, you didn't dare to answer me and that you didn't recognize me. And he started running again, beating himself in the chest, getting angry, and pacing, and when they told him about you, he said, “Well, climb over the partition, sit there until further notice, don't move, no matter what you hear, and bring me a stool yourself,” and locked me in. “Perhaps,” he said, “I’ll ask you something.” And when they brought Nikolai, he led me out after you: “I'll demand to see you again,” he said, “and I’ll ask you more.”

Fathers and teachers, I think: “What is hell?” I reason thus: “Suffering over what can no longer be loved.” Once, in the infinite being, immeasurable by time or space, a certain spiritual being, upon its appearance on earth, was given the ability to say to itself: “I am, and I love.” Once, only once, was it given the moment of active, living love, and for that it was given earthly life, with its times and seasons. But what: this happy being rejected the priceless gift, did not value it, did not love, looked down upon it and remained insensitive. 

Such a one, already departed from the earth, sees both Abraham's bosom and converses with Abraham, as indicated to us in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, and contemplates Paradise, and can ascend to God, but precisely that is his torment, that he will ascend to God, unloving, having spurned the love of those who loved. For he sees clearly and says to himself: "Now I know and even though I yearned to love, there will be no movement in my love, there will be no sacrifice, for earthly life is finished and Abraham will not come even with a drop of living water (that is, a new earthly life, the former and active) to quench the flame of the spiritual thirst with which I am now burning, having neglected it on earth; there is no life anymore, and time will not be!” Though he would be willing to give his life for others, it is no longer possible, for the life which could have been sacrificed for love has passed. And now there is a chasm between that life and this being."

They speak of the material fire of hell: I do not investigate this secret and am afraid, but I think that if there were a material fire, they would truly rejoice in it, because, I imagine, in material suffering even for a moment the most terrible spiritual suffering would be forgotten. And it is impossible to take away this spiritual suffering from them, for this suffering is not external, but within them. And if it were possible to take it away, I think they would become even more unhappy. For even if they were forgiven by the righteous from Paradise, who see their suffering, and called to themselves, loving infinitely, they would still multiply their torments, because they would stir in them even stronger the flame of the longing for reciprocal, active, and grateful love, which is no longer possible.

In the humility of my heart, I think, however, that the very awareness of this impossibility would eventually serve them as some relief, for, accepting the love of the righteous with the impossibility of reciprocating it, in this submission and in the act of this humility, they would finally find as it were an image of that active love which they neglected on earth, and as it were some action, similar to it…

I grieve, brothers and friends, that I cannot express this clearly. But woe to those who have destroyed themselves on earth, woe to suicides! I think that there can be no one more unhappy than these. They say that sin is to pray to God for them, and the church outwardly seems to reject them, but I think in the secret of my soul, that it is possible to pray for them. Christ will not be angry for love, after all. For such I have inwardly prayed throughout my life, I confess to you, fathers and teachers, and even now I pray for them every day.

Zhang Shao said, “Li Ding, we two are truly congenial, need no grand rituals or gold-rimmed cups. Let us simply exchange verses, see how our conversation flows like a fisherman and a woodcutter chatting by the shore.” Li Ding said, “Brother Zhang speaks with great wisdom, please recite first.”

“A boat rests within the green waters, smoke and waves rippling. I dwell deep in the mountains and open plains. I prefer the spring waters rising over bridges, most pity the peaks shrouded in the mist of dawn.  Fresh carp from Dragon Gate are cooked at times, dried firewood is consumed, embers flicker daily. Fishing nets catch enough to sustain my old age, carrying ropes are my two concerns to fill my years. I lie back in a small boat, watching geese in flight, on a grassy path, I slant a willow branch and listen to the cries of cranes. I have no part in the clamor of the marketplace, in the affairs of the world, my tracks are seldom found. By the creekside, linen dries like brocade, upon the stone, the axe grinds sharp like a blade. Under the autumn moon's soft glow, I fish alone. In the quiet spring mountains, no one meets me. I catch many fish, exchange them for wine, to drink with my wife. The leftover firewood I use to fill the pot, to share with my son.”

Zhang Shao said, "Li Ding, we two are truly kindred spirits, we need not ornate wine cups or carved tables. Casual verses are nothing special, let's each compose a few lines and see how our fisherman-scholar conversation fares?" Li Ding said, "Brother Zhang, you speak most wisely, please recite first."

"The boat rests on the green water amidst ripples,
My dwelling is in the deep mountains and open fields.
I favor the creek bridge where spring water rises,
Most fond of the misty clouds over the rock peaks at dawn.

Dragon Gate carp, when freshly caught, are simmered,
Insect-eaten dry wood crackles in the daily hearth.
My fishing nets of various types suffice to sustain my old age,
The carrying rope, two things enough to fill my life.

Small boat reclining, gazing at flying geese,
On the grass path, I lean and listen to the cries of the cranes.
In the court of tongues, I have no place,
In the affairs of the world, my trace is scarce.

By the creek, I hang drying cloth like silk,
On the stone, I sharpen the axe, like a honed blade.
Under the autumn moon's bright glow, I fish alone,
In the spring mountains, I am in silent solitude.

I trade fish for wine, drink with my wife,
With leftover firewood, I brew pot liquor to share with my children."

Zhang Shao said, "Li Ding, we two are truly kindred spirits, needing no polished words or ornate vessels. Let us simply exchange a few verses and see how our humble conversation flows." Li Ding replied, "Brother Zhang speaks with wisdom. Please, Brother, begin first." 

"My boat rests within the verdant water, amidst smoke and waves,
My home lies in the deep mountains, amidst vast wildernesses.
I favor the spring water rising by the creek bridge,
Most I pity the rocks and peaks shrouded in the dawn's mist. 
Fresh carp from Longmen, cooked at the time of their season,
Dry, worm-eaten firewood, ever burning on the hearth.
A myriad fishing nets, enough to sustain my old age,
A shoulder pole and two tasks, enough to fill my remaining years.

My small boat lies on its side, gazing at the flying geese,
Along the grassy path, I lean against the willow, listening to the cry of the crane.
Within the marketplace of words, I have no share,
In the world's affairs, my trace is seldom found. 

Silk like cloth hangs to dry by the creek,
My axe, honed upon the stone, sharp as a blade.
Under the autumn moon's bright radiance, I fish alone,
In the spring mountains, silent and deserted, no one encounters me. 
With plenty of fish, I share wine with my wife,
With leftover firewood, I imbibe a flask with my children."

Little boat reclining, gazing at flying geese,

Aschenbach was tempted to threaten him with his finger. "But I advise you, Kritobulos," he thought, smiling, "take a year's journey! For that is at least the amount of time you need to recover." And then he ate large, fully ripe strawberries, which he had bought from a vendor. It had become very warm, though the sun was unable to pierce the haze in the sky. Laziness held the mind captive, while the senses enjoyed the immense and intoxicating entertainment of the sea's stillness.  To guess, to investigate, which name it was that sounded roughly like "Adgio," seemed to the serious man a suitable, perfectly fulfilling task and occupation. And with the help of some Polish memories, he determined that it must be "Tadzio," an abbreviation of "Tadeusz" and pronounced "Tadziu" when calling out. 

Tadzio was swimming. Aschenbach, who had lost sight of him, discovered his head, his arm, with which he was rowing, far out at sea; for the sea might be shallow quite a distance out. But already one seemed concerned for him, already women's voices called out to him from the huts, uttering again that name that dominated the beach almost like a motto, and with its soft, prolonged u-sound at the end, had something both sweet and wild: "Tadziu, Tadziu!" He obeyed, he ran, churning the water to foam with his feet, his head thrown back, swept back by the waves; and to see the living form, before-manly handsome and wild, with dripping curls and beautiful like a tender god, emerging from the depths of heaven and sea, escaping the elements: This sight gave mythical ideas, it was like poetic knowledge from primeval times, from the origin of form and the birth of the gods. Aschenbach listened with closed eyes to this song resonating within him; and again he thought that it was good here and that he wanted to stay.

"Being a righteous monk means enduring hardship and suffering, that's how you become a disciple." Eight Precepts said, "Brother, look at how heavy this baggage is!"  The行者 said, "Brother, since I've had you and Sha Seng, I haven't had to carry it myself, so how would I know how heavy it is?" Eight Precepts said, "Brother, take a look: four lengths of yellow rattan, eight ropes of varying lengths. You need to protect against rain and sun, layering the felt three or four times. The burden is prone to slipping, so you nail both ends. The nine-ring staff has bronze inlaid iron, the large cloak is wrapped in rattan and hemp. With so much baggage, it's difficult for a lazy pig like me to carry it every day, and you, following the Master as a disciple, make me the laborer!" The行者 laughed, "Fool, who are you talking to?" Eight Precepts said, "Brother, I'm talking to you." The行者 said, "You're wrong, you're talking to me. Old Sun only worries about the Master's well-being, you and Sha Seng, you just take care of the baggage and mounts. But if you slack off even a little, Old Sun will give you a beating with his staff first!"

Later, Nikolai Kuschmitch always maintained that on that Sunday evening, although he was understandably in a rather depressed mood, he had not drunk anything. He was therefore completely sober, as much as one can say that about what happened next. Perhaps he had dozed off a bit in his corner, one could at least think that. This brief nap had initially brought him considerable relief. "I've gotten entangled with numbers," he told himself. "Well, I don't understand numbers. But it's clear that one shouldn't attach too much importance to them; they're just a state-made contrivance, for the sake of order. No one had ever seen them anywhere else but on paper. It was impossible to encounter a seven or a twenty-five in a gathering, for example. They simply didn't exist. And then there had been this little mix-up, out of pure absent-mindedness: time and money, as if those couldn't be kept apart. Nikolai Kuschmitch almost laughed. It was good, really, to have stumbled upon this insight, and in good time, that was the important thing, in good time. Now it would be different. Time, yes, that was a painful thing. But did it only concern him? Didn't it also affect the others, as he had discovered, in seconds, even if they didn't know it?

Hearing this, the Great Sage chuckled silently. "This Buddha is awfully easy to fool! With a single somersault, I travel 100,000 to 80,000 li. With his palm barely a foot in diameter, how can I not escape?"  He blurted, "If you say so, then you are willing?"

The Buddha said, "Willing! Willing!"

He extended his right hand, appearing the size of a lotus leaf. The Great Sage retracted his R如意 Stick, gathered his divine might, leaped, and stood in the palm of the Buddha's hand, then declared, "I'm going out now!"  You see, he moved through a streak of clouds, disappearing without a trace.

The Buddha, with his wise eyes, saw that the monkey king moved like a gust of wind, never ceasing in his advance. As the Great Sage journeyed, he suddenly encountered five vermilion pillars, supporting a column of azure energy. He said, "This is the end of the road. Upon my return, with Buddha as witness, the Lingxiao Palace will be mine!" He pondered for a moment and then said, "Wait! Let me leave some mark so I can speak to Buddha." He plucked a hair, breathed a puff of fairy qi, and cried, "Transform!" It transformed into a thick ink double-haired brush.  On the middle pillar, he inscribed a large inscription: "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven, visited here." After finishing, he put the hair away.  Uncharacteristically, he then urinated on the root of the first pillar.  He flipped over his somersault cloud and returned to his original spot, standing before Buddha, saying, "I have been and I am back. You tell Jade Emperor to yield the Heavenly Palace to me."

Hearing this, the Great Sage let out a silent laugh, "This Buddha is so easily fooled! My old Sun can cover one hundred and eight thousand li in a single somersault. With his palm, barely a foot in diameter, how could I not escape?" He quickly declared, "If you say so, then make good on your promise!" The Buddha replied, "Yes, yes!," and extended his right hand, which was no larger than a lotus leaf. 

The Great Sage put away his Ruyi staff, shook his spirit, and with a leap, stood in the Buddha's palm, and said, "I've gone! " You see him shoot through the clouds, vanishing without a trace. The Buddha, with his insightful gaze, saw that the Monkey King moved like a chariot, stopping for nothing. As the Great Sage traveled, he suddenly saw five crimson pillars, supporting a surge of green energy. 

He said, "This must be the end of the road. On my return, I'll have Buddha as my witness, and the Lingxiao Palace shall be mine."  He pondered for a moment, "Wait! Let me leave a mark so I can have something to speak to Buddha about." He plucked a single hair, blew on it with divine energy, and cried out, "Change!"  It transformed into a pen made of concentrated ink and a double horsehair, and he wrote on the middle pillar in large characters: "The Great Sage Equaling Heaven, has passed by." 

He finished writing, then gathered the hair. Not acting with reverence, he urinated on the base of the first pillar. He turned and leaped back on his cloud, returning to the Buddha's palm. He declared, "I've gone and now I've returned. Tell Jade Emperor that the Heavenly Palace shall be mine!"

Hearing this, the Great Sage chuckled to himself, "This Buddha is so easy to fool!  My old Sun can travel ten thousand eight hundred li with a single somersault.  How could his palm, which isn't even a foot wide, possibly contain me?"  He blurted out, "If you say so, then can you make it happen?"  Buddha said, "I can, I can!" He extended his right hand, its size like a lotus leaf. The Great Sage tucked away his Ruyi staff, shook his divine power, leaped, and stood on the Buddha's palm, then declared, "I'm leaving now!" You saw him streak away through the clouds, leaving no trace. Buddha, with his wise eyes, saw the monkey king's departure resemble a wind chariot, unstoppable. As the Great Sage traveled, he suddenly encountered five crimson pillars, each supporting a wave of green energy.  "This is the end of the road," he thought.  "On my return, I'll have Buddha as my witness, and the Lingxiao Palace will surely be mine!" He pondered, "Wait! I'll leave a mark here so I can have something to tell Buddha about." He plucked out a single hair, breathed a puff of immortal qi, and cried, "Change!" It transformed into a thick, double-hair ink brush.  On the middle pillar, he wrote in large characters, "Great Sage Equal to Heaven, arrived here for a visit." After finishing, he retracted his hair.  With a mischievous glint in his eye, he urinated at the base of the first pillar.  With a turn of his somersault cloud, he returned to his starting point and stood before Buddha, "I've been and come back.  Tell the Jade Emperor to make the Heavenly Palace submit to me."

Hearing this, the Great Sage secretly laughed, "This Tathagata is so gullible! With one somersault of mine, I can travel a hundred thousand eight thousand li. With his palm, barely a foot in diameter, how could I possibly not be able to jump out?" He boldly said, "If that's the case, can you vouch for it?" The Buddha said, "I can vouch! I can vouch!" He opened his right hand, as if it were the size of a lotus leaf. The Great Sage retracted his Ruyi Rod, shook his divine might, leaped forward, and stood on the Buddha's palm, saying, "I'm out! Now!" You see, he rode a streak of cloud light, becoming formless and invisible, departing. The Buddha, with his wise eyes, saw that the Monkey King was like a shooting star, rushing forward. As the Great Sage traveled, he suddenly saw five meat-red pillars supporting a stream of green qi. He said, "This must be the end of the path. This time when I return, with the Tathagata as witness, the Lingxiao Palace shall be mine." He thought to himself, "Let me leave a mark here, so that I can have something to tell the Tathagata about." He plucked a single hair, blew a breath of immortal qi, and said, "Transform!" It transformed into a thick ink double-pointed brush. He wrote a line of large characters on the central pillar: "The Great Sage Equaling Heaven, has visited here." After finishing, he tucked the hair away. Then, unRespectfully, he peed a puddle of monkey urine under the base of the first pillar. He turned and somersaulted on his cloud, returning to his starting point, standing before the Tathagata. "I have gone, and now I'm back. You tell Jade Emperor that Heaven shall be mine."

The Great Sage hearing this, secretly smiled and said, “This Tathagata is so easily fooled! My old Sun can leap ten thousand eight thousand miles with a single somersault. With his palm, barely a foot in diameter, how could I not jump out?”  He urgently said, “If you say so, can you make good on your word?” The Buddha said, “Yes, yes!” He stretched out his right hand, appearing the size of a lotus leaf. The Great Sage put away his Ruyi Stick, shook his divine might, leaped, and stood on the Buddha’s palm, then declared, “I am out, indeed!” You see, he shot forth like a streak of cloud light, vanishing without a trace. The Buddha watched with his wise eyes and saw the Monkey King’s form, resembling a chariot, advancing ceaselessly. As the Great Sage journeyed, he suddenly saw five crimson pillars, supporting a surge of green qi. He said, “This must be the end of the road. On this return, with the Tathagata as witness, the Lingxiao Palace will surely be mine!” He further thought, “Wait! Let me leave a mark here so I can speak with the Tathagata.” He plucked a single hair, blew a puff of fairy air, and cried, “Transform!” It changed into a thick ink-dipped double-bristle brush, and he wrote a large line on the middle pillar: “Qi Tian Great Sage, arrived here for a visit.” Having finished writing, he collected the hair.  Uncharacteristically, he then urinated at the base of the first pillar. He somersaulted back on his Cloud and returned to his original position, standing before the Tathagata’s palm.  “I have gone, and now I am back. Tell Jade Emperor to cede the Heavenly Palace to me.”

When the Jade Emperor had sent a golden decree, the celestial Venus descended from the heavens, landing upon the cloud outside the Hua Guo Mountains, where the Flower and Fruit Forest lay hidden. He addressed the throngs of small monkeys: “I am an emissary of the Heavenly Court, bearing a sacred decree. Please summon your Great King. Act swiftly!” 
The news was relayed from monkey to monkey, layer by layer, until it reached the depths of the cave. "Great King, an old man with a scroll bearing a celestial seal has arrived, claiming to be an emissary from Heaven, bearing a decree for you.”  The Monkey King, overjoyed, declared, "These past few days, I’ve been thinking of visiting Heaven. Now, just as I was contemplating it, an angel arrives to summon me!" He exclaimed, "Bring him in quickly!" The Monkey King hurriedly adjusted his robes and stepped out to greet him.

Venus entered the cave, stood facing south, and declared, "I am the Western White Jade Star, Venus. I am sent by the Jade Emperor to grant you a decree, summoning you to Heaven to receive your immortal record."  Sun Wukong laughed, “I am honored by the Star's presence." He instructed, "You little ones! Prepare a feast to entertain our guest." Venus replied, "The decree is in my possession. I cannot linger long; please accompany me to Heaven. After your promotion, we shall have time for leisurely conversation." Wukong said, “Thank you for your consideration. Please excuse me for my haste." Immediately, he summoned his four valiant generals, and instructed them: "Carefully instruct your offspring, wait for me as I ascend to Heaven to explore the way, so that I may later bring you all to live there with me.”  The four generals agreed. The Monkey King and Venus then leaped upon a cloud and ascended to the heights of the heavens, achieving the exalted position of a Heaven immortal, their names inscribed on the celestial roster. What official rank would he be bestowed, we shall hear in the next chapter.

Golden Star took the imperial decree and exited the Southern Heaven gate, pressing down on auspicious clouds, until he reached the waterfall cave of the Flower and Fruit Mountains. He addressed the throng of little monkeys, saying: “I am a celestial messenger from Heaven. I have a decree here. Please, Your Majesty, come receive it quickly!” The monkeys outside the cave, layer by layer, relayed the message to the depths of the cave, saying: “Your Majesty, an old man is outside, carrying a cornered scroll, claiming to be a messenger from Heaven, bringing an imperial decree requesting your presence.” Monkey King, upon hearing this, rejoiced greatly and said: “These past few days, I was just thinking of going up to Heaven, and now a messenger has arrived to invite me.” He exclaimed: “Quickly invite him in!” The Monkey King hurriedly straightened his clothing and greeted him at the gate. Golden Star strode into the center and, facing south, stood firm, saying: “I am the Western Tai Bai Golden Star. I am entrusted by the Jade Emperor to deliver an imperial decree, inviting you down to Heaven to receive an immortal scroll.” Monkey King laughed and said: “I am greatly honored by the old Star’s visit.” He instructed: “My children! Prepare a feast to entertain him.” Golden Star said: “The decree is in my possession, so I cannot linger. Please, Your Majesty, come with me. After your promotion, we can converse at leisure.” Monkey King said: “Thank you for your grace. Please, excuse yourself! Please, excuse yourself!” He immediately summoned his four strongest generals, assigning them: “Carefully instruct my descendants to watch over things. I am going up to Heaven to explore the way, so that later I can bring you all up to live with me.” The four strong generals accepted the order. Monkey King and Golden Star then rose on clouds, ascending to the heights of the sky, and reaching the rank of celestial immortals. Their exact positions on the celestial scroll were still unknown.  We will hear about their specific titles in the next chapter.

Jin Xing received the imperial edict and left the South Heaven Gate, riding on auspicious clouds until she reached the Flower and Fruit Mountain curtain cave. Addressing the many young monkeys, she said, "I am a heavenly messenger, bearing an imperial decree. I ask that your king ascend to the celestial court and report promptly." 

Monkeys outside the cave, layer by layer, relayed the message to the depths of the cave, saying, "Your Majesty, an old man is outside, carrying a cornered scroll, claiming to be a heavenly messenger, bearing an imperial decree to summon you." 

Monkey King heard this and was overjoyed, saying, "These past few days, I've been contemplating going to heaven, and now a messenger has arrived." He called out, "Quickly, bring him in!" The Monkey King hurriedly straightened his attire and went out to greet him at the door. Jin Xing entered directly into the center, standing with her face towards the south, and said, "I am the Western White-Robed Star, Jin Xing, sent by the Jade Emperor to issue a decree. I have come down to summon you to heaven to receive a heavenly scroll." 

Sun Wukong laughed, saying, "It is a great honor for the old star to descend." He instructed, "You all, arrange a feast to entertain our guest."

Jin Xing said, "The decree is with me, so I cannot linger long; please accompany me to heaven, and after the official transfer, we can then converse leisurely."

Sun Wukong said, "Thank you for your visit, please depart! Please depart!" He immediately summoned his four strongest generals, distributing orders, "Carefully look after the young ones, while I ascend to heaven to see the way. Then, I will bring you all up to live with me." The four generals accepted the order.

The Monkey King and Jin Xing leaped onto the cloud heads, ascending into the boundless heavens,

truly achieving the exalted rank of celestial immortals, listed in the Cloud Banner’s Sacred Roster. The specific official position bestowed upon him remains unknown; we shall listen to the next installment to learn more.

Gold Star received the imperial decree and left the gate of the Southern Heavens, riding on auspicious clouds until he reached the Flower-Fruit Mountain Grotto. Addressing the many little monkeys, he said: “I am a heavenly messenger, bearing an imperial decree. Arrange a banquet to entertain our guest.” Gold Star said: “The decree is in my possession, so I cannot linger; please, Great King, come with me. After you are bestowed with your position, we shall have time to converse at leisure.” Monkey King replied: “Thank you for your courtesy, but please refrain from delaying! Please refrain from delaying!” He immediately summoned his four valiant generals and instructed: “Carefully instruct the children and grandchildren. While I ascend to heaven to scout the way, you may then follow me and reside in heaven as well.” The four valiant generals pledged their obedience.  Thus, the Monkey King and Gold Star soared up on a cloud, rising high above the earthly realm, fulfilling the verse: Ascending to a lofty celestial position, his name inscribed on the celestial register of clouds. His official rank remains unknown for now. We shall learn more in the next installment.

The Star of the Evening led the way, leaving the South Heaven Gate and riding down auspicious clouds until she reached the waterfall curtain cave of Flowers and Fruits Mountain. Addressing the group of small monkeys, she said, “I am a heavenly messenger, bearing a decree from Heaven. Please invite your Great King, and have him come quickly!” The monkeys outside, layer by layer, relayed the message to the depths of the cave, saying, “Great King, there is an old man outside, carrying a corner of a document, claiming to be a heavenly messenger, bringing a decree for you.” Sun Wukong, hearing this, was overjoyed. He said, “These past two days, I’ve been thinking about going to Heaven for a visit, and now a messenger has come to invite me.” He called out, “Quickly, invite him in!”  The Monkey King hurriedly adjusted his clothes and went out to greet him. 

The Star of the Evening stepped into the center, facing south and standing still, saying, “I am the Taibai Gold Star from the West, carrying the Jade Emperor’s decree to invite you to Heaven to receive your immortal record.” Sun Wukong laughed and said, “I am grateful for the old star’s arrival.” He instructed, “You little ones! Arrange a banquet to entertain him.”

The Star of the Evening said, “The decree is in my possession, so I cannot linger. Please, Great King, follow me. After you are elevated, we can discuss matters at leisure.” Sun Wukong said, “Thank you for your visit. Please excuse me!” Then, he summoned his four strongest generals and gave them instructions: “Carefully instruct the younger generations to look after yourselves. I am going to Heaven to see the way, so that later, I can bring you all to live there as well.” The four generals agreed. Sun Wukong and the Star of the Evening soared up on a cloud, rising above the clouds. This is when he was granted a celestial position among the immortals, his name recorded in the Treasured Register of the Cloud Banners. They don’t yet know what rank he will be given. Let’s hear how it unfolds next time.

Suddenly she stopped, placed her hand on K.'s, as if to soothe him, and whispered, "Quiet, Berthold is looking at us." K. slowly lifted his gaze. In the doorway of the sitting room stood a young man, small in stature, with slightly crooked legs, who searched for dignity in a short, thin, reddish full beard, constantly running his fingers through it. K. looked at him curiously; it was the first student of the unknown legal science that he had encountered, in a manner of speaking, as a human being, a man who would probably also ascend to higher positions in the civil service. The student, however, seemed not to care about K. at all. He only beckoned with a finger, which he drew out of his beard for a moment, to the woman and went to the window. The woman bent down to K. and whispered, "Please don't be angry with me, I beg you, don't think badly of me either, I must go to him now, to this hideous man, just look at his crooked legs. But I'll be right back, and then I'll go with you, if you'll take me. I'll go wherever you want, you can do whatever you want with me, I'll be happy if I'm away from here for as long as possible, ideally forever." She stroked K.'s hand again, jumped up and ran to the window. Unconsciously, K. reached out for her hand into the void. The woman truly enticed him; despite all his thinking, he found no solid reason why he shouldn't give in to her temptation. The fleeting objection that the woman would have him arrested by the court, he easily brushed aside. How could she possibly arrest him? Wasn't he always so free that he could shatter the whole court, at least as far as it concerned him, immediately? Couldn't he have this little trust in himself? And her offer of help sounded sincere and was perhaps not worthless. And there was perhaps no better revenge on the investigating judge and his entourage than to take this woman away from them and make her his own. It might happen that the investigating judge, after much toil over fabricated reports about K., would one day find the woman's bed empty in the late night. And empty precisely because she belonged to K., because this woman at the window, this lush, supple, warm body in the dark dress of coarse, heavy fabric, utterly belonged only to K.

Ba Ching recounted the dreams of the three young children to San Zang, who was pleased.  After they had received the plain vegetarian meal, Ba Ching offered a silver tael in thanks. San Zang refused it. The family persisted in their pleas, and San Zang, though he still refused any payment, said, "Your kindness in offering me this journey is enough to touch my heart." Ba Ching and his wife, unable to convince him otherwise, hastily made some coarse steamed buns and dried rations, and had Ba Ching see San Zang off. San Zang was happy to receive them. 

Tai Bao, having received his mother's orders, also called for two or three house servants, each with their hunting implements, and they went together along the main road, marveling at the mountain scenery and the views from the ridges. After traveling for half a day, they came to a mountain across the way, which truly reached up to the heavens, its peak lofty and perilous. San Zang, however, did not hesitate and quickly reached the front. For Tai Bao, ascending this mountain was like walking on level ground.  As they walked halfway up, Ba Ching turned around and stood at the foot of the road, saying, "Elder, please go ahead. I shall return." San Zang, hearing this, dismounted and said, "Please, do not trouble Tai Bao to accompany me any further!" Ba Ching replied, "Elder, you don't know, this mountain is called Liang Jie Shan. The eastern half belongs to the territory of our Tang Dynasty, but the western half is the territory of the Tatars. The wolves and tigers over there don't submit to my authority, so I cannot cross the border. You go on." San Zang was startled, his hands trembling, he clasped his robe and wept tears that he could not contain.  Just as he was saying farewell, a thunderous shout came from the foot of the mountain, "My master is here! My master is here!" This startled San Zang, causing him to become dumbfounded. Ba Ching struggled to defend himself. In the end, he didn't know who was shouting, so listen to the next installment.

Master Chen was told of the three young boys' dream narratives by Master Bao. Master Chen was pleased. He had received a vegetarian meal and was given a tael of silver as a thank you. Master Chen refused the money. The family begged him repeatedly, but Master Chen still wouldn't accept it. Finally, he said, "It is enough that you are willing to send me on my way with compassion." Master Bao and his wife, unable to do anything else, quickly made some coarse flatbread and dried grain, and had Master Bao escort him far along the road. Master Chen was happy to accept it. 

The Taobao, having received his mother's orders, summoned two or three house servants, each carrying hunting gear, and they all went up the main road, enjoying the scenery of the mountains and wilderness. They walked for half a day when they came to a mountain on the opposite side, towering high and piercing the heavens, steep and formidable. Master Chen arrived at the mountain edge without hesitation. The Taobao ascended the mountain as if walking on flat ground. Just as they reached the middle of the mountain, Master Bao turned back and stood at the foot of the road, saying, "Elder, please go ahead. I will return." Hearing this, Master Chen dismounted and said, "Please don't trouble the Taobao to send me any further!" Master Bao said, "Elder, you do not know, this mountain is called Liangjie Mountain. The eastern half belongs to the territory of our Tang dynasty, while the western half belongs to the Tatars. The wolves and tigers over there do not submit to my command, so I cannot cross the border. You should go on your own." Master Chen was startled, he clasped his hands together, clutched his robes, and tears streamed down his face. 

Just as he was about to say his farewells, a roar like thunder came from the foot of the mountain: "My master is here! My master is here!" Master Chen was stunned, while Master Bao struggled. Still unsure who was shouting, he could only wait to hear what happened next.

So, I settled in, you see, with the German merchant, in the entryway. Things were going well, but he sent me to work in the buffet. What did that have to do with me? Once, I was carrying some kind of Bohemian glassware, the floors were so smooth and slippery — good thing they didn’t shatter! Suddenly, my legs went out from under me, and the whole lot of it, plate and tray, crashed to the floor. Well, they kicked me out, of course. 

Another time, I caught the eye of an old countess. "Respectable-looking," she said, and hired me as a Swiss. A good position, an old-fashioned one: just sit on the stool with an air of importance, cross your legs, and don't answer right away when someone comes in. First, bark orders, then decide whether to let them in or shove them aside, as needed; as for decent guests, of course: a good whack with a baton, like this! —  Zakhary made a sweeping motion with his hand. — Flattering, isn’t it! But the lady turned out to be such a pain — God have mercy on her soul! Once she popped into my little room, saw a flea, and went ballistic, as if I’d invented fleas! What household is without fleas? Another time, she passed by and thought she smelled wine on me…  such a woman! And she rejected me.

“Look at you all huddled together!” Leni cried, returning with the cup and stopping in the doorway. They were indeed pressed close, so that with the slightest turn they bumped heads. The merchant, who, besides his small stature, also stooped, had forced K. to hunch down too if he wanted to hear everything. “Just a little while longer!” K. called out to Leni, waving her off impatiently with the hand he still had resting on the merchant’s. “He wanted me to tell him about my trial,” the merchant said to Leni. “Go on, tell him,” she said. She spoke to the merchant affectionately, but also condescendingly, which K. disliked; as he had now realized, the man had some worth, at least he had experiences he knew how to relate well. Leni was probably judging him wrongly. He glared angrily as Leni now took the candle from the merchant, who had been holding it the whole time, wiped his hand with her apron, and then knelt beside him to scrape off some wax that had dripped from the candle onto his trousers. “They wanted to tell me about the Winkel advocats,” K. said and, without further comment, pushed Leni’s hand away. “What do you want?” Leni asked, lightly slapping K. and resuming her work. “Yes, about the Winkel advocats,” the merchant said, stroking his forehead as if in thought. K. wanted to help him and said, “They wanted immediate success and so they went to the Winkel advocats.” “Quite right,” the merchant said, but didn’t continue. “He probably doesn’t want to talk about it in front of Leni,” K. thought, suppressing his impatience to hear the rest immediately, and no longer pressed him further.

K. turned around, the merchant hardly noticing as he immediately stood up.  "Sit down," said K. and pulled a chair next to him. "Have you been an old client of the lawyer's?" asked K. "Yes," said the merchant, "a very old client." "How many years has he been representing you?" asked K. "I don't know how you mean that," said the merchant, "in business law matters – I have a grain business – the lawyer has represented me since I took over the business, so about twenty years. In my own case, the one you are probably referring to, he has represented me since the beginning, it's been longer than five years. Yes, well over five years," he added, and pulled out an old wallet, "here I have it all written down; if you want, I can tell you the exact dates. It's hard to keep track of everything. My case has probably been going on for much longer, it began shortly after my wife's death, and that's been longer than five and a half years." K. leaned closer to him. "So the lawyer also takes on ordinary legal cases?" he asked. This connection of courts and law seemed extremely comforting to K. "Certainly," said the merchant, and then whispered to K., "People even say that he is better at those cases than at the others." But then he seemed to regret it, placed a hand on K.'s shoulder, and said, "Please, don't tell anyone." K. tapped him reassuringly on the knee and said, "No, I'm no betrayer." "He's vindictive," said the merchant. "He certainly won't do anything to such a loyal client," said K. "Oh yes," said the merchant, "when he's excited, he knows no distinctions; by the way, I'm not actually loyal to him." "Why not?" asked K. "Should I confide in you?" asked the merchant doubtfully. "I think you may," said K. "Well," said the merchant, "I will tell you part of it, but you must also tell me a secret so that we can support each other against the lawyer." "You are very cautious," said K., "but I will tell you a secret that will completely reassure you. What is your disloyalty to the lawyer?" "I have," said the merchant hesitantly, in a tone as if confessing something dishonorable, "I have other lawyers besides him." "That's not such a bad thing," said K., a little disappointed. "Here, yes," said the merchant, who was still breathing heavily from his confession, but gained more confidence due to K.'s remark. "It's not allowed. And it is especially not allowed to take so-called  winkle lawyers in addition to a lawyer. And that's exactly what I've done, I have five winkle lawyers besides him." "Five!" exclaimed K., the number set him in astonishment, "five lawyers besides this one?" The merchant nodded. "I'm currently negotiating with a sixth." "But why do you need so many lawyers?" asked K. "I need them all," said the merchant. "Don't you want to explain that?" asked K. "Certainly," said the merchant. "Above all, I don't want to lose my case, that goes without saying. Consequently, I can't ignore anything that might be of use to me, even if the hope of benefit in a particular case is only very small, I can't dismiss it. That's why I have used everything I own on the case. For example, I have withdrawn all the money from my business; earlier, my business offices filled almost a whole floor, today a small room in the back house is enough, where I work with an apprentice. This decline has naturally not only been caused by the withdrawal of money, but even more so by the withdrawal of my working capacity. If one wants to do something for one's case, one can hardly deal with anything else." "So you're also working at court yourself?" asked K. "I'd like to learn more about that." "I can't say much about that," said the merchant, "at first, I probably tried it too, but I soon gave up. It's too exhausting and doesn't bring much success. Even working and negotiating there has proven impossible for me. It's hard enough to just sit and wait there. You know the heavy air in the courtrooms yourself." "How do you know I was there?" asked K. "I was in the waiting room when you walked through." "What a coincidence!" exclaimed K., completely accepting it and forgetting the merchant's previous flippancy. "You saw me! You were in the waiting room when I walked through. Yes, I was there once." "It's not such a big coincidence," said the merchant, "I'm there almost every day." "I will probably have to go there more often now," said K., "but I probably won't be received as honorably as before. Everyone stood up. They probably thought I was a judge." "No," said the merchant, "we greeted the bailiff then. That you are a defendant, we knew." "You already knew that," said K., "then my behavior probably seemed arrogant. Did you talk about it?" "No," said the merchant, "on the contrary. But those are stupidities." "What kind of stupidities?" asked K. "Why do you ask that?" said the merchant irritably. "You seem not to know the people there yet and will probably misunderstand them. You have to consider that in this proceedings, many things are constantly discussed that are beyond the reach of reason, one is simply too tired and distracted for many things, and one substitutes superstition for reason. I'm talking about the others, but I'm no better myself. One such superstition is that many people judge the outcome of the case from the defendant's face, especially from the shape of the lips. These people claimed that, judging by your lips, you would certainly and soon be condemned. I repeat, it's a ridiculous superstition and in most cases completely refuted by the facts, but when you live in that society, it's hard to escape those opinions. Think about how strongly this superstition can work. You spoke to someone there, didn't you? He could hardly answer you. There are, of course, many reasons for this, but one of them was the sight of your lips. He later told me he even thought he saw the sign of his own condemnation on your lips." "My lips?" asked K., pulled out a pocket mirror, and looked at himself. "I can't see anything special about my lips. And you?" "Neither can I," said the merchant, "absolutely nothing." "How superstitious these people are!" exclaimed K. "Didn't I tell you?" asked the merchant. "Do they exchange opinions with each other so much?" asked K. "I've mostly kept to myself," said the merchant. "Generally, they don't get along with each other," said the merchant, "it would be impossible, there are so many. There are also few common interests. If sometimes a belief in a common interest emerges in a group, it soon turns out to be a mistake. Together, nothing can be achieved against the court. Each case is examined individually, it is the most meticulous court after all. You can't achieve anything together, only an individual sometimes achieves something secretly; only when it's achieved do others find out; no one knows how it happened. There is no community, although they occasionally meet in the waiting rooms, but little is discussed there. The superstitious opinions have existed for ages and multiply by themselves." "I saw the gentlemen there in the waiting room," said K., "their waiting seemed so pointless." "Waiting is not pointless," said the merchant, "pointless is independent action. I said that I now have five lawyers besides this one. One would think – and I myself thought so at first – now I could leave the matter entirely to them. But that would be completely wrong. I can trust them less than if I had only one. You don't understand that, do you?" "No," said K., and placed his hand reassuringly on the merchant's hand to slow him down, "I just want to ask you to speak a little slower, these are all very important things for me, and I can't quite follow you." "It's good that you remind me," said the merchant, "you are new, a young man. Your case is half a year old, isn't that right? Yes, I've heard that. Such a young case! I've thought about these things countless times, they are the most obvious things in the world to me." "You are probably glad that your case has progressed so far?" asked K., he didn't want to ask directly about the merchant's situation. He didn't get a clear answer either. "Yes, I've been running my case for five years," said the merchant, and lowered his head, "it's no small feat." Then he was silent for a while. K. listened, wondering if Leni was coming. On one hand, he didn't want her to come, because he had many more questions and didn't want to be caught in this confidential conversation with the merchant by Leni.
