For several years now, the Indian cholera had shown a heightened tendency to spread and migrate. Originating from the warm marshes of the Ganges delta, rising with the miasmatic breath of that lush yet unsuitable, by humans shunned primeval wilderness and island-wildness, in whose bamboo thickets the tiger lurks, the disease had raged continuously and unusually fiercely throughout all of Hindustan. It had spread eastward to China, westward to Afghanistan and Persia, and, following the main caravan trade routes, carried its terrors as far as Astrakhan, indeed even to Moscow. But while Europe trembled, fearing the specter might make its entry from there, overland, it had, carried by Syrian merchants across the sea, almost simultaneously appeared in several Mediterranean ports, had raised its head in Toulon and Malaga, shown its mask repeatedly in Palermo and Naples, and seemed determined to leave Calabria and Apulia no more. The northern part of the peninsula had remained untouched. However, in the middle of May of this year, on the same day, the dreaded vibrios were found in the emaciated, blackened corpses of a ship's boy and a green goods merchant in Venice. The cases were concealed. But after a week, there were ten, then twenty, thirty, and so on, in various quarters. A man from the Austrian province, who had stayed in Venice for his pleasure for a few days, died, upon returning to his home town, under unmistakable signs, and thus it came to pass that the first rumors of the plague of the lagoon city reached German newspapers. Venice’s authorities responded that the health conditions of the city had never been better and took the necessary measures to combat it. But it was likely that food had been infected, vegetables, meat, or milk, for what was denied and hushed up, devoured death in the narrowness of the alleyways. And the prematurely arrived summer heat, which warmed the water of the canals, was particularly favorable to its spread. Yes, it seemed as if the pestilence were experiencing a revival of its strength, as if the tenacity and fertility of its pathogens had doubled. Cases of recovery were very rare; eighty percent of those infected died, and in a horrifying manner, for the disease manifested with extreme ferocity and often showed that most dangerous form, which is called "the dry."  Here, the body was unable to even expel the masses of water separated from the blood vessels. Within a few hours, the patient would dry up and suffocate on the pitch-like viscous blood, amidst cramps and hoarse laments.  Woe betide him, if, as sometimes happened, the outbreak occurred after slight discomfort in the form of a deep swoon, from which he did not or scarcely ever awaken. By the beginning of June, the isolation barracks of the Ospedale civico were filled in the stillness, in the two orphanages space began to be scarce, and a terrifyingly lively traffic reigned between the pier of the new foundations and San Michele, the island cemetery. But the fear of general damage, the consideration for the recently opened art exhibition in the public gardens, for the immense losses, from which, in the event of panic and uproar, hotels, shops, the entire diverse tourist trade were threatened, proved to be mightier in the city than truthfulness and respect for international agreements; it enabled the authorities to stubbornly maintain their policy of silence and denial. Venice's chief medical officer, a respected man, had resigned in disgust from his post and been replaced by a more compliant personality behind the scenes. The people knew that; and the corruption of the upper classes, combined with the prevailing uncertainty, the state of emergency, in which the impending death had placed the city, brought about a certain desensitization of the lower classes, an encouragement of dark and antisocial impulses, which manifested in excess, shamelessness, and growing criminality. Against the norm, one observed many drunkards in the evenings; malicious gangs, so it was said, made the streets unsafe at night; robberies and even murders repeated themselves, for it had already been proven twice that persons supposedly succumbed to the plague had been removed from life by their own relatives with poison; and professional mendicancy took on intrusive and extravagant forms, such as were otherwise unknown here but at home in the south of the country and in the Orient.

But likely, foodstuffs had been infected: vegetables, meat, or milk, for concealed and hushed up, death consumed itself in the cramped alleys, and the prematurely arrived summer heat, which warmed the water of the canals pleasantly, was particularly favorable to its spread. Yes, it seemed as if the pestilence had experienced a resurgence of its powers, as if the tenacity and fertility of its pathogens had doubled. Cases of recovery were very rare; eighty out of one hundred of the afflicted died, and in a terrifying manner, for the ailment erupted with utmost ferocity and often exhibited that most dangerous form, which is called "the dry one." In this form, the body was unable to expel even the mass of water separated from the blood vessels. Within a few hours, the patient withered and suffocated on the pitch-thickened blood, convulsing and groaning hoarsely. Well was it, if, as occasionally happened, the outbreak occurred after slight discomfort in the form of a deep swoon from which he did not or scarcely awaken again. By the beginning of June, the isolation barracks of the Ospedale civico were filling up in silence, space was beginning to run out in the two orphanages, and a chillingly brisk traffic prevailed between the quays of the new foundations and San Michele, the island cemetery. But the fear of widespread damage, the consideration for the recently opened art exhibition in the public gardens, for the massive losses, from which, in the event of panic and rampage, hotels, businesses, the entire diverse tourist trade were threatened, proved more powerful in the city than truthfulness and respect for international agreements; it enabled the authorities to stubbornly maintain their policy of concealment and denial. Venice's chief medical officer, a worthy man, had resigned in indignation from his post and been replaced underhand by a more compliant personality. The people knew this; and the corruption of the elite, coupled with the prevailing uncertainty, the state of emergency in which the imminent death had plunged the city, brought about a certain moral degradation in the lower classes, an encouragement of shady and antisocial impulses, which manifested itself in excess, shamelessness, and growing crime. Against the rule, one noticed many drunkards in the evenings; vicious gangs were said to make the streets unsafe at night; robberies and even murders were repeated, for it had already been proven twice that people supposedly fallen victim to the plague had been eliminated from life by their own relatives with poison; and professional lechery took on intrusive and extravagant forms, such as were not known here otherwise and only prevalent in the south of the country and the Orient.

As always, Cavalier slipped from under the table and ran toward her.  I saw it, Malte, I saw it. He ran toward her, even though she wasn't coming; for him, she was coming. We understood that he was running towards her. Twice he looked back at us, as if asking. Then he darted towards her, as always, Malte, just as always, and reached her; for he began to jump around, Malte, around something that wasn't there, and then up at her, to lick her, right up. We heard him whine with joy, and as he jumped so high, several times in quick succession, one might have thought he was covering us with his leaps. But then a cry suddenly arose, and he turned from his own swing in the air and crashed down, oddly ungainly, and lay there quite peculiarly flat and still. From the other side the servant from the house came out with the letters. He hesitated for a moment; apparently it wasn't easy to approach our faces. And your father waved him off to stay. Your father, Malte, didn't love animals; but now he did go, slowly, as it seemed to me, and bent over the dog. He said something to the servant, something short, monosyllabic. I saw the servant jump to lift Cavalier. But then your father took the animal himself and went with it, as if he knew exactly where he was going, into the house.

Every day for a few hours I went to Dronningens Tværgade, to the cramped rooms that looked offended, like all rental apartments where someone had died. I paced between the desk and the large white tiled stove and burned the Jägermeister’s papers. I had started throwing the letters, as they were bundled, into the fire, but the small packages were too tightly bound and only charred at the edges. It took effort to untie them. Most had a strong, persuasive scent that permeated me, as if it wanted to stir memories in me as well. I had none. Then it could happen that photographs slipped out, heavier than the rest; these photographs burned incredibly slowly. I don’t know how it came to be, suddenly I imagined it could be Ingeborg’s picture underneath. But every time I looked, it was mature, magnificent, distinctly beautiful women who made me think of other things. It turned out, in fact, that I wasn’t entirely without memories. It was exactly such eyes that I sometimes found myself in, when, during my growing-up years, I walked with my father across the street. Then they could surround me from within a carriage, with a gaze from which it was hardly possible to escape. Now I knew that they compared me to him then, and that the comparison was not in my favor. Certainly not, the Jägermeister had nothing to fear from comparisons.

Perhaps that was the trick the captive illness used to overcome him.  The will had broken in two places, and the yielding had left a soft, alluring allure in the possessed muscles and a compelling second beat. But the stick was still in its place, and his hands looked mean and angry; so we stepped onto the bridge, and it went. It went. Now something uncertain entered the gait, now he ran two steps, and now he stood.  Stood. His left hand gently released itself from the stick and rose so slowly that I saw it trembling in the air; he pushed his hat back a little and ran his hand over his forehead. He turned his head slightly, and his gaze drifted over sky, buildings, and water without focusing, and then he gave in. The stick was gone, he stretched out his arms as if he wanted to take flight, and it burst out of him like a natural force, bending him forward and pulling him back, making him nod and sway, and hurling dance power out of him into the crowd. For already many people were around him, and I could no longer see him.

No, he didn't consider her a child! Certain looks of hers lately, certain words, terrified him. Sometimes it seemed to him that she was clinging on too tightly, restraining herself too much, and he recalled that this was what frightened him. True, all these days he tried not to think about it, he pushed away the heavy thoughts, but what was hidden in this soul? This question had been tormenting him for a long time, although he believed in this soul. And here it was all about to be resolved, to reveal itself today!  A terrible thought! And again— "this woman"! Why did it always seem to him that this woman would appear at the very last moment and tear apart his entire destiny like a rotting thread? He was now ready to swear to this, even though he was almost delirious. If he had tried to forget about her lately, it was only because he was afraid of her. What was it: did he love this woman or hate her? He hadn't asked himself this question today; his heart was pure: he knew who he loved... He wasn't so afraid of their rendezvous, not the strangeness of it, not the reason for this meeting, which was unknown to him, not its resolution in any way— he was afraid of Nastasya Filippovna herself. My dear Alyosha, I love you, I have loved you since childhood, since Moscow, when you were not at all like you are now, and I will love you for my whole life. I have chosen you with my heart to be united with you, and to end our lives together in old age. Of course, on the condition that you leave the monastery. As for our age, we shall wait until the law decrees. By then I shall have certainly recovered, I will be walking and dancing. There can be no other way."

Someone must have slandered Josef K., for one morning he was arrested without having done anything wrong. The cook for Mrs. Grubach, his landlady, who brought him breakfast every day around eight o'clock, didn't come this time. This had never happened before. K. waited a while longer, saw the old woman who lived opposite him observing him with an unusual curiosity, and then, both bewildered and hungry, he rang the bell. Immediately, someone knocked, and a man, whom he had never seen in this apartment before, entered. He was slender yet sturdy, wearing a close-fitting black suit that, like a traveler's outfit, was adorned with various pleats, pockets, buckles, buttons, and a belt, making it appear particularly practical, although it wasn't clear what it was intended for. "Who are you?" asked K., sitting up halfway in bed. The man, however, ignored the question, as if his appearance should be taken for granted, and simply said, "You rang the bell?" "Anna should bring me breakfast," said K. and tried, first silently, to determine, through observation and thought, who this man actually was. But the man didn't subject himself to his gaze for long, but turned towards the door, which he opened slightly, to say to someone who was apparently just behind the door, "He wants Anna to bring him breakfast." A small laugh came from the next room; it wasn't certain from the sound whether it wasn't several people involved. Although the stranger couldn't have learned anything from this that he didn't already know, he said to K. in a tone of announcement, "It's impossible." "That would be news," said K., jumped out of bed, and quickly pulled on his trousers. "I want to see who's in the next room and how Mrs. Grubach will justify this disturbance to me." It occurred to him immediately that he shouldn't have said that out loud and that he was thereby acknowledging a kind of supervisory authority of the stranger, but it didn't seem important to him now. At any rate, the stranger took it that way, for he said, "Wouldn't you rather stay here?" "I don't want to stay here, nor be addressed by you as long as you don't introduce yourself," said K. "It was meant well," said the stranger, and now voluntarily opened the door wider. In the next room, which K. entered more slowly than he wanted to, it looked almost exactly the same as the night before. It was Mrs. Grubach's living room, perhaps there was a little more space in this room overflowing with furniture, blankets, porcelain and photographs today, one didn't notice it immediately, all the more so because the main change consisted in the presence of a man who was sitting by the open window with a book, from which he now looked up. "You should have stayed in your room! Didn't Franz tell you?" "Yes, what do you want?" said K., looking from the new acquaintance to the man named Franz, who had remained in the doorway, and then back again. Through the open window, one could see the old woman again, who had moved with truly senile curiosity to the window opposite, to continue to see everything. "I want to see Mrs. Grubach," said K., made a movement as if he wanted to pull himself away from the two men, who were standing far from him, and wanted to move on. "No," said the man by the window, threw the book onto a small table, and stood up. "You can't leave, you are arrested." "It seems so," said K. "And why?" he then asked. "We are not obliged to tell you that. Go to your room and wait. The proceedings have now been initiated, and you will learn everything in due time. I'm exceeding my mandate if I speak to you so amicably. But I hope it won't be overheard by anyone else besides Franz, and he himself is friendly to you against all rules. If you continue to have as much luck as you had in the selection of your guards, then you can be confident." K. wanted to sit down, but now he saw that there was no seating arrangement in the whole room except for the armchair by the window. "You will see how true all this is," said Franz, and at the same time moved towards K. with the other man. Particularly the latter towered over K. considerably and patted him on the shoulder repeatedly. Both of them examined K.'s nightgown and said that he would now have to wear a much better shirt, that they would keep this one, as well as the rest of his laundry, and, if his case turned out favorably, would return it to him. "It's better that you give the things to us than to the depot," they said, "because there are often thefts in the depot, and besides, they sell all things after a certain time, regardless of whether the relevant proceedings have ended or not. And how long do such processes last, especially recently! You would then eventually receive the proceeds from the depot, but this proceeds is firstly already small in itself, because when selling, the amount offered doesn't decide, but the amount of the bribe, and furthermore, such proceeds decrease over time, the more they are passed from hand to hand and from year to year." K. hardly paid attention to these speeches, the right of disposal over his belongings, which he might still have, he didn't value highly; what mattered to him was to gain clarity about his situation; but in the presence of these people, he couldn't even think, the belly of the second guard - they had to be guards, after all - kept bumping into him in a friendly way. When he looked up, he saw a dry, bony face with a strong, sideways-turned nose, which didn't quite match the thick body, that communicated with the other guard. Who were these people? What were they talking about? What authority did they belong to? K. lived in a state of law, there was peace everywhere, all the laws were in force; who dared to storm his apartment? He always tended to take everything as lightly as possible, believing only the worst when the worst actually happened, not making any provisions for the future, even when everything threatened. But here, it didn't seem right, although it could be viewed as a joke, as a crude joke played on him for unknown reasons, perhaps because today was his 30th birthday, the colleagues from the bank had organized it – it was possible, maybe he just had to laugh at the guards' faces, and they would laugh along, maybe they were civil servants from the street corner, they didn't look dissimilar – nevertheless, he was determined from the very first glance at the guard Franz not to give up even the smallest advantage he might have over these people. He saw little danger in the fact that later people would say he hadn't understood the joke, but he remembered – without it being his habit to learn from experience – some insignificant cases where he had, unlike his friends, behaved recklessly, without the slightest sense of the possible consequences, and had been punished for the result. It shouldn't happen again, at least not this time; if it was a comedy, he wanted to play along.

Immediately, someone knocked, and a man, whom he had never seen in the apartment before, entered. He was slender yet solidly built, wearing a close-fitting black suit, which, like traveling outfits, was equipped with various pleats, pockets, buckles, buttons, and a belt, and thus, without one clearly understanding its purpose, appeared particularly practical. "Who are you?" asked K., sitting up half-straight in bed. The man, however, ignored the question, as if his appearance needed no explanation, and merely said in return: "You rang the bell?" But this one didn't subject himself to his gaze for too long, but turned to the door, which he opened a crack, to say to someone clearly standing just behind it: "He wants Anna to bring him breakfast." A small chuckle came from the adjoining room; it was not certain from the sound whether several people were involved. Although the stranger couldn't have learned anything from this that he didn't already know, he now said to K. in a tone of announcement: "It's impossible." "That would be new," said K., jumped out of bed and quickly pulled on his pants. "I want to see who's in the next room and how Frau Grubach intends to justify this disturbance to me." It occurred to him immediately that he shouldn't have said that aloud and that he was thereby recognizing a certain right of supervision on the part of the stranger, but it didn't seem important to him now. After all, the stranger took it that way, because he said: "Wouldn't you rather stay here?" Even at the beginning of the trial, Raskolnikov's mother fell ill. Dunya and Razumikhin decided it was best to take her out of Petersburg for the duration of the proceedings. Razumikhin chose a town on the railway line, not too far from Petersburg, so that he could keep abreast of all the developments in the trial and at the same time see Avdotya Romanovna as often as possible. Pulcheria Alexandrovna's illness was of a strange, nervous sort, accompanied by something like insanity, if not complete, then at least in part. When Dunya returned from her last meeting with her brother, she found her mother already very ill, delirious with fever. That very evening, she and Razumikhin agreed on what to tell their mother about her son, and even invented a whole story about Raskolnikov's departure to a distant part of Russia on a private mission that would ultimately bring him both money and fame. But they were struck by the fact that Pulcheria Alexandrovna never asked about any of this, neither then nor later. On the contrary, she herself had a whole story about her son's sudden departure; she tearfully recounted how he had come to say goodbye, hinting that only she knew many very important and mysterious circumstances, and that Rodion had many very powerful enemies, so that he had to go into hiding. As for his future career, she too seemed to consider it certain and brilliant, once some hostile circumstances had passed; she assured Razumikhin that her son would eventually become a state man, which was evidenced by his article and his brilliant literary talent. She read the article constantly, sometimes even aloud, barely sleeping without it, and yet she hardly ever asked where Rodion was now, despite the fact that, apparently, they avoided talking about it with her, – which in itself could have heightened her suspicions. Finally, they began to fear this strange silence of Pulcheria Alexandrovna about certain points. She, for example, did not even complain about the lack of letters from him, whereas before, living in her small town, she had lived only on the hope and expectation of receiving a letter from her beloved Rodion as soon as possible. This last circumstance was too inexplicable and deeply troubled Dunya; the thought came to her that her mother, perhaps, foresaw something terrible in her son's fate and was afraid to ask, lest she learn something even worse. In any case, Dunya clearly saw that Pulcheria Alexandrovna was not in her right mind.

In the mountains, for eight sections I roam freely, in the lake, for four seasons I follow my inclinations. Gathering firewood brings me the joy of immortals, angling yields no trace of worldly form. Outside my door, wild flowers bloom vibrantly, on the boat, the green water laps gently. My heart at ease, I care not for the lofty positions of the Three Officials; my nature is strong, steadfast as a ten-mile city wall. The ten-mile city wall stands high, defending against foreign threats; the position of the Three Officials brings only a hearing of proclamations. The joy of mountains and water is truly rare, to heaven, to earth, to the gods I offer my thanks. 

Having shared verses and linked poetic lines, they reached the fork in the road and bowed in farewell. Zhang Shao said, "Brother Li, be careful on your journey! When climbing the mountain, be sure to watch out for tigers. Should any danger arise, it will be like missing a few acquaintances in the marketplace tomorrow!" Li Ding, upon hearing this, grew furious and said, "You lazy dog! Even as a close friend, you speak of death! If I were to encounter a tiger and meet harm, you would surely be caught in a raging river!" Zhang Shao replied, "I will never in this lifetime encounter such a raging river." Li Ding said, "The heavens have unforeseen winds and clouds, people have temporary fortunes and misfortunes. How can you be so certain of safety?" Zhang Shao said, "Brother Li, though you speak thus, you still haven't grasped it. Unlike your ventures, mine are predictable. I will certainly avoid such dangers." Li Ding said, "Your livelihood on the water is both perilous and treacherous, veiled in secrecy. What could be predictable about it?" Zhang Shao said, "You don't understand. In Chang'an City, on West Street, there's a diviner. Every day, I give him a golden carp, and he secretly imparts a lesson, according to directions, before the nets are cast. Today, I bought a reading from him. He instructed me to set my net at the east edge of the Jing River bend and cast my line on the west bank, guaranteeing a full haul of fish and shellfish. Tomorrow, I will sell them in the city, buy some wine, and join you again." Thus, the two parted ways.

I wandered more through the busiest, industrial streets, along Meshchanskaya, along Sadovaya, past Yusupov Garden. I always particularly loved to stroll along these streets at dusk, especially when the crowds of passersby, industrial and tradespeople, with faces contorted with irritation, dispersed to their homes from their day's earnings, grew thicker. I liked this very petty bustle, this blatant prosaicism. This time, all this street commotion irritated me even more. I couldn't control myself, couldn't find peace. Something kept rising in my soul, relentlessly, with pain, and wouldn't be silenced. Completely distraught, I returned home. It was as if some kind of crime weighed on my soul.

I put six rubles in the letter, sealed it, and begged Apollo to take it to Simonov. Learning that the letter contained money, Apollo became more respectful and agreed to go. By evening I went for a walk. My head still ached and spun from the day before. But the more evening approached and the thicker the dusk became, the more my impressions changed and jumbled, and with them, my thoughts. Something wouldn't die within me, in the depths of my heart and conscience, didn't want to die, and manifested itself in a burning longing. I wandered mostly through the busiest, industrial streets, the Meshchansky, the Sadovaya, near Yusupov's garden. Well, alright, my little angel, alright! You decided that it's not a disaster that I haven't managed to get the money. Well, alright, I'm calm, I'm happy on your account! Even glad that you, my old man, are not leaving me and will stay in this apartment. Yes, if I'm honest, my heart overflowed with joy when I saw how well you wrote about me in your letter and paid due praise to my feelings. I'm not saying this from pride, but because I see how you love me, how you worry about my heart. Well, alright; what's the use of talking about my heart now! The heart is on its own; but you, my dear, you punish me so that I won't become a coward. Yes, my little angel, I'll probably even say myself, that there's no need for cowardice; but at the same time, decide for yourself, my dear, what boots I'll go to work in tomorrow! That's the thing, my dear; but a thought like this can destroy a man, completely destroy him. And most importantly, my dear one, I'm not suffering for myself, I'm not sad for myself; to me, it's all the same if I have to walk in freezing weather without a coat and without boots, I'll endure it all, it doesn't matter to me; I am a simple, small man – but what will people say? My enemies, those wicked tongues of theirs, what will they say when I go out without a coat? After all, I dress for people, and I wear boots for them too. Boots in this case, my dear, my soul, are needed for me to maintain my honor and good name; in worn-out boots, both are lost – believe me, my dear, believe the experience of my many years; listen to me, an old man who knows the world and people, and not some young punks and runners.

A shout from the next room startled him so badly that he bit down on the glass. “The guard is calling you!” it said. It was only the shouting that had frightened him, that short, clipped, military shout, which he wouldn’t have dared to attribute to Guard Franz. The order itself was very welcome to him. “Finally!” he called back, barred the cupboard and hurried into the next room. There the two guards stood and hustled him back into his room as if it were perfectly natural. “What do you think you’re doing?” they called. “Going before the guard in your shirt? He’ll have you beaten and us with you!” “Let me be, damn it!” cried K., already pushed back to his wardrobe, “if they attack me in bed, you can’t expect me to be found in my evening clothes.” “It won’t do any good,” said the guards, who always, whenever K. shouted, became quite calm, almost sad, and thus bewildered or somehow brought him to his senses. “Ridiculous ceremonies!” he grumbled, but he lifted a coat from the chair and held it for a moment with both hands, as if submitting it to the judgment of the guards. They shook their heads. “It has to be a black coat,” they said. K. threw the coat to the floor and said – he didn’t even know in what sense he said it –: “It’s not the main trial yet.” The guards smiled but stuck to their: “It has to be a black coat.” “If it hastens things,” said K., opened the wardrobe himself, searched long among the many clothes, chose his best black dress, a jacket dress that had almost caused a stir among acquaintances for its tailoring, pulled out another shirt, and began to dress carefully. In secret, he believed he had accelerated the whole affair by making the guards forget to force him to take a bath. He watched them, to see if they might perhaps remember, but of course, they didn’t.  Willem, however, didn’t forget to send Franz the message that K. was getting dressed.

Here Ippolit Kirillovich laid out the whole picture of the defendant’s fatal passion for Grushhenka. He began with the moment the defendant went to “the young lady” to “beat her up,” as he put it in his own words, explained Ippolit Kirillovich, “but instead of beating her, he stayed at her feet—that was the start of this love. At the same time, the same young lady catches the eye of the defendant’s father—a remarkable and fateful coincidence, for both hearts suddenly flared up, at the same time, although both had previously known and met this lady—and these two hearts ignited with the most unrestrained, the most Karamazovian passion. Here we have her own admission: “I,” she says, “laughed at both of them.” Yes, she suddenly felt like laughing at both of them; she hadn’t felt like it before, but suddenly this intention came to her mind—and it ended with both falling before her, defeated. The old man, who worshipped money like a god, immediately prepared three thousand rubles just for her to visit his home, but he was soon driven to the point where he would have gladly offered her his name and all his fortune, just to have her become his lawful wife. We have solid evidence for that. As for the defendant, his tragedy is obvious, it’s before us. But that was the “game” of the young lady. The unfortunate young man, the seductress did not even offer hope, because real hope was only given to him in the very last moment, when he, kneeling before his tormentor, stretched out to her hands already stained with the blood of his father and rival: it was in this position that he was arrested. “Take me, me with him, to Siberia! I drove him to it, I am most to blame!” – cried out this woman herself, already in sincere remorse, at the moment of his arrest. The talented young man who took it upon himself to describe this case—the same Mr. Rakitin whom I have already mentioned—in a few concise and characteristic phrases defines the character of this heroine: “Early disillusionment, early deception and downfall, the betrayal of a seducer-fiance who left her, then poverty, the curse of an honest family, and finally, the patronage of a rich old man, whom she, however, still considers her benefactor. In the young heart, which may have contained much good, anger has festered since a very early age. A calculating character has formed, accumulating capital. Cynicism and resentment towards society have formed.” After this description, it is clear that she could have laughed at both only for the sake of the game, for a malicious game. And so, in this month of hopeless love, moral downfall, betrayal of his fiancée, appropriation of other people’s money entrusted to his honor, the defendant, in addition, is driven to near madness, to frenzy, by ceaseless jealousy, and to his father! And what’s more, the crazy old man tempts and seduces the object of his affection—with the very same three thousand rubles that his son considers his family heritage, his mother’s inheritance, and berates his father for. Yes, I agree, it was hard to bear! It could even have brought on madness. It wasn’t about the money, but the fact that with such disgusting cynicism these same funds were shattering his happiness!”

One of the ghost kings replied, "I have long heard of Your Majesty's recruitment of talent, but had no opportunity to meet you. Today, seeing Your Majesty bestowed with the celestial record, enjoying triumphant glory, I specially present this ochre-yellow robe as a celebratory gift. Please, do not cast aside my humble self and accept me as your subordinate, allowing me to serve as your faithful dog or horse." The Monkey King was delighted and donned the ochre-yellow robe. All present, pleased, lined up to pay their respects. He then appointed the ghost king as the vanguard commander of the front forces.

After expressing his gratitude, the ghost king inquired, "Your Majesty, during your time in Heaven, what position was bestowed upon you?" The Monkey King replied, "The Jade Emperor considered me worthy and appointed me as a 'stable keeper'!" 
Hearing this, the ghost king proposed, "With Your Majesty's divine powers, why bother tending horses? Why not become the 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven'? What reason could there be against it?" 
The Monkey King, upon hearing this, was overjoyed and repeatedly exclaimed, "Good! Good! Good!" He ordered his four loyal generals, "Quickly prepare a banner for me, with the inscription 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven' emblazoned upon it. Raise it immediately!" 

From that day forward, he was known only as the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. No longer would anyone address him as Your Majesty. 

The order was also relayed to all the demon kings of the various caves, ensuring everyone was informed.

He walked for a long time along the entire long, narrow corridor, finding no one, and was about to shout loudly when suddenly, in the dark corner, between an old cabinet and the door, he spotted some strange object, something that seemed to be alive. He bent down with his candle and saw a child – a girl of no more than five years old, in a dress that was worn out like a dishcloth, shivering and crying. She didn’t seem to be afraid of Svidrigailov at all, but looked at him with dull surprise with her big black eyes and occasionally hiccuped, like children who had cried for a long time but had stopped and even comforted themselves, but then suddenly hiccuped again. The girl's face was pale and emaciated; she was stiff from the cold, but "how did she get here?  So she hid here and didn't sleep all night." He began to question her. The girl suddenly came to life and began chattering quickly to him in her childish language. There was something about "Mama" and that "Mama splashed," about some kind of cup that "Lyazbilia" (broke). The girl spoke non-stop; it was somehow possible to make out from all these stories that this was an unloved child, whom her mother, some eternally drunken cook, probably from this very hotel, had scolded and frightened; that the girl had broken her mother's cup and was so frightened that she had run away since the evening; she had probably been hiding somewhere in the yard, in the rain, and finally crept in here, hid behind the cabinet and had sat here in the corner all night, crying, shivering from dampness, darkness, and fear that she would now be beaten for all this. He took her in his arms, went to his room, sat her on the bed, and began to undress her. Her holey little shoes, on her bare foot, were so wet as if they had been lying in a puddle all night.  After undressing her, he laid her on the bed, covered her up, and tucked her completely under the covers. She immediately fell asleep. After finishing everything, he again fell into a gloomy thought.

An hour passed before she appeared. We had arrived, and yet not arrived; we were not in a hurry, and yet felt driven by impatience. The young Poles, patriotically dressed, perhaps also spurred on by the military bugle calls that echoed across the water from the area of the public gardens, had come on deck. And, intoxicated by the Asti, they raised cheers to the Bersaglieri drilling over there. But it was repulsive to see in what state the primped old man's false camaraderie with youth had left him. His old brain had not been able to keep up with the wine like the youthful, vigorous ones. He was wretchedly drunk. With glazed eyes, a cigarette trembling between his fingers, he swayed, laboriously maintaining his balance, drawn back and forth by the effects of the alcohol. Because he would have fallen at the first step, he dared not move from his spot, but he showed a pitiful exuberance, grasped anyone who approached him by the buttonhole, babbled, winked, giggled, raised his ringed, wrinkled index finger in childish mockery, and licked his mouth corners with a disgustingly ambiguous gesture. Aschenbach looked at him with furrowed brows, and once again a feeling of dizziness came over him, as if the world were showing a slight, yet not to be contained, inclination to distort itself into the peculiar and grotesque; a feeling to which the circumstances, however, prevented him from succumbing, since the stamping of the machine had once again begun and the ship resumed its voyage through the Canal of San Marco, which had been so near completion. And so he saw him again, the most astonishing landing place, that dazzling composition of fantastical architecture that the Republic presented to the awestruck gaze of approaching sailors: the delicate grandeur of the Palace and the Sighing Bridge, the columns with lions and saints on the bank, the magnificently protruding flank of the fairytale temple, the view through the gate and the giant clock, and he pondered thoughtfully that upon landing, at the train station in Venice, one entered a palace through a back door, and that one could only reach the unlikeliest of cities, just as now he, like a ship, across the high sea.

The行者 exclaimed, "I've never seen this before. But I've always heard people say that ginseng fruit is a grass elixir, and eating it can greatly prolong one's life. Where can I find it now?"
"It's here," said the 八戒. "That boy brought two for Master to eat. The old monk didn't recognize it, saying it was the fruit of a three-day-old child, and he didn't dare eat it. The boy was lazy. Since Master wouldn't eat, he must have taken them for himself. He's been eating them one by one in the next room, crunching and crunching. It makes my mouth water just thinking about it. How can we not try some? I think you're clever; why don't you sneak into his garden and steal a few?"
"This is easy," said the行者. "Old Sun will get them." He was about to leave when the 八戒 grabbed him and said, "Brother, I heard him say in here that he was going to use a golden mallet to hit something. We have to be careful and not alert him."
"I know, I know," said the行者.

The pain did not lessen; but Ivan Ilyich made an effort to convince himself that he was getting better. And he could deceive himself as long as nothing disturbed him. But as soon as there was some trouble with his wife, a failure at work, or bad cards in whist, he would immediately feel the full force of his illness. Sometimes he would endure these misfortunes, waiting for things to improve, for him to overcome the bad luck, for success, a big win. But now every failure would undermine him and plunge him into despair. He would tell himself: just when I was starting to get better, the medicine was beginning to work, and then this accursed misfortune or unpleasantness… And he would be angry at the misfortune or at the people who were causing him trouble and killing him, and he would feel this anger killing him too; but he couldn't help it. It would seem to him that he should be clear that this resentment towards circumstances and people was worsening his illness and that therefore he should ignore unpleasant incidents; but he reasoned quite the opposite: he said that he needed peace, he watched everything that disturbed this peace, and at the slightest disturbance, he would become irritated. The fact that he read medical books and consulted doctors made matters worse. The deterioration was so even that he could deceive himself by comparing one day with another — there was little difference. But when he consulted doctors, it seemed to him that things were getting worse and very quickly at that. And despite this, he constantly consulted doctors.

He roared, and they rose like in a storm, dressed themselves, and remained, without a word, sitting by the lamp until it passed. And the women, who were close to giving birth, were put in the remotest rooms and under the thickest bed coverings; but they heard it, they heard it, as if it were in their own bodies, and they begged to be allowed to rise too, and came, pale and wide-eyed, and sat down with the others with their blurred faces. And the cows, which were calving at this time, were helpless and shut in, and one was forced to pull the dead fruit with all its entrails from its body, as it didn't want to come at all. And everyone did their work poorly and forgot to bring in the hay, because they were afraid of the night by day and because from the constant wakefulness and the frightened rising they were so exhausted that they couldn't think straight. And when they went to the white, peaceful church on Sunday, they prayed that there would be no more Lord on Ulsgaard: for this one was a terrible Lord. And what they all thought and prayed, that the parson said aloud from the pulpit, for he too had no nights anymore and couldn't understand God. And the bell said it, which had gotten a terrible rival, who thundered all night long and against whom it, even if it began to ring out of all its metal, could do nothing. Yes, everyone said it, and there was one among the young people who had dreamed that he had gone into the castle and had killed the gracious Lord with his pitchfork, and so upset were they, so at an end, so overstimulated, that they all listened as he told his dream, and looked at him, without knowing it, to see if he was capable of such a deed. Thus they felt and spoke throughout the entire area, where they had still loved and mourned the chamberlain a few weeks earlier. But although they spoke like that, nothing changed. – No, you see, you don't believe me, you think I'm just pulling your leg, – Porfiry picked up, growing more and more joyful and incessantly giggling with pleasure, and again beginning to pace the room, – of course, you're right; my figure is so divinely made that it only inspires comical thoughts in others; a buffoon, you see;[56] but I'll tell you, and I'll repeat it again, that you, father, Rodion Romanovich, forgive me, an old man, am still young, so to speak, in the first bloom of youth, and therefore value human intellect above all, just like all young people. Playful wit and detached reasoning delight you. And that's precisely like the old Austrian war council,[57] as much as I can judge of military events: on paper, they defeated Napoleon, captured him, and in their offices, they calculated and summed it all up in the most clever way, but look, General Mac surrenders with his whole army, hee-hee-hee! I see, I see, father Rodion Romanovich, you are laughing at me, that I, such a civil servant, am bringing up examples from military history. What can I do, it's a weakness, I love military affairs, and I love to read all these military reports... I practically missed my calling. I should have served in the military, for sure. Maybe not have become Napoleon, but at least a major, hee-hee-hee! Well, now I'll tell you, my dear fellow, the whole truth about this particular case: reality and nature, sir, are important things, and how often the most insightful calculations are thwarted! Hey, listen to the old man, I'm speaking seriously, Rodion Romanovich (saying this, the barely thirty-five-year-old Porfiry Petrovich truly seemed to have aged suddenly; even his voice changed, and he seemed to hunch over), – besides, I am an open man-s… Am I an open man or not? What do you think? It seems so: I am sharing these kinds of things with you for free, and I don't even ask for a reward for it, hee-hee! Well, so, I continue-s: wit, in my opinion, is a magnificent thing-s; it is, so to speak, a beauty of nature and a solace of life, and what kind of tricks can it play, that sometimes it's impossible even for a poor detective, who is also enthralled by his own imagination, as always happens, because he is also a man-s! But the poor detective's nature saves him, that's the trouble! And the youth, captivated by wit, doesn't even think about this. They "walk through all obstacles," (as you so cleverly and cunningly expressed it). He may lie, that is, the man-s, in this particular case-s, incognito-s, and lie brilliantly, with the utmost cunning; here, it seems, would be the triumph, and enjoy the fruits of his wit, but then, bam! Right in the most interesting, in the most scandalous place, he faints. It's a sickness, sometimes there's stuffiness in the room too, but still-s! It's still a thought! He lied flawlessly, but couldn't calculate for his nature. There's the cunning, see-s! Another time, carried away by the playfulness of his wit, he will begin to fool the one suspecting him; he will pale as if intentionally, as if in a game, but he will pale too naturally, too truly, and again, a thought is presented! Even if he bluffs the first time, he'll think it over by night, if the other fellow isn't a fool himself. But this happens at every turn-s! What's more, he himself will start to run ahead, he'll start to intrude where he's not asked, he'll start to talk incessantly about what he should be silent about, he'll start to bring up various allegories, hee-hee! he'll even come and ask: why don't they arrest me for so long? hee-hee-hee! And this can happen to even the most witty person, to a psychologist and a writer-s! Nature is a mirror, a very transparent one-s! Look into it and admire, that's all-s! But what is this, you have paled so much, Rodion Romanovich, aren't you feeling stuffy, shouldn't we open a window?

Peter Ivanovich sighed even deeper and more sorrowfully, and Praskovya Fedorovna gratefully clasped his hand. Entering her drawing-room, lined with rose-colored chintz and lit by a gloomy lamp, they sat down at the table: she on the sofa, and Peter Ivanovich on a low pouf, whose springs were broken and uncomfortably offered him as a seat. Praskovya Fedorovna wanted to warn him to sit in another chair, but she found such a warning unbecoming of her position and changed her mind.  As he sat down on the pouf, Peter Ivanovich recalled how Ivan Ilyich had furnished this drawing-room and consulted with him about this very rose-colored chintz with green leaves. As she sat down on the sofa and passed by the table (the drawing-room was, in fact, full of trinkets and furniture), the widow’s black lace veil snagged on the carving of the table. Peter Ivanovich rose to unhook it, and the released pouf began to sway and nudge him. The widow herself began to unhook her lace, and Peter Ivanovich sat down again, pressing down on the rebellious pouf. But the widow hadn’t unhooked it all, and Peter Ivanovich rose again, and the pouf rebelled once more, even clicking. When it was finally over, she pulled out a clean batiste handkerchief and began to cry. The episode with the lace and the struggle with the pouf chilled Peter Ivanovich, and he sat frowning. This awkward situation was interrupted by Sokolov, Ivan Ilyich’s waiter, with a report that the plot of land at the cemetery, which Praskovya Fedorovna had chosen, would cost two hundred rubles. She stopped crying and, with the air of a victim, looked at Peter Ivanovich and said in French that she found it very difficult. Peter Ivanovich made a silent gesture expressing his unshakeable conviction that this was inevitable.

Three years had passed, and the Master ascended the sacred seat once more to discourse with the multitude. He spoke of paradoxical sayings and debated the encompassing nature of appearances. He suddenly asked, “Where is Wukong?” Wukong stepped forward and knelt, saying, “Disciple is here.” The Master said, “What path have you been cultivating all this while?” Wukong replied, “Disciple's understanding of the Dharma nature has become profound, and the roots have also grown firm.” The Master said, “Since you have grasped the Dharma nature and gained a solid foundation, you have entered the state of embodied spirit, yet you are merely guarding against the ‘three calamities.’” Hearing this, Wukong pondered for a long time before saying, “Master, your words are amiss. I often hear that those of great virtue and high attainment live as long as Heaven, traversing fire and water unscathed, immune to a hundred diseases. How can there be these ‘three calamities’?” The Master said, “This is an exceptional path: one that defies the natural order of Heaven and Earth, encroaching upon the profound mysteries of sun and moon. After the elixir is perfected, even spirits and demons cannot abide. Though your appearance may remain youthful for millennia, after five hundred years, a thunderbolt will descend from Heaven, striking you. You must see into your true nature and clear your mind to escape. If you evade it, you will live as long as Heaven; if not, you will perish instantly. Another five hundred years later, a fire calamity will descend from Heaven. This is not Heaven’s fire, nor is it ordinary fire; it is called ‘Yin fire,’ arising from the source well at the base of your spine, searing upwards through the palace of your body, turning your five viscera to ash and your four limbs to dust. Your thousand years of arduous practice will be rendered utterly hollow. Five hundred years after that, a wind calamity will strike. This is not the wind from the east, west, north, or south, nor the wind that blows gold or the wind that rustles leaves or bamboo; it is called ‘Bi wind.’ It will blow in from the fontanelle at the top of your head, passing through your six internal organs, dantian, and nine orifices, causing your flesh and bone to disintegrate. You will cease to exist.”

Wukong, upon hearing this, was chilled to the bone. He bowed his head in prostration and said, “Grandmaster, out of compassion, you have revealed the method to evade these three calamities. I will never forget your kindness.”

The Master said, “This is not difficult, but since you are different from others, I cannot pass it on.”

Wukong said, “I too have a round head reaching for the heavens and feet that touch the ground, with nine orifices, four limbs, five viscera, and six bowels. How am I different?”

The Master said, “Though you resemble a human, you lack cheeks.” Wukong realized his cheekbones were flat and his face was narrow and pointed. He reached out and touched his face, smiling and saying, “Master, your calculation is wrong! Though I lack cheeks, I have this pouch, which can be used to avert disaster just as well.”

The Master said, “Very well, if you wish to learn like an ordinary person, there are thirty-six celestial transformations and seventy-two terrestrial transformations.”

Wukong said, “Disciple is willing to delve into the depths and learn one terrestrial transformation.”

The Master said, “If that’s your wish, come closer, and I will impart the secret mantra.” He leaned in and whispered something to him. It was a wondrous method. This Monkey King was a quick learner, understanding immediately. Once he grasped the mantra, he practiced diligently, and mastered all seventy-two terrestrial transformations.

Sun Wukong, upon hearing this, pondered deeply and said, "Master, your words are mistaken. The Master said, "This is the extraordinary way: it steals Heaven and Earth's transformations, violates the mysteries of the sun and moon; after the elixir is formed, spirits and demons cannot bear it. If you evade it, you will live as long as Heaven; if you cannot, your life will end. Another five hundred years later, a heavenly fire will descend upon you. This fire is not heavenly fire nor mortal fire; it is called 'yin fire.' It rises from the wellspring beneath your body, burning through your earthen palace, turning your five organs to ash and your limbs to decay, rendering your thousand years of ascetic practice illusory. Another five hundred years, and a wind calamity will blow upon you. This wind is not the southeast wind, northwest wind, wind of incense, moon, gold, nor the wind of flowers, willows, pine, or bamboo; it is called 'bi wind.' It blows from the fontanelle, enters your six organs, passes through the dantian, pierces the nine orifices, causing your bones and flesh to become loose, and your body to dissolve. Sun Wukong said, "I have a round head, stand on two feet, possess nine orifices and four limbs, five organs and six internal organs. How am I different from others?" The Master said, "Although you resemble a human, you lack cheeks." It turned out that the monkey had a narrow face, sunken cheeks, and a pointed mouth. The Master said, "Very well, if you wish to learn like an ordinary person, you need to understand the celestial and terrestrial transformations. Early the next morning, the monk saddled his horse, packed his belongings, and set out. The monks sent him off from afar. The traveler led the way, it being the season of spring thaw. One could see: the grass carpeted the jade-colored horse's hooves with soft trails, willow branches swayed with golden threads of dew, newly blooming. Peaches and apricots filled the forest, vying for beauty. Ivy vines wound around the paths, exuding vibrant energy. On the sandy dike, warmed by the sun, mandarin ducks slept. In the mountain stream, the fragrance of flowers attracted butterflies. It was as if spring was halfway through, having chased away autumn and winter. It was impossible to know when, after walking for so long, he would truly attain the literary merit he sought.

The master and disciple traveled for seven days on desolate roads. Suddenly, one day as dusk approached, they saw a village in the distance. The Master said, "Sun Wukong, look, there's a mountain villa near the wall. Let's rest there for the night and continue our journey tomorrow." Sun Wukong said, "Wait a moment, let me see if it's a place of good or ill fortune before deciding."  The Master held his reins, while Sun Wukong fixed his gaze upon it. Truly:

bamboo fences stood thick, thatched roofs covered many houses.  Towering wild trees greeted them at the gate, and a curved water bridge reflected the house windows. Beside the path, willow trees stood green and rustling. Within the garden, flowers bloomed, filling the air with fragrance. As the sun sank in the west, the forest echoed with birdsong. Smoke rose from hearths, and winding paths led to grazing cattle and sheep. Chickens and pigs lay sleeping in the corners of houses, and a drunk old man sang from nearby.

Sun Wukong said, "Master, let's go. It's definitely a good family, and we can rest there." The Master urged his white horse forward and soon arrived at the village entrance.  A young man emerged, wrapped in a cotton cloth, wearing a blue robe. He carried an umbrella and a bag, his clothes tucked in and tied at the waist, and wore three-eared straw sandals. He walked briskly, like a determined warrior. Sun Wukong grabbed his arm and asked, "Where are you going? Tell me, what is this place called?" The man struggled furiously, shouting, "I'm going back to my village! I need to deliver a message!" Sun Wukong laughed and said, "Don't be upset, friend. Helping others is also helping yourself. Tell me the name of the place, it'll solve your problem." The man couldn't break free, panicking and hopping around, "Screech! Screech! My father is under so much pressure, and I run into this bald head, his aura is suffocating!"

Sun Wukong said, "If you have the ability, break free from my hand, then go on." The man twisted and turned, but he couldn't move, feeling like a vise had clamped onto him. He was furious, dropping his bag and umbrella, and attacking Sun Wukong with fists like rain. Sun Wukong held his luggage in one hand, blocking the man's attacks with the other.  No matter how the man struggled, he couldn't reach him. Sun Wukong held on tighter, growing increasingly irritated. The sound of his anger was like thunder.

The Master said, "Sun Wukong, doesn't anyone else live here? You're just holding onto him, why not ask someone else?" Sun Wukong smiled, "Master, if we asked someone else, it would be pointless. We need to ask him, that's where the business lies." 

The man, unable to escape Sun Wukong's grip, finally revealed, "This is the borderland of U-Shi-T'ang, called Gao Lao Village. Most of the people here are surnamed Gao, hence the name Gao Lao Village. Please let me go." Sun Wukong replied, "You're dressed for a journey, not someone who travels easily. Tell me honestly where you're going and what you're doing. Then I'll let you go." The man, desperate, finally revealed his true situation: "I'm Gao Taigong's grandson, named Gao Cai. My grandfather has a daughter, twenty years old, who's never been married. Three years ago, she was taken by a demon. The demon has been acting as her husband for three years. My grandfather is unhappy, saying that having a demon as a daughter-in-law is bad for his family's reputation. He wants to expel the demon, as it brings no fortune and no in-laws to visit. The demon refuses to leave, locking my sister in his backyard. He'll keep her for half a year, refusing to let her see any of us. My grandfather gave me some silver and told me to find a master to exorcise the demon.  I've been searching for months, hiring several monks and Taoists. They're all useless, unable to defeat the demon. They scolded me, saying I'm incompetent, and gave me five copper coins to travel further and find a capable master.  Unexpectedly, I ran into you, Sun Wukong, grabbing me and delaying my journey. I'm furious! But you seem to have some means, and I can't break free from your grip. So, I'm telling you everything."

Sun Wukong said, "Your fate has brought us together. This is a fortunate coincidence. You don't need to travel far and waste your money. We are not those useless monks or inept Taoists. We have some methods and are skilled at dealing with demons. We're here to help you. We are holy monks sent from the Eastern Land on a pilgrimage to the West to seek the scriptures. We are also skilled in exorcising demons."

Gao Cai said, "Don't fool me! I'm a very angry man. If you're just making empty promises and can't actually exorcise the demon, I'll be even more miserable!" Sun Wukong said, "Don't worry, we won't disappoint you. Come, lead us to your house."

The man had no choice but to lead them. He picked up his bag and umbrella and turned back, guiding the master and disciple to the front door.  "Masters," he said, "please wait on the platform for a moment while I inform my father." Sun Wukong then released his grip. He unshouldered his luggage and led the horse. The master and disciple waited at the side of the house.

This ordered presentation startled K. at first, then he said as quietly as the painter, “I believe you contradict yourself.”

“How so?” the painter asked patiently, leaning back with a smile. 

This smile gave K. the feeling that he was now about to discover contradictions not in the painter’s words, but in the court proceedings themselves. Nonetheless, he didn’t back down and said, “You earlier remarked that the court is inaccessible for reasons of evidence, later you restricted this to the public court, and now you even say that the innocent don’t need help from the court. That’s a contradiction. Furthermore, you earlier said that judges can be personally influenced, but now you deny that a real acquittal, as you call it, can ever be achieved through personal influence. That’s the second contradiction.”

“These contradictions are easy to clear up,” the painter said. “Here two different things are being discussed: what the law states and what I have personally experienced; you mustn’t confuse the two. The law, which I haven’t actually read, naturally states on the one hand that the innocent are acquitted, but on the other hand it doesn’t state that judges can be influenced. Now, however, I have experienced the opposite. I know of no real acquittals, but many influences. It’s of course possible that in all the cases I know of there was no innocence. But isn’t that unlikely?  Even as a child, I listened closely to my father when he talked about trials at home, even the judges who came to his atelier talked about the court; in our circles we talk about nothing else; as soon as I had the opportunity to go to court myself, I always took it; I’ve attended countless trials in important stages, and as far as they are visible, I have followed them, and – I must admit – not experienced a single real acquittal.”

“Not a single acquittal then,” K. said, as if speaking to himself and his hopes. “That confirms the opinion I already had of the court. So it’s useless from this side as well. A single executioner could replace the whole court.”

“You mustn’t generalize,” the painter said, dissatisfied, “I’ve only spoken from my experiences.”

“That’s enough,” said K., “or have you heard of acquittals from earlier times?”

“Such acquittals,” the painter replied, “may have existed. But it’s very difficult to ascertain that. The final decisions of the court are not published, they aren’t even accessible to the judges; as a result, only legends have survived about old court cases. These even contain, in the majority, real acquittals; you can believe them, they are verifiable, but not completely. Nonetheless, we mustn’t completely disregard them; they certainly contain a certain truth, and they are very beautiful; I myself have painted some pictures based on these legends.”

“Bare legends don’t change my mind,” K. said, “can you not appeal to these legends in court either?” 

The painter laughed. “No, you can’t,” he said.

“Then it’s pointless to talk about it,” K. said; he was willing to accept the painter’s opinions for now, even if he found them unlikely and contrary to other reports. He didn’t have the time to check or even refute everything the painter said; it was the utmost he could achieve to convince the painter to help him in some way, even if it wasn’t decisive. Therefore, he said, “Let’s set aside the question of a real acquittal, you mentioned two other possibilities.”

“The apparent acquittal and the postponement. That’s all that remains,” the painter said. “But before we discuss them, don’t you want to take off your coat? It’s getting quite warm in here.”

“Yes,” said K., who had been paying attention only to the painter’s explanations, but now, reminded of the heat, broke out in a sweat. “It’s almost unbearable.”

The painter nodded, as if he understood K.’s discomfort very well. “Couldn’t we open the window?” K. asked.

“No,” the painter said. “It’s just a fixed glass pane, you can’t open it.” Now K. realized that he had been hoping all along that the painter or he himself would suddenly go to the window and fling it open. He had been prepared to breathe in the mist with his mouth agape. The feeling of being completely shut off from the air caused him dizziness. He lightly struck the feather bed beside him and said in a weak voice, “This is uncomfortable and unhealthy.”

“Oh no,” the painter said, defending his window, “because it can’t be opened, even though it’s just a simple pane, it holds the heat better than a double-glazed window. If I want to air out the room, which isn’t really necessary, since air seeps in through the joists, I can open one of my doors, or even both.” 

K., comforted slightly by this explanation, looked around for the second door. The painter noticed this and said, “It’s behind you, I had to push it in with the bed.” 

Only now did K. see the small door in the wall. “It’s just too small for an atelier here,” the painter said, as if anticipating K.’s criticism. “I had to make do as best as I could. The bed in front of the door is of course in a very bad place. The judge, for example, whom I’m painting now, always comes through the door when he’s by the bed, and I’ve also given him a key to this door, so that he can wait for me here in the atelier even when I’m not at home. However, he usually comes early in the morning, while I’m still asleep. He naturally always rouses me from the deepest sleep when he opens the door next to the bed. You would lose all respect for the judges if you heard the curses I hurl at him when he steps over my bed in the morning. I could take the key away from him, but it would just make things worse. You can break down any door here with the slightest effort.”

While the painter was speaking, K. pondered whether he should take off his coat. In the end, he realized that if he didn’t, he wouldn’t be able to stay here any longer; he took off his coat, but laid it over his knees so that he could put it back on if the discussion ended.

As soon as he had taken off his coat, one of the girls cried out, “He’s taken off his coat already!” and you could hear them all crowding around the slits to see the spectacle. 

“The girls think,” the painter said, “that I’m going to paint you, and that’s why you’re taking off your clothes.”

“Well,” K. said, not very amused, because he didn’t feel much better than before, although he was now sitting in his shirt sleeves. He asked almost gruffly, “What were those two other possibilities you mentioned?”

“The apparent acquittal and the postponement,” the painter said. “It’s up to you which one you choose. Both are achievable with my help, of course, not without effort; the difference lies in this: the apparent acquittal requires a collected, temporary effort, while the postponement demands a much smaller, but enduring one.” 

“First, then, the apparent acquittal. If you wish that, I’ll write on a piece of paper a confirmation of your innocence. The text for such a confirmation has been passed down to me from my father and is completely unassailable. With this confirmation, I’ll go on a round of visits to the judges I know.  I’ll start, for example, by presenting the confirmation to the judge I’m painting now this evening when he comes to the session. I’ll lay it before him, explain that you’re innocent, and vouch for your innocence. That’s not just a superficial, but a real, binding guarantee.”

"The girls believe," said the painter, "that I am going to paint you and that that's why you are taking off your clothes." "Well," said K., not very amused, because he didn't feel much better than before, although he was now sitting in his shirt sleeves. Almost gloomily, he asked, "What were the two other possibilities again?" He had already forgotten the terms. "The apparent acquittal and the deferral," said the painter. "It is up to you which one you choose. Both are achievable with my help, of course not without effort, the difference in this respect is that the apparent acquittal demands a collective, temporary one, the deferral a much smaller, but lasting effort. First then the apparent acquittal. If you should desire this, I will write a confirmation of your innocence on a sheet of paper. The text for such a confirmation was passed down to me by my father and is quite unassailable. With this confirmation, I will then make the rounds among the judges I know. So I will start by presenting the confirmation to the judge I am currently painting, this evening, when he comes to the session. I will present the confirmation to him, explain that you are innocent, and vouch for your innocence. This is not just a superficial, but a real, binding guarantee." There was a reproachful look in the painter's eyes as if K. wanted to burden him with such a guarantee. "That would be very kind," said K. "And the judge would believe you and still not really acquit me?" "As I said," answered the painter. "By the way, it's not at all certain that everyone would believe me, some judges, for example, will demand that I bring you to them myself. Then you would have to come along once. However, in such a case, the matter is already half won, especially since I would, of course, inform you beforehand about how you should behave before the betreffende judge. It is worse with the judges who, and this will also happen, reject me from the outset. On these we must, if I don't fail at multiple attempts, certainly not give up, but we are also allowed to, because individual judges cannot decide the outcome here. If I now have a sufficient number of judges' signatures on this confirmation, I will go to the judge who is currently presiding over your trial with it. Maybe I even have his signature, then everything will develop even faster than usual. In general, there are then no more major obstacles, it is then the time of highest hope for the accused. It is remarkable, but true, that people are more hopeful in this time than after the acquittal. Now no special effort is needed. The judge has the guarantee of a number of judges in the confirmation, can acquit you unburdened and will, after going through various formalities, undoubtedly do so for me and other acquaintances. You then leave the court and are free." "Then I am free," said K., hesitantly. "Yes," said the painter, "but only seemingly free, or, better expressed, temporarily free. It was a very rainy, stormy morning when K., full of annoyance at the day ahead, arrived at the office at seven o’clock, in order to get some work done before the visitor took everything away from him. He was very tired, because he had spent half the night studying an Italian grammar in preparation; the window, which he had spent far too much time sitting by recently, was more tempting than the desk, but he resisted and sat down to work. Unfortunately, the servant just then entered and reported that the Director had sent him to see if the Commercial Manager was already there; if he was, he was to be so kind as to come to the reception room, as the gentleman from Italy was already there. “I’ll be right there,” said K., tucked a small dictionary into his pocket, took an album of city sights, which he had prepared for the foreigner, under his arm, and went through the Deputy Director’s office into the Director’s room. He was pleased to have arrived at the office so early and to be immediately available – something that no one had probably seriously expected. The Deputy Director’s office was, of course, still empty as on a dark night; the servant had probably tried to summon him to the reception room as well, but without success. When K. entered the reception room, the two gentlemen rose from the deep armchairs. The Director smiled amiably; he was obviously very pleased about K.’s arrival; he immediately arranged for introductions, the Italian shook K.’s hand heartily and, smiling, called someone a “early bird.” K. did not quite understand who he meant; it was also a strange word, the meaning of which K. only guessed after a while. He replied with a few polite phrases, which the Italian accepted with laughter, while he repeatedly ran his nervous hand over his gray-blue, bushy mustache. This mustache was apparently perfumed; one was almost tempted to approach and smell it. As everyone sat down and a small, introductory conversation began, K. noticed with great discomfort that he only understood the Italian in fragments. When he spoke very calmly, K. understood him almost completely; these were only rare exceptions, mostly the words poured out of his mouth, he shook his head as if enjoying it. At such times, however, he would regularly get into some dialect, which held nothing Italian for K., but which the Director not only understood but also spoke, which K. could, of course, have foreseen, as the Italian came from southern Italy, where the Director had lived for some years. In any case, K. realized that the possibility of understanding the Italian was largely denied to him, since his French was also difficult to understand; besides, the mustache concealed the movements of his lips, whose sight might have helped with comprehension. K. began to foresee many inconveniences; for the time being, he gave up trying to understand the Italian – in the presence of the Director, who understood him so easily, it would have been an unnecessary effort – and he limited himself to watching him with displeasure as he reclined deeply but lightly in the armchair, as he often tugged at his short, sharply cut jacket, and as he once raised his arms and with loosely moving hands tried to depict something that K. could not grasp, although he kept his eyes fixed on the hands. Finally, the earlier fatigue took hold of K., who otherwise followed the back and forth of the conversation mechanically with his eyes, and he caught himself, fortunately just in time, in the act of wanting to get up distractedly, turn around and walk away. Finally, the Italian looked at his watch and jumped up. After bidding farewell to the Director, he pressed himself against K., so close that K. had to push his armchair back to be able to move. The Director, who certainly recognized K.’s distress in his dealings with this Italian, intervened in the conversation, so cleverly and delicately that it seemed as if he was only adding small pieces of advice, while in reality he explained everything that the Italian, tirelessly interrupting him, was saying, in the shortest possible way to K. K. learned from him that the Italian still had some business to attend to, that unfortunately he only had a little time in general, that he certainly did not intend to rush through all the sights, that he had, however, – although only if K. agreed, the decision rested with him – decided to visit only the Cathedral, but to do so thoroughly. He was extremely happy to be able to take this tour in the company of such a learned and amiable man – this referred to K., who was busy with nothing other than eavesdropping on the Italian and quickly catching the Director’s words – and he asked him, if he was free, to meet him in the Cathedral in two hours, around ten o’clock. He himself hoped to be there for sure by then. K. replied accordingly, the Italian shook hands first with the Director, then with K., then again with the Director and went out, followed by the two of them, only half turned towards them, still not stopping talking, towards the door. K. then remained with the Director for a while longer, who looked particularly miserable today. He seemed to want to apologize to K. in some way and said – they stood close together confidentially – that at first he had intended to go with the Italian himself, but then – he did not give a closer reason – he had decided to send K. instead. If K. didn’t understand the Italian at the beginning, he shouldn’t be surprised, comprehension would come quickly, and even if he didn’t understand much at all, it wouldn’t be so bad, because it wasn’t so important for the Italian to be understood. By the way, K.’s Italian was surprisingly good, and he would certainly get along well with it. With that, K. was dismissed. The time that remained to him, he spent writing down rare words from the dictionary that he needed for guidance in the Cathedral. It was extremely tedious work; servants brought in the mail, officials came with various requests and remained by the door, as they saw K. busy, without moving away, until they had been heard by him; the Deputy Director did not miss the opportunity to disturb K., often came in, took the dictionary out of his hand and apparently leafed through it meaninglessly; even parties appeared in the semi-darkness of the antechamber when the door opened and bowed hesitantly – they wanted to draw attention to themselves, but were unsure if they had been seen – all of this moved around K. as if he were its center, while he himself put together the words he needed, then looked them up in the dictionary, then wrote them down, then practiced their pronunciation and finally tried to memorize them. His former good memory seemed to have deserted him completely; sometimes he became so angry with the Italian who caused him this effort that he buried the dictionary under papers with the firm intention of no longer preparing, then he realized that he could not simply walk around with the Italian silently before the works of art in the Cathedral, and he pulled the dictionary out again with even greater anger.

Right after the greetings – settling into the armchair, which K. invited him to do, he had no time – he asked K. for a short private conversation. K. was silent, he knew what was coming, but, suddenly relaxed from the strenuous work he had been doing, he initially gave himself over to a pleasant lethargy and looked out the window at the opposite side of the street, of which only a small, triangular section was visible from his seat, a piece of bare wall between two shop windows.
