Today I received the letter and naturally drove over immediately. For no other reason, but it seems like a sufficient reason. I can read you the passage of the letter that concerns you." He pulled the letter out of his wallet. "Here it is." She writes: 'Josef, I haven't seen you for a long time, last week I was once at the bank, but Josef was so busy that I wasn't allowed in; I waited for almost an hour, but then I had to go home because I had a piano lesson. I would have liked to speak to him, perhaps an opportunity will arise soon. For my name day, he sent me a large box of chocolates, it was very kind and thoughtful. I had forgotten to write to you about it back then, only now, since you are asking, do I remember. Chocolates, you must know, disappear from the boarding house immediately, as soon as one becomes aware that one has been gifted with chocolates, they are already gone. But as for Josef, I wanted to tell you something else. As mentioned, I wasn't allowed in to him at the bank because he was negotiating with a gentleman. After I had waited quietly for a while, I asked a servant if the negotiation would last long. He said that it probably would, because it was probably about the trial against the head clerk. I asked what kind of trial it was, if he wasn't mistaken, but he said he wasn't mistaken, it was a trial, and a serious one, he didn't know more. He himself would like to help the head clerk, because he is a good and just man, but he doesn't know how to start, and he just wishes that influential gentlemen would take over. This will certainly happen, and it will eventually have a good ending, but for now, as he could gather from the mood of the head clerk, it is not going well at all. I didn't pay much attention to this speech, of course, I also tried to reassure the simple servant, forbade him to talk about it to anyone else, and consider the whole thing as nonsense. Nevertheless, it might be good if you, dearest father, looked into the matter during your next visit, it will be easy for you to find out more and, if it really becomes necessary, to intervene with your great, influential acquaintances. Should it not be necessary, which is probably the most likely, then it will at least give your daughter the opportunity to hug you soon, which would make her happy.' – 'A good child,' said the uncle when he finished reading, and wiped away some tears. K. nodded, he had completely forgotten Erna due to the various disturbances of recent times, even her birthday had slipped his mind, and the story about the chocolate was apparently only invented to protect him from his uncle and aunt. It was very touching, and with the theatre tickets, which he intended to send her regularly from now on, certainly not sufficiently rewarded, but he didn't feel suited to visiting the boarding house and having conversations with an eighteen-year-old schoolgirl right now. "And what do you say now?" asked the uncle, who had forgotten all his haste and excitement through the letter and seemed to be reading it again. "Yes, Uncle," said K., "it's true." I did not attach much importance to this speech, of course, I also tried to reassure the simple servant, forbade him to speak about it to others, and consider the whole thing as nonsense. Nevertheless, it might be good if you, dearest father, would look into the matter during your next visit, it will be easy for you to find out more and, if it really is necessary, to intervene with your great, influential acquaintances. Should it not be necessary, which is probably the most likely, then it will at least soon give your daughter the opportunity to hug you, which would please her." "A good child," said the uncle, when he had finished reading, and wiped some tears from his eyes. K. nodded; as a result of the various disruptions of the last few weeks, he had completely forgotten about Erna, he had even forgotten her birthday, and the story about the chocolates was apparently only invented to protect him from his uncle and aunt. It was very touching, and with the theatre tickets that he wanted to send her regularly from now on, certainly not adequately rewarded, but visits to the pension and conversations with an eighteen-year-old schoolgirl did not feel right to him at the moment. "And what do you say now?" asked the uncle, who had forgotten all haste and excitement thanks to the letter and seemed to be reading it again. "Yes, Uncle," said K., "it's true." "True?" the uncle exclaimed.

Immediately after the greetings – he had no time to settle into the armchair which K. offered him – he asked K. for a short private conversation. "It's necessary," he said, swallowing with effort, "for my peace of mind, it's necessary." K. immediately sent the servants out of the room, with instructions not to let anyone in. "What have I heard, Josef?" cried the uncle, once they were alone, sat down on the table and, without looking up, stuffed various papers under himself to sit more comfortably. K. was silent; he knew what was coming, but, suddenly relaxed from the exhausting work he had been doing, he at first surrendered to a pleasant lethargy and looked out the window at the opposite side of the street, which, from his seat, offered only a small, triangular glimpse – a piece of bare wall between two shop windows. "You are looking out the window!" cried the uncle, his arms raised, "For heaven's sake, Josef, answer me! Is it true, can it possibly be true?" "Dear Uncle," said K., pulling himself away from his distraction, "I don't even know what you want from me." "Josef," said the uncle warningly, "you have always told the truth, as far as I know. Should I take your last words as a bad omen?" "I guess I know what you want," said K. obediently, "you've probably heard about my trial." "That's right," replied the uncle, nodding slowly, "I heard about your trial." "From whom?" asked K. "Erna wrote to me," said the uncle, "she doesn't have much contact with you, you unfortunately don't care much for her, but she found out. Today I received the letter and, of course, came immediately. For no other reason, but it seems to be a sufficient one. I can read you the passage that concerns you." He took the letter out of his wallet. "Here it is."  She writes: 'Josef, I haven't seen you for a long time. Last week I was once at the bank, but Josef was so busy that I wasn't allowed in; I waited for almost an hour, but then had to go home because I had piano lessons. I would have liked to speak to him, perhaps there will be an opportunity next time. For my name day he sent me a large box of chocolates, it was very kind and thoughtful. I had forgotten to write to you about it then, only now, since you asked me, do I remember. Chocolates, you must know, disappear immediately in the pension, as soon as one becomes aware that one has been given chocolates, they are already gone. "And what do you say now?" asked the uncle, who had forgotten all the urgency and excitement due to the letter and seemed to be reading it again. "Yes, Uncle," said K., "it's true." Nobody paid any attention to him, though. The family was completely absorbed in the violin playing; the lodgers, who at first, with their hands in their pockets, had positioned themselves far too close behind the sister's music stand, so that they could all see the notes—which must have been a nuisance to her—soon withdrew to the window with half-whispered conversations and heads bowed. The father watched them with evident concern, and they stayed there. It really seemed as though, disappointed in their assumption of hearing beautiful or entertaining music, they were tired of the whole performance and only allowed themselves to be disturbed in their tranquility out of politeness. Especially the way they all puffed smoke from their cigars upwards from their noses and mouths gave an impression of great nervousness. And yet, the sister played so beautifully. Her face was tilted to the side, her gaze searching and sad, following the lines of the notes. Gregor crept a little further forward and held his head close to the floor, hoping perhaps to meet her gaze. Was he an animal, to be so moved by music? It felt as if the path to the longed-for, unknown nourishment was being shown to him. He was determined to push his way to his sister, to tug at her skirt and thereby hint to her that she should come into his room with her violin, for no one here deserved her music as he did. He didn't want to let her out of his room anymore, at least not as long as he lived; his frightening form would be useful to him for the first time; he wanted to be at all the doors of his room at once, barking at the attackers; but his sister should stay with him voluntarily; she should sit next to him on the sofa, lean her ear to him, and he would then confide in her that he had the firm intention of sending her to the Conservatory, and that he would have told everyone that, if not for the misfortune that had intervened, last Christmas—Christmas was surely over by now?—without paying any attention to any objections. After this explanation, the sister would burst into tears of emotion, and Gregor would rise up to her shoulder and kiss her neck, which she had been wearing free of any collar or band since she started working.

Heidi had probably waited ten minutes and looked around on all sides to see if the children with the goats were anywhere in sight.  As they weren't, she climbed a little higher, so that she could better oversee the entire meadow, and from there she looked back and forth with signs of great impatience on her face and in her movements. Meanwhile, the children approached on a long detour, because Peter knew many places where there were all sorts of good things for his goats to nibble on in the bushes and shrubs; therefore he made many turns on the path with his flock. At first, the child had climbed wearily, panting from the heat and discomfort in his heavy armor, straining every muscle. He didn't say a word, but looked uncomprehendingly first at Peter, who with his bare feet and light trousers jumped back and forth effortlessly, and then at the goats, who with their thin, slender legs climbed even more easily over bushes and stones and steep slopes.  Suddenly the child sat down on the ground, quickly took off his shoes and socks, stood up again, pulled his red, thick scarf away, opened his petticoat, quickly pulled it off, and had to unhook another one because Base Dete had put on his Sunday dress over his everyday clothes out of haste so that no one had to wear it.  As quickly as that, the everyday petticoat was gone too, and now the child stood in its light under-petticoat, its bare arms joyously stretching out of the short shirt sleeves. Then he neatly placed everything in a pile, and now he sprang and climbed after the goats and beside Peter, as light as one of the whole company. Peter hadn't paid attention to what the child was doing while it was left behind. As it now came bounding up in its new clothes, he grinned broadly and stretched his whole face, and when he saw the pile of clothes lying below, his face spread even wider, and his mouth almost went from ear to ear; but he said nothing. Since the child felt so free and light, it started a conversation with Peter, and he also began to talk and had to answer many questions because the child wanted to know how many goats he had, where he was going with them, and what he would do when he arrived.  Finally, the children, along with the goats, reached the hut and came face to face with Base Dete. As soon as she saw the approaching company, she cried out loudly: "Heidi, what are you doing? What do you look like? Where is your skirt and your second one and your scarf? And I bought you brand new shoes for the mountain and made you new socks, and all gone! All gone! Heidi, what are you doing, where is everything?"

He dozed off on the bench, but his anxiety persisted even in his dreams. Right before falling asleep, he recalled that Hippolyte would kill ten people and chuckled at the absurdity of the thought. A beautiful, clear silence surrounded him, broken only by the rustle of leaves, which, it seemed, made the world around him even quieter and more secluded. He had many dreams, all of them disturbing, from which he would jolt awake every moment. Finally, a woman appeared to him; he knew her, knew her to the point of suffering; he could have always named her and pointed her out—but strangely, her face now seemed completely different from the one he had always known, and he was painfully reluctant to recognize her as that woman. There was so much remorse and horror in her face that it seemed she was a terrible criminal who had just committed a terrible crime. A tear trembled on her pale cheek; she beckoned to him with her hand and pressed her finger to her lips, as if warning him to follow her more quietly. His heart stopped; he wouldn't, under any circumstances, acknowledge her as a criminal; but he felt that something terrible was about to happen, something that would affect him for the rest of his life. She seemed to want to show him something, right there, in the park. He stood up to follow her, and suddenly a light, fresh laughter rang out beside him; someone's hand suddenly appeared in his; he grasped that hand, squeezed it tightly, and woke up. In front of him stood Aglaya, laughing loudly.

Finally, a woman came to him; he knew her, knew her to the point of suffering; he could have always named her and pointed her out — but strangely, she seemed to have a completely different face than the one he always knew, and he was painfully reluctant to recognize her as that woman. There was so much remorse and terror in her face that it seemed she was a terrible criminal who had just committed a horrible crime. A tear trembled on her pale cheek; she beckoned him with her hand and pressed her finger to her lips, as if warning him to follow her quietly. His heart froze; he didn't want to recognize her as a criminal for anything in the world; but he felt that something terrible was about to happen, something that would affect him for the rest of his life. It seemed she wanted to show him something, right there, nearby, in the park. He stood up to follow her, and suddenly a cheerful, fresh laugh rang out beside him; someone’s hand suddenly found his; he grabbed it, squeezed it tightly, and woke up. Before him stood Aglaya, laughing loudly.

He dozed off on the bench, but his anxiety persisted even in his dreams. Right before falling asleep, he remembered that Hippolytus would kill ten people, and he chuckled at the absurdity of the thought. All around him stood a beautiful, clear silence, broken only by the rustling of leaves, which, it seemed, made the world even quieter and more solitary. As K. passed the corridor separating his office from the main staircase that evening – he was going home almost last, only two servants were still working in the small pool of light from a bare bulb – he heard sighs coming from behind a door, a door behind which he had always assumed was just a storeroom, though he had never actually seen inside. He stopped, surprised, and listened again to make sure he wasn’t mistaken – for a while there was silence, then the sighs came again. At first he wanted to call for one of the servants, one might need a witness, but then an overwhelming curiosity seized him, and he practically flung the door open. It was, as he had rightly suspected, a storeroom. Useless, old printing plates and discarded empty ink bottles lay scattered just beyond the threshold. But inside the chamber, three men were crouched in the low-ceilinged space. A single candle fastened to a shelf gave them light. “What are you doing here?” asked K., rushing forward in excitement, though not loudly. The one man, who seemed to be in charge of the others and was the first to look at him, was dressed in a kind of dark leather, which left his neck exposed down to his chest and his entire arms bare. He didn’t reply. But the two others cried out, “Sir, we’re being punished because you complained about us to the investigator.” And now K. realized that it was truly the guards Franz and Willem, and that the third man held a rod in his hand, ready to strike them. “Well,” said K., staring at them, “I didn’t complain; I merely stated what happened in my apartment. And you certainly didn’t behave impeccably.” “Sir,” said Willem, while Franz seemed to seek safety behind him, “if you knew how poorly paid we are, you would judge us differently. I have a family to feed, and Franz here wanted to get married, one has to make ends meet somehow, simple work doesn’t do it, not even the hardest work. Your fine laundry enticed me; it’s naturally forbidden for guards to act this way, it was wrong, but it’s tradition that the laundry belongs to the guards, it’s always been that way, believe me; it’s understandable, after all, what it means for someone unfortunate enough to be arrested, to have to endure this. If they then bring it to public attention, then punishment must follow.” “What you’re saying now I didn’t know, and I certainly didn’t demand your punishment; it was a matter of principle for me.” “Franz,” Willem turned to the other guard, “didn’t I tell you the gentleman didn’t want our punishment? Now you hear that he didn’t even know we were to be punished.” “Don’t let yourself be swayed by his words,” said the third man to K., “the punishment is as just as it is unavoidable.” “Don’t listen to him,” interrupted Willem, “we are only being punished because you reported us. Otherwise nothing would have happened to us, even if they had found out what we did. Can that be called justice? We two, especially I, had proven ourselves to be very reliable guards for a long time – you yourself must admit that, from the authority’s point of view, we did a good job – we had prospects of advancement and would certainly have become beaters like this one, who simply had the good luck of never being reported; such reports are truly rare. And now, sir, everything is lost, our careers are finished, we will have to do even more menial work than guard duty, and on top of that we get these terribly painful beatings.” “Can a rod really cause such pain?” asked K. and examined the rod the beater was brandishing. “We will have to take our clothes off,” said Willem. “Ah, so,” said K., looking at the beater closely; he had a tanned, sun-baked face like a sailor. “Is there no way to spare the two of them?” he asked him. “No,” said the beater, shaking his head with a smile. “Strip!” he ordered the guards. And to K. he said, “You mustn’t believe everything they say, they’ve gone a bit mad with fear of the rod. What this one,” he pointed at Willem – “is saying about his possible career is simply ridiculous. Look at him, how fat he is – the first blows will disappear into the fat entirely. Do you know why he’s so fat? He has a habit of eating all the breakfast of the arrested. Didn’t he also eat yours?” “Well, I told you so.” “But a man with such a belly can never be a beater, that’s out of the question.” “There are beaters like that,” Willem asserted. “No,” said the beater, stroking Willem’s neck with the rod in such a way that he flinched, “you’re not supposed to listen, but to strip.” Franz, who had perhaps been quite reserved in anticipation of a good outcome from K.’s intervention, now stepped forward, still only wearing his trousers, leaned down and whispered to K., “If you can’t secure leniency for us both, at least try to free me. Willem is older than I am, in every way less sensitive, he also received a light beating a few years ago, but I am still pure and I was only led astray by Willem, who has been my teacher in both good and bad. My poor bride awaits me downstairs at the bank, I am so ashamed.” He wiped his tear-streaked face with K.’s coat. “I won’t wait any longer,” said the beater, grasping the rod with both hands and striking Franz, while Willem cowered in a corner, secretly watching without turning his head. At that moment Franz let out a scream that was entirely and irrevocably his own, it didn’t sound like a human scream, it sounded like the scream of a tortured instrument; it echoed through the whole corridor, the whole building must have heard it. “Don’t scream,” cried K., unable to hold back, and as he strained his gaze towards the direction from which the servants should be coming, he pushed Franz, not hard, but hard enough so that the stunned man fell and writhed on the floor searching for something with his hands; but he didn’t escape the blows, the rod found him even on the ground; as he rolled under it, its tip rose and fell rhythmically. And in the distance appeared one servant, and a few steps behind him a second. Look at him, how fat he is – the first blows will be lost in the fat altogether. – Do you know why he’s so fat? He has a habit of eating the breakfast of all the detainees. Didn’t he also eat yours? Well, I told you so. But a man with such a belly can never become an inquisitor, that’s completely out of the question.” “There are inquisitors like that,” Willem insisted. “No,” said the inquisitor, and stroked his neck with the rod in such a way that Willem winced, “You are not supposed to listen, but to undress.” “I would reward you handsomely if you let them go,” said K., and without looking at the inquisitor again – such transactions are best handled with downcast eyes on both sides – he pulled out his wallet. “You want to bribe me, then?” said the inquisitor, “and also get me beaten. No, no!” “Be reasonable,” said K., “if I had wanted these two punished, I wouldn’t be trying to buy them off now. I could simply have shut the door here, not see or hear anything more, and gone home. But I’m not doing that, I’m really determined to free them; if I had known they were going to be punished, or even could be punished, I would have never mentioned their names. I don’t think they are guilty, it’s the organization that is guilty, the high officials.” “That’s right!” cried the guards, and immediately received a blow on their already undressed backs. “If there were a high judge here under your rod,” said K., and as he spoke, he pressed the rod down, which was already trying to rise again, “I would not stop you from hitting him, on the contrary, I would give you more money to carry out this noble deed.” “What you say sounds plausible,” said the inquisitor, “but I’m not easily swayed. I’m paid to beat people, so I will beat them.” Franz, the guard, who had perhaps, in anticipation of a good outcome from K.’s intervention, been fairly restrained until now, stepped forward, still only in his trousers, and leaned down, whispering to K.’s arm, “If you can’t secure pardon for us both, at least try to free me. Willem is older than me, in every way less sensitive, and besides, he has already been lightly punished once, years ago. But I am still innocent and only came to do this through Willem, who is my teacher, for good and for bad. Downstairs, in front of the bank, my poor bride waits for the outcome, I am so ashamed.” He wiped his tear-stained face with K.’s jacket. “I’m not waiting any longer,” said the inquisitor, grasped the rod with both hands and struck Franz, while Willem cowered in a corner and watched secretly, without turning his head. Then Franz let out a scream that was unburdened and unchanging, it didn’t sound like that of a human being, but of a tortured instrument. The whole corridor resounded with it, the whole house must have heard it. “Don’t scream,” cried K., he couldn’t hold back, and as he looked intently towards the direction from which the servants must come, he pushed Franz, not hard, but hard enough that the senseless man fell and, struggling, searched the floor with his hands; but he didn’t escape the blows, the rod found him on the ground; as he writhed under it, its tip swung regularly up and down. And just then, a servant appeared in the distance, and a few steps behind him a second one. To prevent the servants from approaching, K. shouted, “It’s me!” “Good evening, Mr. Clerk!” came the reply. “Has something happened?” “No, no,” answered K., “only a dog is barking in the courtyard.” As the servants still didn’t move, he added, “You can stay at your work.” To avoid engaging in conversation with the servants, he leaned out of the window. After a while, when he looked back into the corridor, they were gone. K., however, remained by the window; he didn’t dare go into the storeroom, and he didn’t want to go home. He looked down at the small, square courtyard, surrounded by office rooms, all the windows of which were now dark, only the upper ones caught a glimmer of moonlight. K. strained his eyes to penetrate the darkness of a corner of the courtyard where some handcarts were piled up. He was tormented by the fact that he hadn’t been able to prevent the beating, but it wasn’t his fault that it had happened; if Franz hadn’t screamed – certainly, it must have hurt, but in a crucial moment, one must be able to control oneself – if he hadn’t screamed, then K., at least very probably, would have still found a way to persuade the inquisitor. If the entire lower bureaucracy was riff-raff, why should the inquisitor, who had the most inhuman job, have made an exception? K. had also observed well how his eyes had lit up at the sight of the banknote; he had apparently only carried out the beating in order to increase the bribe. And K. wouldn’t have spared the money; he was truly determined to free the guards; if he had already begun to fight against the corruption of this judicial system, it was naturally to be expected that he would intervene on this side too. But the moment Franz started to scream, of course, everything was over. K. couldn’t allow the servants and perhaps all sorts of other people to come and surprise him in negotiations with the company in the storeroom. No one could reasonably expect this sacrifice from K. If he had intended to do this, it would have been almost easier for K. to have stripped himself and offered himself to the inquisitor as a replacement for the guards.

One cannot, however, say that the nature of our hero was so harsh and callous, and his feelings so dulled, that he knew nothing of compassion or pity; he felt both, and he would even have liked to help, but only not in any significant amount, so as not to touch those funds that were not meant to be touched; in a word, his father's instruction: "Save and hoard every penny"—proved useful. But he had no real attachment to money for money's sake; neither greed nor miserliness controlled him. No, these were not what drove him: he envisioned a life before him, filled with comfort and abundance; carriages, a well-appointed house, delicious meals—this is what incessantly occupied his thoughts. And in order to finally taste all this, in time, that's what he guarded, carefully refusing himself and others, for a while. When a wealthy man galloped past him in splendid carriages, on fine steeds in a rich harness, he would stand rooted to the spot and then, waking up as if from a long sleep, would say: "But I used to be a clerk, wearing my hair in a circle!" And everything that evoked wealth and contentment had an effect on him that was incomprehensible even to himself. 

Leaving school, he didn't even want to rest; his desire to begin his work and service was so strong. However, despite his commendable testimonials, he struggled greatly to find a position in the government office. And even in remote areas, patronage is needed! He was given a negligible position, a salary of thirty or forty rubles a year. But he resolved to devote himself passionately to his work, to overcome everything. And indeed, he showed unheard-of self-denial, patience, and restraint of his needs. From early morning until late evening, he toiled without respite, neither mentally nor physically, writing, buried in mountains of paperwork, he wouldn't go home, slept in the office on desks, sometimes ate with the guards, and all the while managed to keep himself neat, dress respectably, wear an agreeable expression, and even impart something noble in his movements. It must be said that the office clerks were particularly distinguished by their mediocrity and unattractiveness. Some had faces that looked like poorly baked bread: one cheek puffed out in one direction, the chin slanted in another, the upper lip protruded like a bubble, which, in addition, cracked; in a word, simply unattractive. They spoke all in a harsh voice, as if they were about to strike someone; they made frequent offerings to Bacchus, showing that there were still many vestiges of paganism in the Slavic nature; they even sometimes arrived for work apparently drunk, which made the presence unpleasant and the air far from fragrant. Among such clerks, Chiklov could not help but be noticed and distinguished, representing a complete opposite in his amiable face, his friendly voice, and his complete abstinence from any strong drink.

But his path remained difficult; he fell under the authority of an already elderly official, who was a monument to some kind of stone insensitivity and impassivity: always the same, inaccessible, never once showing a smile on his face, never greeting anyone, not even with a question about their health. No one had ever seen him be anything other than what he always was, whether on the street or at home; he never showed any participation in anything, nor did he ever get drunk and laugh in his drunken revelry; not even the slightest shadow of anything like that existed in him. There was nothing in him, exactly, neither villainous nor good, and something terrible appeared in this absence of everything. His austere, marble-like face, without any sharp irregularity, did not hint at any resemblance; the features were in austere proportion to one another. Only frequent wrinkles and pockmarks, deeply ingrained, made him resemble those faces on which, as the saying goes, the devil came at night to pound peas. It seemed that there were no human forces capable of approaching such a man and winning his favor, but Chiklov tried. At first, he started by indulging him in all sorts of subtle ways: he carefully examined the ink pen with which he wrote and, having prepared a few copies of it, always placed them near his hand; he blew and swept the sand and tobacco off his desk; he found a new rag for his inkwell; he found his hat somewhere, a truly awful hat, which had ever existed in the world, and always placed it near him a minute before the end of the audience; he even cleaned his back if he had smeared it with chalk from the wall—but all this remained absolutely unnoticed, as if nothing of it had been done. Finally, he learned about his home, family life, and found out that he had a mature daughter, with a face that also looked as if the devil had come to pound peas at night. From this side, he devised a plan to win his favor. He found out which church she attended on Sundays and would stand opposite her every time, neatly dressed, with his shirt starched crisply—and the plan worked: the stern official faltered and invited him for tea! And in the office, they had hardly had time to blink when things turned out so that Chiklov moved in with him, became a necessary person, bought flour and sugar, treated the daughter like a bride, called the official "Daddy," kissed his hand; everyone in the office assumed that there would be a wedding at the end of February, before Lent. The stern official even started to intercede for him with his superiors, and after a while, Chiklov himself was appointed to the vacant position. This, it seemed, was the main goal of his connections with the old official, because immediately after that, he secretly sent his trunk home and the next day found himself in a different apartment. He stopped calling the official "Daddy" and no longer kissed his hand, and the wedding idea fizzled out as if nothing had happened. However, when they met, he always warmly shook his hand and invited him for tea, so that the old official, despite his perpetual immobility and cold indifference, would always shake his head and mutter under his breath: "He fooled me, he fooled me, that devil's son!"

Finally, he learned about his domestic, family life and found out that he had a mature daughter, with a face that also looked as if the devil had been grinding peas on it at night. From this side, he devised a plan to make an impression. He learned which church she attended on Sundays and would stand opposite her every time, neatly dressed, his white collar starched to crispness—and his plan worked: the stern official softened and invited him for tea! And in the office, no one had time to blink an eye before things were arranged so that Chikchov moved into his house, became a necessary and indispensable person, bought flour and sugar, treated the daughter like a fiancée, called the official "father," and kissed his hand; everyone in the office assumed that there would be a wedding before Lent. The stern official even started to vouch for him with superiors, and after a while Chikchov himself took over the vacant position. It seemed that this was the main purpose of his connection with the old official, because he immediately secretly sent his trunk home and the next day was already in a different apartment. He stopped calling the official "father" and no longer kissed his hand, and the wedding fizzled out, as if nothing had happened at all. However, when they met, he always greeted him warmly, shaking his hand and inviting him for tea, so that the old official, despite his eternal immobility and callous indifference, would shake his head every time and mutter to himself: "He tricked me, the devil's son!"

"And now?" Gregor wondered, looking around in the darkness. He soon discovered that he could no longer move at all. He wasn't surprised, rather it felt unnatural that he had actually been able to move about with those thin legs until now.  On the other hand, he felt relatively comfortable. He had pain all over his body, but it felt as if it were gradually weakening and would eventually disappear entirely. He hardly felt the rotten apple in his back anymore, nor the inflamed area around it, which was completely covered in soft dust.  He thought back to his family with tenderness and love. His own conviction that he had to disappear was perhaps even stronger than his sister's. He remained in this state of empty, peaceful contemplation until the tower clock struck three in the morning. He still experienced the beginning of the general brightening outside the window. Then his head sank down without his will, and his last breath weakly streamed out of his nostrils.

The small room the young man entered was yellow-wallpapered, with geraniums and sheer curtains at the windows, brightly lit by the setting sun. "And so, then, the sun will shine just like this!" – a thought flickered through Raskolnikov's mind as if by chance, and with a quick glance he surveyed everything in the room, trying to study and memorize the arrangement. But there was nothing particularly special about the room. The furniture, all very old and made of yellow wood, consisted of a sofa with a huge curved wooden back, a round table oval in shape in front of the sofa, a toilet with a mirror in the alcove, chairs along the walls, and two or three cheap pictures in yellow frames, depicting German maidens with birds in their hands – that was all the furniture. In the corner in front of a small icon lamp was lit. Everything was very clean: both the furniture and the floors had been polished to a sheen; everything sparkled. "Lizabetha's work," the young man thought. Not a speck of dust could be found in the whole apartment. "This kind of cleanliness is common among evil and old widows," Raskolnikov continued to himself, and with curiosity he glanced at the cotton curtain in front of the door to the second tiny room, where the old woman's bed and chest of drawers stood, and which he had never entered. The whole apartment consisted of these two rooms.

Ippolit Kirillovich deemed it necessary to sketch the character of the late Smerdyakov, “who ended his life in a fit of morbid mental delusion and insanity.” He portrayed him as a feeble-minded man, with a rudimentary education, bewildered by philosophical ideas beyond his comprehension and frightened by other modern notions of duty and obligation, which had been instilled in him in a reckless manner through the life of his master, the deceased Fyodor Pavlovich, and perhaps also by his father, and theoretically by strange philosophical discussions with the master’s elder son, Ivan Fyodorovich, who indulged in this pastime willingly – perhaps out of boredom or a desire to ridicule, finding no better outlet for it.  He himself told me about his mental state in the last days of his time at his master’s house, – Ippolit Kirillovich explained – but other witnesses confirm this too: the defendant himself, his brother, and even the servant, Grigory, that is, everyone who knew him intimately. Besides, being afflicted with a worsening illness, Smerdyakov was "timid as a chicken." “He fell at my feet and kissed my feet,” the defendant himself recounted at that moment, when he still did not realize the potential disadvantage of such a disclosure, – “He was a chicken in his ailing state,” he expressed it in his characteristic way. And so, this defendant (as he himself testifies) chose him as his confidant and intimidated him so much that he finally agreed to serve him as a spy and messenger. In this capacity as a household spy, he betrayed his master, reported to the defendant about the existence of a package of money, and about the signs by which one could gain access to the master – and how could he have not told him? “They would kill me, I saw it directly, that they would kill me,” he said at the investigation, trembling and shaking even before us, despite the fact that the tormentor who had frightened him was already under arrest and could no longer punish him. "They suspected me every minute, I myself, in fear and trembling, eager only to appease their anger, rushed to tell them every secret, so that they might see my innocence before them and release me alive for repentance,”  These are his own words, I recorded and remembered them: “When they would yell at me, I would fall to my knees before them.” Being inherently honest by nature, and having gained the trust of his master, who had distinguished this honesty in him when he had returned the money he had lost, the unfortunate Smerdyakov, one must think, was terribly tormented by remorse for betraying his master, whom he loved as his benefactor. As is well known, people suffering greatly from epilepsy, according to the deepest psychiatrists, are prone to continuous and, of course, painful self-accusation. They suffer from their “guilt” for something and to someone, tormented by pangs of conscience, often, even without any reason, they exaggerate and even invent for themselves various sins and crimes. And so, such a subject becomes truly guilty and criminal from fear and intimidation. Moreover, he strongly anticipated that something unpleasant might arise from the circumstances that were unfolding before his eyes. When Ivan Fyodorovich, the elder son of Fyodor Pavlovich, left for Moscow just before the catastrophe, Smerdyakov begged him to stay, though, however, out of his cowardly habit, he did not dare to express all his fears to him in a clear and categorical manner. He only contented himself with hints, but the hints were not understood. It is worth noting that in Ivan Fyodorovich he saw as if his protection, as if a guarantee that as long as he was at home, nothing bad would happen. Remember the expression in Dmitri Karamazov’s “drunk” letter: “I’ll kill the old man if only Ivan leaves”; therefore, the presence of Ivan Fyodorovich seemed to everyone as a guarantee of peace and order in the house. And so he leaves, and Smerdyakov, almost an hour after the young master’s departure, immediately falls ill with his affliction. But this is perfectly understandable. Here it should be mentioned that, tormented by fears and a kind of despair, Smerdyakov in the last days especially felt the possibility of approaching fits, which had always happened to him in moments of moral tension and shock. It is, of course, impossible to predict the day and hour of these fits, but every epileptic can feel the predisposition to them in advance. This is what medicine says. And so, just as Ivan Fyodorovich leaves the yard, Smerdyakov, under the impression of his so-called “orphanhood” and helplessness, goes to the cellar for some household chore, descends the stairs and thinks: “Will there be a fit or not, but what if it comes now?” And it is precisely from this mood, from this anxiety, from these questions, that a throat spasm, always preceding an epileptic fit, grips him, and he falls headlong unconscious to the bottom of the cellar. And so, in this very natural chance, they try to see some kind of suspicion, some kind of indication, some kind of hint that he feigned illness! But if he feigned it, then the question arises: for what purpose? With what calculation, with what goal? I'm not even talking about medicine; science, they say, lies, science is mistaken, doctors failed to distinguish truth from pretense, – let it be, let it be, but answer me this: what was the point of pretending? Was it not so that, having planned the murder, he would attract attention to himself in the house as soon as possible with the sudden seizure?  You see, gentlemen jurors, there were and stayed five people in Fyodor Pavlovich’s house on the night of the crime: first, Fyodor Pavlovich himself, but he didn’t kill himself, it’s clear; second, his servant Grigory, but he was almost killed himself; third, Grigory’s wife, the maidservant Marfa Ignatievna, but to imagine her killing her master is simply shameful. This leaves, therefore, two people in sight: the defendant and Smerdyakov. But since the defendant insists that he did not kill, then, therefore, Smerdyakov must have killed, there is no other way out, because you cannot find anyone else, you cannot imagine any other murderer. Here, here, therefore, comes this “ingenious” and colossal accusation against the unfortunate, recently deceased, idiot! It is solely based on the fact that there is no one else to blame! If there was even a shadow, even a suspicion about someone else, some sixth person, I am convinced that even the defendant would have been ashamed to point to Smerdyakov then, and would have pointed to this sixth person, because to accuse Smerdyakov of this murder is utter nonsense.

You see, gentlemen jurors, there were and there were five people in the house of Fyodor Pavlovich on the night of the crime: firstly, Fyodor Pavlovich himself, but he did not kill himself, this is clear; secondly, his servant Grigory, but that very Grigory was almost killed; thirdly, Grigory’s wife, the maidservant Marfa Ignatyevna, but to imagine her as the murderer of her master is simply shameful.  Therefore, there remain, it turns out, two people in sight: the defendant and Smirdyakov. But since the defendant asserts that he did not kill, then, it follows, Smirdyakov must have killed, there is no other way out, because there is no one else to find, there is no other murderer to come up with. That is exactly where this “cunning” and colossal accusation against the unfortunate, who had just taken his own life, idiot arose! Just because there is no one else to blame! If there were even a shadow, even a suspicion about someone else, about some sixth person, then I am convinced that even the defendant himself would have been ashamed to point to Smirdyakov then, and would have pointed to this sixth person, because to accuse Smirdyakov of this murder is complete absurdity.

Here Ippolit Kirillovich deemed it necessary to sketch out somewhat the character of the late Smerdyakov, “who ended his life in a fit of morbid frenzy and insanity.” He presented him as a man of feeble intellect, with a vague smattering of education, bewildered by philosophical ideas beyond his grasp, and frightened by other contemporary teachings on duty and obligation, broadly presented to him practically – recklessly so – by the life of his master, the late Fyodor Pavlovich, and perhaps even by his father, and theoretically – by various strange philosophical conversations with his master’s elder son, Ivan Fyodorovich, who readily indulged in this pastime – probably out of boredom or a need for amusement, finding no better outlet. He himself told me of his mental state in the last days of his stay in his master’s house, – Ippolit Kirillovich explained, – but this is also attested by others: the defendant himself, his brother, and even the servant, Grigory, that is, all those who ought to have known him well. Moreover, being tormented by a failing illness, Smerdyakov was “timid as a chicken.” “He fell at my feet and kissed my feet,” – the defendant himself reported to us at that very moment, when he still did not realize what disadvantage this revelation held for him, – “he was like a chicken in a failing illness,” – he expressed his opinion about him in his characteristic manner. And so it was that the defendant (as he himself testifies) chose this man as his confidant and intimidated him to such an extent that he agreed to serve him as a spy and courier. In this capacity, as a domestic informer, he betrayed his master, reporting to the defendant about the existence of a package of money and about the signs by which one could penetrate to the master – and how could he not have reported! “They will kill me, I saw directly that they will kill me,” – he said at the trial, trembling and shivering even before us, despite the fact that the tormentor who had frightened him was already under arrest and could no longer come to punish him. “They suspected me every minute, I myself was in fear and trembling, only in order to appease their wrath, I hastened to report every secret to them, so that they might see my innocence and release me alive in penitence,” – these were his own words, I recorded and memorized them: “As soon as he yelled at me, I fell to my knees before them.”  

Being by nature an exceptionally honest young man and having thus gained the trust of his master, who had distinguished this honesty in him, when he returned the money he had lost, the unfortunate Smerdyakov, one can assume, was terribly tormented by remorse for betraying his master, whom he loved as his benefactor. As is known, people suffering intensely from failing illnesses, according to the deepest psychiatrists, are prone to constant and, of course, painful self-recrimination. They torment themselves with their “guilt” to someone, suffer from pangs of conscience, often, even without any basis, exaggerating and even inventing various sins and crimes for themselves. And so, this type of subject becomes truly guilty and criminal from fear and intimidation. Moreover, he strongly sensed that something bad might come out of the circumstances that were unfolding before his eyes. When Ivan Fyodorovich, the elder son of Fyodor Pavlovich, left for Moscow just before the catastrophe, Smerdyakov begged him to stay, but, however, not daring, in his cowardly way, to express all his anxieties to him clearly and categorically. He was content with hints, but the hints were not understood. It is worth noting that in Ivan Fyodorovich, he saw as it were his protection, as a guarantee that as long as he was at home, nothing bad would happen. Remember the expression in Dmitry Karamazov's "drunken" letter: “I will kill the old man if only Ivan leaves.” Thus, the presence of Ivan Fyodorovich seemed to everyone as if a guarantee of peace and order in the house. And so, he leaves, and Smerdyakov, almost an hour after the departure of the young master, immediately falls ill with a failing illness. But this is perfectly understandable. Here it should be mentioned that, tormented by fears and a kind of despair, Smerdyakov in the last days especially felt in himself the possibility of approaching fits of failing illness, which had always happened to him in moments of moral stress and shock. The day and hour of these fits, of course, cannot be predicted, but each epileptic can feel the predisposition to a fit beforehand. This is what medicine says. And so, as soon as Ivan Fyodorovich leaves the courtyard, Smerdyakov, under the impression of his, so to speak, orphanhood and helplessness, goes to the cellar for some domestic chore, descends the stairs and thinks: “Will there be a fit or not, but what if it happens right now?” And it is precisely from this mood, from this anxiety, from these questions, that a throat spasm grabs him, which always precedes a failing illness, and he falls headlong unconscious to the bottom of the cellar. And so, in this very natural accident, they try to see some kind of suspicion, some kind of indication, some kind of hint that he pretended to be sick! But if he pretended, then the question arises: for what purpose? What calculation, what goal? I’m not even talking about medicine; science, they say, lies, science makes mistakes, doctors failed to distinguish the truth from pretense – let it be, let it be, but answer me, please, what was the point of pretending? Not to draw attention to himself with the occurrence of a fit, in order to prepare and hasten the attention of the household to the murder he had conceived? You see, esteemed jurors, on the night of the crime in Fyodor Pavlovich's house there were and stayed five people: first, Fyodor Pavlovich himself, but he certainly didn’t kill himself, that’s clear; second, his servant Grigory, but he was almost killed himself; third, the wife of Grigory, the maid Marfa Ignatievna, but to imagine her as the killer of her master is simply shameful. Good Prince, hands grasping iron staff, a robe with embroidered sleeves, leapt out the gate, and bellowed, "Which one of you is the Great Sage, Equal to Heaven?" The Great Sage, brandishing his Ruyi staff, responded, "It is old Sun. Who are you, daring to ask me?" The Iron Staff said, "I am Li Tianwang's second prince, Iron Staff. I am here before Guanyin Bodhisattva's seat, protecting my disciples, my dharma name is Hui'an." The Great Sage said, "You are not practicing in the South Sea, yet come here to see me? What is your purpose?" The Iron Staff said, "I have been sent by my master to scout the enemy situation. Seeing you so rampant, I have come to capture you!" The Great Sage said, "You dare utter such bold words! Stand still! Eat old Sun's staff!" Iron Staff was completely fearless, wielding his iron staff to meet the attack. The two of them stood amidst the mountains, outside the gate, and the good fight began.

The old woman, Belokonskaya, listened to all of Lizaveta Prokofyevna’s feverish and desperate confessions and not a single tear stirred in her eyes for the bewildered head of the household. She even looked at her with a touch of mockery. This was a terrifying tyrant; in friendship, even the oldest, she could not tolerate equality, and she looked at Lizaveta Prokofyevna resolutely as her protégé, just as she had thirty-five years ago, and could not reconcile herself with the sharpness and independence of her character. Besides, she noticed that, “it seems, they’ve all, as always, rushed ahead and made a mountain out of a molehill; that no matter how she listened, she couldn’t be convinced that anything truly serious had happened; that it might be better to wait until something more concrete emerged; that the prince, in her opinion, was a decent young man, although sick, eccentric, and far too insignificant. Worst of all, that he openly kept a mistress.”  Lizaveta Prokofyevna very well understood that Belokonskaya was slightly angry about the failure of Yevgeny Pavlovich, whom she had recommended. She returned to Pavlovsk in even greater agitation than when she had left, and immediately unleashed her ire on everyone, mainly for “going mad,” that nobody else conducted their affairs like this, only theirs; “what was the rush? What had happened? No matter how she looked at it, she couldn't conclude that anything had really happened! Wait until something more comes out! Who knows what Ivan Fyodorovich might have imagined, don’t make a mountain out of a molehill?” and so on, and so on.

If it does rain tomorrow, according to the precise time you’ve predicted, I will offer you fifty taels of silver as a reward. But his silent standing must have been noticeable, and indeed the girl and the court officer looked at him as if some great transformation were about to happen to him in the next minute, which they couldn't miss observing. And in the doorway stood the man whom K. had earlier noticed in the distance; he held himself on the rail of the low door and swayed a little on his toes, like an impatient spectator. The girl, however, first recognized that K.'s demeanor was due to a slight discomfort; she brought a chair and asked, "Would you like to sit down?" K. sat down immediately and, to get even better support, rested his elbows on the arms. "You have a little dizziness, don't you?" she asked him. His face was now close before her, it had the stern expression that some women have even in their most beautiful youth. "Don't worry about it," she said, "it's nothing unusual here, almost everyone gets such an attack when they come here for the first time. You're here for the first time? Well, that's nothing unusual then. The sun beats down on the roof frame here, and the hot wood makes the air so dull and heavy. That's why this place is not very suitable for office spaces, although it offers other great advantages. But as for the air, on days of great party traffic, and that's almost every day, it's hardly breathable. And if you also consider that laundry is often hung out to dry here – you can't entirely forbid the tenants – then you won't be surprised that you feel a little sick. But one gets used to the air very well. When you come here for the second or third time, you'll hardly feel the heaviness here anymore. Do you feel better already?" K. didn't answer, it was embarrassing for him to be so exposed to the people here because of this sudden weakness, moreover, now that he knew the cause of his nausea, he didn't feel any better, but rather a little worse.

How well the Deputy Director managed to appropriate everything that K. was now forced to give up! But did K. not give up more than absolutely necessary? While he went to an unknown painter with vague and, as he had to admit, very slim hopes, his reputation suffered an irreparable damage here. It would probably have been much better to take off the winter coat again and at least win back the two gentlemen who were still waiting next door. K. might have even tried it, if he hadn’t just seen the Deputy Director in his room, searching in the bookcase as if it were his own. As K. approached the door excitedly, he exclaimed, "Oh, you haven't left yet!" He turned to him, his face with its many tight wrinkles seeming to evidence not age but strength, and immediately began searching again. "I'm looking for a contract," he said, "which, as the company representative claims, is in your possession. Won't you help me look for it?" K. took a step, but the Deputy Director said, "Thank you, I've found it," and returned to his room with a large bundle of papers that contained not only the contract, but certainly many other things.

As he was speaking, the head monk of the upper courtyard was arranging a vegetarian meal for Master Sun. The Monkey King, after taking a few bites, hopped back onto his cloud and continued his search. Just then, he saw a strange creature, with a rosewood box clutched under his left armpit, coming along the main road. The Monkey King thought there must be some kind of message inside the box, so he raised his staff and struck it down, smashing it into a flat pancake. He dragged it to the side of the road and opened the box, revealing a formal invitation. It read: "Bears-and-Tigers pays his respects with his head bowed low, to the venerable Master of the Great Revealing Golden Pond, residing in the Purple Chamber: He humbly expresses his gratitude for your many kindnesses. Observing the hardships of my return, I am afraid of not receiving protection; I implore that the immortal's powers will not cause me any harm. By chance, I have obtained a Buddha's robe, and wish to hold a gathering in your honor, with fine wine and delicacies. I respectfully request your presence on that day. Sincerely, Yours, Bear-and-Tigers. Two days hence." The Monkey King saw this and burst into laughter. "That old monk, dying a thousand deaths still isn't enough! He has teamed up with demons! No wonder he lived for two hundred and seventy years. It must be that demon who taught him some trivial incantations, granting him such longevity. The old monkey remembers his appearance. I'll transform myself into a monk and visit his cave, just to see where my robes are kept. If I can get them back, it will save me a lot of trouble."

Just as he was saying this, the abbot of the upper chamber, having prepared vegetarian food, invited Master Sun to eat. I was so stunned by his proposal that I don't even know why I burst into tears. He took my tears as gratitude and said that he had always been sure that I was a kind, sensitive, and educated young woman, but that he had not dared to make this move until he learned the whole truth about my current behavior. Then he began to ask about you, saying that he had heard everything, that you were a man of noble principles, and that he did not want to be in your debt and that five hundred rubles would be enough for all that you had done for me. When I explained to him what you had done for me, something that no amount of money could repay, he said that it was all nonsense, that it was all just romantic stories, that I was still young and that I read poetry, that novels ruined young women, that books only corrupted morals, and that he could not stand books at all; he advised me to live his years and then speak about people; "Then," he added, "you will get to know people." He then said that I should think carefully about his proposals, that it would be very unpleasant for him if I took such an important step without thinking it through, adding that rashness and infatuation ruin inexperienced youth, but that he very much desired a favorable answer from me, and that, finally, if I refused, he would be forced to marry a merchant's daughter in Moscow because, as he said, I had sworn to deprive my worthless nephew of his inheritance. He left five hundred rubles in my hands, on my spindles, as he said, for sweets; he said that in the village I would get fat like a pancake, that I would be rolling around with him like cheese in oil, that he had a terrible lot of work now, that he had spent the whole day running errands, and that he had just popped in to see me between business. That's how he left.

I thought for a long time, I thought a great deal, I suffered, thinking, my friend, and finally, I made a decision. My friend, I will marry him; I must agree to his proposal. If anyone can save me from my shame, restore my good name, and prevent poverty, hardship, and misfortune in the future, then it is he alone. What else can I expect from the future, what else can I ask of fate? Fedya says that one should not lose one's happiness; he says, then what is happiness called in such a case? At least, I cannot find another way for myself, my precious friend. What should I do? Work has already ruined my health; I cannot work constantly. Go into society? - I will simply waste away from longing, besides, I will never please anyone. I am sickly by nature, and therefore I will always be a burden on someone else's hands. Of course, I am not going to paradise now, but what should I do, my friend, what should I do? What am I to choose from?

Nevertheless, there were moments of reflection and half-conscious consideration. By what paths!, he then thought with astonishment. By what paths! Like any man to whom natural merit instills an aristocratic interest in his lineage, he was accustomed to remember his ancestors when reflecting on the achievements and successes of his life, to seek assurance of their approval, their satisfaction, their begrudging respect in his spirit. He thought of them now too, entangled in such an inappropriate experience, immersed in such exotic extravagance of feeling; he thought of their dignified austerity, their decent manhood, and smiled wistfully. What would they say? But of course, what would they have said about his whole life, which had deviated from theirs to the point of degeneration, about this life under the spell of art, about which he himself, in the bourgeois spirit of his fathers, had once let slip such mocking youthful pronouncements and which was ultimately so similar to theirs? He too had served, he too had trained himself in strict discipline; he too had been a soldier and a warrior, like many of them—for art was a war, a draining struggle, for which one did not stay strong for long. A life of self-overcoming and yet, a harsh, steadfast, and abstinent life, which he had fashioned into a symbol for a tender and contemporary heroism—he surely could call it manly, he could call it brave, and it seemed to him that Eros, who had mastered him, was in some way particularly suited and inclined to such a life. Had he not been highly regarded among the bravest peoples, yes, was it not said that he had flourished in their cities through courage? Numerous war heroes of yore had willingly borne his yoke, for no humiliation was too great that the god inflicted, and deeds that would have been scorned as marks of cowardice if they had been done for other purposes: falls, oaths, insistent pleas, and slavishness—such things did not bring shame to the lover, but rather he reaped praise for them.

The Bodhisattva led the assembly inside, paid their respects to the Jade Emperor, and then greeted the Old Master and the Queen Mother, all taking their seats. 

"How was the Peach Banquet?" the Bodhisattva inquired.

"Every year it's a joyous occasion," the Jade Emperor replied, "but this year, it was disrupted by the monkey demon, so it was a mere formality."

"Where did this monkey demon come from?" the Bodhisattva asked.

"The monkey demon was born from a stone egg in Flower Fruit Mountain, Ao Lai Country, in the Eastern Victory Divine Continent. From the moment he was born, his eyes emitted golden light, shooting straight up to the Constellation Palace. At first, we ignored it, but as he grew, he became increasingly powerful, subduing dragons and tigers. He even eradicated himself from the roster of the underworld. The Dragon King and the King of Hell both reported this to me. I intended to capture him, but the Star Chang Geng advised, 'Between the Three Realms, all beings with nine orifices can become immortals.' I then offered him a position as an official, ushering him to the Heavenly Realm and appointing him as the Stablemaster in charge of the Heavenly steeds. That fellow disliked the position, so he rebelled against the Heavenly Palace. I then dispatched the Heavenly King Li and Prince Nezha to subdue him, and I also issued an edict to appease him, promoting him to the Heavenly Realm, and appointed him as the 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven,' but he had no salary.  With nothing to do, he wandered east and west. I feared he would cause further trouble, so I had him manage the Peach Garden. But he disregarded the laws and ate all the large, old peaches. At the time of the banquet, since he was a staff member without pay, he wasn't invited. He devised a plan to deceive the bare-footed immortal, changing his appearance to enter the banquet, and stole all the immortal delicacies and wine. He also stole the Old Master's elixir and a quantity of celestial wine, to enjoy with the monkeys back on his mountain. I was distressed by this, so I dispatched 100,000 heavenly soldiers, setting a net of heaven and earth to capture him.  Today, there's been no news, and I don't know the outcome."

The Bodhisattva led the crowd inside and, after paying respects to the Jade Emperor, greeted Laozi and the Queen Mother, and they all sat down.  He then asked, "How was the Peach Feast?"

The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year it's a joyous occasion, but this year it was disrupted by the Monkey King, making it a hollow affair."

The Bodhisattva asked, "Where does this Monkey King come from?"

The Jade Emperor said, "The Monkey King was born from a stone egg on Flower Fruit Mountain in the Aolai Country of the Eastern Victory Continent. When he was born, he shot a golden light that pierced to the Hall of the Martial God. At first, we paid him no mind, but then he grew stronger, subduing dragons and tigers, and erased his own name from the death register.  When the Dragon King and the King of Hell reported this, I wanted to capture him. But then Chang Geng Xing reported, 'In the Three Realms, anyone with nine orifices can become an immortal.' I then bestowed upon him the position of  Instructor of the Celestial Stables, governing the Emperor's horses. He disliked the position and rebelled against Heaven. I sent Li Tianwang and Nezha, the Prince of the Sea, to subdue him, and then issued an edict to calm the situation and invited him to the upper realm, where he was given the title 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven,' but with no salary. Having nothing to do, he wandered east and west. I feared further trouble, so I appointed him to oversee the Peach Garden. But he disregarded the rules and ate all the old trees and peaches. When the feast was set, he, as an uncompensated employee, was not invited.  He then concocted a plan to trick the barefooted immortals, disguised himself, entered the feast, and stole all the celestial delicacies and liquor, as well as stealing Laozi's elixir of immortality and a quantity of imperial wine, which he took back to share with his mountain tribe. I was distressed by this, so I dispatched one hundred thousand heavenly soldiers with nets to subdue him. But I have yet to receive a report, and I don't know the outcome."

I then sent Li Tianwang and Nezha, the Prince, to subdue him. Afterwards, I issued an edict to appease him and promoted him to the Heavenly Realm, granting him the title 'Great Sage Equaling Heaven,' though he received no official stipend. Since he had nothing to do, he roamed east and west. I was afraid of further trouble, so I had him manage the Peach Garden. But he disregarded the laws, devouring the old trees and the large peaches. When the banquet was held, since he was a non-salaried official, he was not invited. He then devised a plan, pretending to be another immortal and joining the banquet. He stole all the immortal food and wine, and also stole Laozi's elixir and some imperial wine to share with the monkeys back on his mountain. This has troubled me greatly, so I dispatched one hundred thousand heavenly soldiers with celestial nets to capture him. But so far, there has been no news of his capture, and I am unsure of the outcome."

The Bodhisattva led the crowd inside and, after paying respects to the Jade Emperor, met with Lao Jun and the Queen Mother, taking their seats. He then inquired, “How was the Peach Feast?” The Jade Emperor replied, “Every year it’s a joyful occasion, but this year, due to the havoc caused by the Monkey King, it was a mere formality.” The Bodhisattva asked, “Where does this Monkey King hail from?” The Jade Emperor said, “He was born from a stone egg in Flower Fruit Mountain, Aolai Kingdom, in the Eastern Victory Divine Continent. When he first emerged, his eyes shone with golden light, shooting straight for the Celestial Court. At first, it wasn’t a concern, but he grew stronger, subduing dragons and tigers, and removing himself from the mortal registry. When the Dragon King and the King of Hell reported it, I wanted to capture him. But then, the Star Chang Geng advised, ‘In the three realms, all beings with nine orifices can become immortals.’ I then bestowed upon him the teachings of a virtuous scholar and summoned him to the celestial realm, appointing him as the Superintendent of Horses under the name Ma Wen. However, he despised his low position and rebelled against Heaven. I then dispatched Li Tianwang and Prince Nezha to subdue him. I also issued an imperial decree to appease him, summoning him to the celestial realm, and appointed him the 'Great Sage Equaling Heaven,’ but he had no official salary. With nothing to do, he roamed freely east and west. Fearful that he would cause further trouble, I had him oversee the Peach Garden. Yet, he disregarded the laws, stealing the large, old peaches and consuming them all. When the feast was set, as he was an uncompensated employee, he wasn't invited. He then devised a plan to trick the Barefoot Immortal, disguising himself and entering the feast, stealing all the immortal delicacies and wine, and even stealing Lao Jun’s elixir and a considerable amount of imperial wine to share with the monkeys back at his mountain. This has caused me great worry, so I deployed one hundred thousand celestial soldiers and set up a heavenly net to capture him. But today, there has been no word of his capture, and I don’t know the outcome.”

Copper snakes and iron dogs vied for their meals, forever falling into the River Nai without a way out. The poem says: I often hear the cries of ghosts and the calls of gods, bloodwater churned into a thousand-zhang high wave. Countless bull-heads and horse-faces, ferociously guarding the Bridge of Nai River. Just as he was speaking, those bridge guardians had already returned. Taizong’s heart trembled with fear again, he nodded in silent lament, sadly accompanying the Judge and Grand Minister as they crossed the evil waters of the River Nai, the blood basin of suffering. They arrived at the City of Wronged Deaths, and only a cacophony of shouts could be heard, clearly saying, "Li Shimin has arrived! Li Shimin has arrived!"  Taizong, upon hearing the shouts, was terrified. He saw a group of ghosts with bent waists, broken arms, and bodies missing limbs, who blocked his way, all shouting, "Return our lives! Return our lives!"  Panic-stricken, Taizong hid and cowered, crying out, "Mr. Cui, save me! Mr. Cui, save me!" The Judge said, "Your Majesty, those people are all the ghosts of the sixty-four places of dust and seventy-two places of bandits, countless princes and leaders; all victims of wrongful deaths, uncollected and unattended, unable to transcend, with no money or offerings, all forlorn and hungry ghosts. Your Majesty should give them some money and offerings, and only then can I save them." Taizong said, "As a ruler with nothing, where can I get money and offerings?" The Judge said, "Your Majesty, there is a man in the yang world who has a large sum of gold and silver deposited here in the underworld. You can use his name and make a vow, I can act as a guarantor, and borrow a treasury from him to distribute to these hungry ghosts, only then can they pass." Taizong asked, "Who is this man?" The Judge said, "He is from Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan Province, named Xiang Liang. He has thirteen treasuries of gold and silver here. If Your Majesty borrows some, you will return it to him in the yang world." Taizong was overjoyed and willingly agreed to borrow it. He then made a written document with the Judge, borrowing a treasury of gold and silver and instructing the Grand Minister to distribute it. The Judge then ordered, "You should divide this gold and silver equally, so that you can allow the great-grandfather of the Tang Dynasty to pass. His life span in the yang world is still long. I have received the decree of the Ten Kings and will send him back to the yang world. I will have him hold a Water-Land Conference to help you transcend and be reborn, so that you will have no more grievances." Upon hearing this, the ghosts, having received the gold and silver, all nodded in agreement and withdrew. The Judge told the Grand Minister to wave the soul-summoning banner, leading Taizong out of the City of Wronged Deaths, onto the Pingyang Road, and drifting away. It remains unknown where he came out from that road.  To be continued next time.

– My friend, I only wanted to make you laugh, but, I swear, this is genuine Jesuit casuistry, and, I swear, all of this happened word for word as I told you. This incident is recent and caused me a great deal of trouble. The unfortunate young man, returning home, shot himself that very night; I was with him until the very last moment… As for those confessional Jesuit booths, they are truly my favorite pastime in gloomy moments. Here's another case, just the other day. A blonde, beautiful girl, twenty years old, comes to the old Father. Beauty, physique, nature – makes you drool. She leans in and whispers her sin into the hole. “What, my daughter, haven't you already fallen again? – exclaims the Father. – O Sancta Maria,[43] what do I hear: not with the same one anymore. But how long will this continue, and how can you not be ashamed!” – “Ah mon père,[44] – replies the sinner, tears of repentance streaming down her face. – Ça lui fait tant de plaisir et а moi si peu de peine!”[45] Well, imagine such a response! I couldn't help but agree then: it's a cry of nature itself, this, if you will, is better than innocence itself! I was about to absolve her and leave, but I was immediately forced to turn back: I heard the Father telling her to meet him later that evening, through the hole. And the old man is a rock, and yet, he fell in an instant! Nature, indeed, nature takes its course! You're turning your nose up again, getting angry? I don't know what to do to please you…

The master passed on the scriptures, stepped on the light of clouds, and was about to ascend to the Cloud Vulture Peak when he was stopped by the Tripitaka, who insisted on asking about the precise route westward. 

The master smiled and said, “The road is not difficult to travel. Just listen to my instructions: thousands of mountains and rivers are deep, with many miasmas and demons. If you encounter the cliff that reaches the heavens, don’t be afraid. When you reach the Mo’er Rock, step sideways. Be careful in the black pine forest, where fox demons often obstruct the way. Elves fill the country city, and the demon king resides on the mountain. A tiger sits in the music hall, a wolf serves as the recorder. Lions and elephants are proclaimed king, tigers and leopards act as guards. Wild boars carry burdens, and water monsters appear ahead. The old monkey, who has lived for many years, dwells there with resentment. You may inquire from him, for he knows the way westward.”

The Monkey King heard this and sneered, “We are going, we need not ask him, ask me instead.”

The Tripitaka still didn’t understand, but the master transformed into a golden light and ascended to the Cloud Vulture Peak. The Elder bowed upwards in gratitude, while the Monkey King was filled with anger and raised his iron rod, striking upwards in a frenzy. However, he only saw tens of thousands of lotus blossoms and auspicious mist protecting the peak. Even with the Monkey King’s strength to stir the sea and overturn rivers, he couldn’t even catch a single vine of the Cloud Vulture Peak.

The Tripitaka saw this and grabbed the Monkey King’s arm, saying, “Monkey, why are you disturbing his dwelling?”

The Monkey King said, “He insulted my two brothers!”

The Tripitaka said, “How could his words about the westward path insult you?”

The Monkey King said, “You don’t understand! He said that wild boars carry burdens, insulting Pigsy; and that the old monkey who has lived for many years insults me. How can you not understand?”

Pigsy said, “Brother, calm down. This master knows past and future events, but let us see if his words about the water monster are true. Let us forgive him.”

The Monkey King saw the lotus blossoms and auspicious mist near the nest, so he could only ask his master to mount his horse and head westward.

He saw that he still had no robes, and felt fear again. He asked, “Why haven’t you robes come this time?” The Monkey King took out a simple note from his sleeve and handed it to the Tripitaka. “Master, that monster and that dead, old skin-shedding fellow were friends.  He had a little demon send this note, inviting him to the Robe Gathering. It was I who beat that little demon to death, transformed into that old monk, entered his cave, tricked him into offering me a pot of tea, and tried to ask him for a robe, but he wouldn’t give one. Just as we were sitting, suddenly a patrolman came by, and a fight broke out between us. We fought until dawn, neither gaining the upper hand. He saw it was late, dashed back to his cave, and shut the stone door tight. The Monkey King, helpless, returned here as well.”

The Tripitaka said, “How do you compare to him in strength?” The Monkey King said, “I am no better than him, we only fought on equal terms.” 

The Tripitaka read the note and handed it to the Abbot. “Is your master also a demon?” The Abbot hurriedly knelt and said, “Master, my master is a human. It’s just that the Black King cultivated human form and often came to the temple to discuss scriptures with my master. He taught my master some techniques for nourishing the spirit and controlling qi, hence their friendship.” The Monkey King said, “These monks don’t seem very demonic. They all have round heads, broad shoulders, and walk with their feet flat on the ground. They are only fatter and bigger than I am. But they are not demons. Look, the note mentions ‘serving bear and rhinoceros,’ this creature must be a black bear who has become a spirit.”

The Tripitaka said, “I’ve heard it said that bears and gorillas are similar creatures, both animals. How could he become a spirit?”

The Monkey King laughed, “The Monkey King is also an animal, and I’ve become the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. What’s the difference? Most things in the world, those with nine orifices, can all cultivate to become immortals.”

That’s what the sisters claimed; of course, Elizabeth Prokofievna had seen and understood everything long ago, and her heart had “ached” for a long time, but—for how long, exactly?—now the thought of the prince suddenly seemed very disagreeable to her, precisely because it confused her. After lunch, he left the beach, returned to the hotel, and had himself taken up to his room. He lingered there for a while in front of the mirror, studying his gray hair, his tired, yet sharp face. At that moment, he thought of his fame and of how many people on the streets recognized him and looked at him with reverence, for the sake of his sure, graceful word – he called to mind all the outward successes of his talent that came to mind and even thought of his ennoblement. He then went down to the dining room for lunch and ate at his little table. As he took the elevator after finishing his meal, young people, also coming from breakfast, crowded into the small cabin after him, and Tadzio entered as well. He stood very close to Aschenbach, for the first time so near that Aschenbach could perceive him not in a pictorial distance, but exactly, with the details of his humanity, and recognized him. Someone addressed the boy, and while he answered with an indescribably sweet smile, he stepped out again, on the first floor, backward, with downcast eyes. Beauty makes one bashful, thought Aschenbach, and pondered deeply why. However, he had noticed that Tadzio's teeth were not quite pleasant: somewhat pointed and pale, lacking the gloss of health and with a peculiar brittle transparency, as sometimes seen in people with paleness. He is very delicate, he is sickly, thought Aschenbach. He probably won't live long. And he refrained from acknowledging a feeling of satisfaction or calm that accompanied this thought.

Dawn again, bamboo knocking against the waning moon, chickens crowing as morning clouds arise. The monks rose and prepared tea and the early meal. Now, I take this vow: wherever I encounter a temple, I will burn incense; where I meet a Buddha, I will bow; where I find a pagoda, I will sweep it. May the Buddha be merciful, soon revealing his six-foot-tall golden form, bestowing the true scriptures, and leaving them for the Eastern lands."

After making this vow, he returned to the abbot's quarters for breakfast. After the meal, the two disciples tended to their horses and set off on their journey.
